An investigation into the decay rate of $B^0_s$ particles decaying into two kaons is presented, yielding the first measurements of the decay rate and mean lifetime of these particles. Additionally, a lifetime ratio with a similar decay channel, $B^0_s \rightarrow K^+K^-$, is determined. These findings are based on 1 inverse picobarns of $p\bar{p}$ collision data collected by the CDF experiment at the Tevatron, and are as follows: for $B^0_s \rightarrow K^+K^-$, a decay rate of $1.448 \pm 0.029 \text{ ps}^{-1}$ and a lifetime ratio with $B^0 \rightarrow K^+K^-$ of $0.460 \pm 0.018$ were obtained. These results demonstrate that the $B^0_s$ decay rate into two kaons is significantly faster than expected, aligning with the predictions of the Standard Model, and provide further insight into the underlying physics of these particles. Furthermore, a new, tighter constraint on the ratio of $B^0_s$ and $B^0$ meson decay rates into two muons has been established, meeting the world's current most stringent benchmark for this quantity. Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. We identified two primary categories: an "Eastward" and a "Westward" component. The characteristics of these components remain nearly constant in spatial patterns and energy spectra. We discovered that the Eastward feature shows a more pronounced presence at higher energies and is orientationally aligned with the Galactic Center, whereas the Westward feature is only visible above a certain detection energy threshold and exhibits an axial orientation. The two features display distinct evolution patterns with the approach of the Sun's perpendicular direction in the sky. We found that the Eastward feature remains steady throughout the year, whereas the West Worth feature's visibility is affected by solar modulation and is more pronounced during certain solar minimum periods. The combination of these features explains nearly 10% of the total anisotropic variation. We found no correlation between the directions of extremely energetic cosmic rays and nearby active galactic nuclei, nor any seasonal variation in energy deposition, leading us to suspect that these features lie outside the Milky Way galaxy and are related to extragalactic sources. Furthermore, we discovered that the orientation of these features does not match the large-scale structure of the universe as seen in optical surveys, suggesting that any underlying large-scale magnetic fields would need to be quite disordered. Building upon these findings, future detectors with enhanced probing capabilities will be able to elucidate the origins of these patterns by detecting a more substantial number of extremely energetic cosmic rays. Scaling up such research will provide a deeper understanding of how extremely energetic cosmic rays interact with the universe en route to Earth. Quantum mechanical systems corresponding to Lie algebras can be reinterpreted through deformation, specifically using noncommutative geometry. This approach replaces fundamental commutation relations with more complex relations derived from the Fock expansion. We demonstrate how deformed quantum mechanical systems can be represented in matrix form, meeting certain closure conditions, and we reestablish previous findings through a more general matrix representation. This generalization also provides closure conditions for specific Lie algebras, including su(2), su(1,2), and so(3). We further show that these conditions can be satisfied with matrix representations involving unitary dual spaces. This satisfaction has significant implications for the uniqueness of these systems' unitary evolution operators. We also discuss the implications of this uniqueness for systems exhibiting spontaneous symmetry breaking. Additionally, we explore how these results can be applied to higher dimensional representations of Lie algebras. We also introduce the concept of "weak commutativity," which provides a more flexible approach to dealing with closed operators in these systems. This new perspective is particularly useful for addressing potential issues with these systems, such as spontaneous symmetry breaking in unitary systems or instability in matrix systems. We apply this concept to a simple system in su(2) where spontaneous symmetry breaking occurs in both the usual and deformed contexts. We examine the differences in outcome when this new concept is used. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings on the study of deformed quantum mechanical systems. We argue that studying these systems can provide valuable insights into both quantum mechanics and Lie algebras. We also suggest that researching these systems can open up new areas of investigation, such as the development of new unitary operators that can be used in both the usual and deformed contexts. We propose that this could involve finding new Casimir operators for these systems, or developing new deformation theories that can be applied to both the usual and deformed contexts. In evaluating the potential of federated learning, we tested its performance in training deep learning models to analyze digitized tissue samples, specifically in classifying tumor cells from whole-slide images. By simulating a FL environment with a large, diverse dataset of publicly available images, we compared the results of training models using both a federated approach and a centralized approach. Our findings indicate that federated learning can produce models with similar accuracy to those trained with centralized data, while avoiding the need to collect extensive training datasets at a single location. This has significant implications for the development of more reliable and accurate image analysis models in histopathology. Furthermore, our study demonstrates the feasibility of applying FL in a scenario that mimics cross-institutional data collaboration, without compromising model performance. Additionally, we explored the effects of varying dataset size and number of participants in the federated learning setting, which provides valuable insights for designing FL studies in this context. These findings are particularly relevant to the cancer research community, which heavily relies on accurate tumor cell detection and classification. Moreover, our study highlights the success of applying federated learning to a critical biomedical analysis task, while also highlighting potential issues with scaling FL in such scenarios that arise from the need for extensive fine-tuning before achieving optimal results. Additionally, we investigated the role of data quality and quantity within each participating institution, which holds significant value for data-rich fields like biomedical research. Overall, our research offers a clear demonstration of the potential of federated learning to address the data challenges facing biomedical researchers, while also providing a framework for evaluating the effects of dataset size and number of participants in FL settings. This has broad implications for any field that relies heavily on image analysis using deep learning models. In terms of future work, we explored potential avenues for further research that could yield even greater advances in the application of federated learning to biomedical research. These potential advancements could provide a new pathway for smooth adoption of cutting-edge deep learning models across the biomedical sector, while addressing the critical issue of ensuring reliable and accurate analysis of biomedical data across multiple institutions. In this study, a high-speed optical transmission system is demonstrated, achieving a data rate of 72Gbit/s using the on-off keying technique, over a distance of 18.8km in a South China Sea submarine cable that lacks dispersion compensation.  Chromatic dispersion in this underwater cable causes four signal nulls in a 36GHz bandwidth, severely hindering BER performance. To address this issue, a decision feedback equalizer was developed and successfully reduced BER below the forward error correction threshold, enabling error-free data transmission without FEC.  However, this approach was limited by the occurrence of burst errors resulting from ocean fiber nonlinear effects, which restricted the achievable data rate.  To tackle this issue, a new BERM-DFFC scheme was proposed and field-tested over the 18.8km South China Sea cable, achieving a maximum data rate of 72Gbit/s with a 7% increase over the previous best result.  This strategy was effective in controlling the growth of BER due to burst errors, outperforming the conventional DFFC method by a 5dB margin, which is expected to further enhance the capacity of this submarine cable.  This work offers a technical solution to mitigate the effects of burst errors in ocean fiber-optic communications and provides valuable insights to enhance the performance of submarine cable communications. Deep Learning models like Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) hold great promise for handling time-series data. TCNs leverage a technique called time-dilated convolution that poses an optimization challenge which typically demands significant experimentation. We've developed a technique to automate the dilation optimization process by casting it as a weight-pruning operation along the time axis. Our method learns dilation factors concurrently with weights during training and achieves notable gains in model compactness and inference efficiency without compromising accuracy. It produces a range of highly optimal TCN variants from a single starting model, surpassing the performance of custom-designed networks in both efficiency and accuracy. Our code is open-sourced under the Pit framework, another simple yet effective optimization technique that can be combined with popular pruning methods to produce state-of-the-art results in both classification and regression tasks. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by obtaining 4.3% top-1 accuracy on the Kinetics-400 human action recognition dataset, a 0.6% improvement over the current leader, and a 1.5% gain on the ActivityNet-1.2 benchmark. Notably, our method produces a TCN that, while being 7 times less parameter-intensive than the original Inception score-based model, still outperforms it in accuracy (34.8% vs 33.5%). This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional relationships. Unlike conventional approaches that require all data values, our method allows for incomplete data sets and incorporates functional dependencies to restrict possible value combinations. We develop techniques for handling inconsistencies by relaxing certain data relationships or filling in missing values, leveraging a score-based framework that considers the trustworthiness of source tables and the strength of functional dependencies. Our approach is designed to minimize value modifications, leveraging techniques like K-nearest Neighbors and Matrix Factorization for missing value estimation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through a case study involving incomplete data from real-world tables and examine its performance using a large public dataset, showing significant improvements over alternative approaches. We also investigate how the level of data incompleteness and functional constraint strength impact our strategy's efficiency and outcome. Additionally, we explore potential improvements, such as integrating additional data sources and utilizing additional algorithms for value estimation. We anticipate our work to be of interest to research on inconsistent data management, value estimation, and query answering techniques. Furthermore, our study may be useful for handling data quality issues common in big data sets that comprise real-world web tables. These sets often entail significant amounts of missing data resulting from incomplete forms, automated data extraction, or legacy database migration. Our approach can as well be applicable to domains outside of web data integration, such as medical diagnosis based on gene function predictions and protein interactions. We have already observed this in our case studies involving real-world web data tables. However, due to the inherent complexity of such datasets, our approach may not entirely eliminate inconsistencies but can still significantly reduce the number of inconsistencies by at least an order of magnitude. This in turn can be further addressed by more refined algorithms for filling in missing data and handling functional constraints. We have already identified potential techniques such as Labeled Multi-dimensional Scaling for filling in missing data based on trustworthiness scores of source tables. We have also identified other algorithms such as Semi-Supervised Non-negative Matrix Factorization that can integrate additional data sources that may contain more precise data relating to certain table entries. We intend to integrate these techniques in our approach as our current evaluation metrics focus on consistency rather than data quality. We anticipate that our approach combined with such techniques will be able to handle a wide range of data completeness levels. The SiD's robust silicon vertex and tracking system, complemented by its high central magnetic field, ensures precise momentum measurement. The detector's finely granulated calorimeter system, designed for particle flow analysis, delivers accurate energy resolution across a wide energy range. Given the SiD's sophisticated design, it's essential to assess the optimal segmentation for the calorimeter and the potential benefits of enhanced vertex and tracking capabilities. By re-examining these components, there's an opportunity to further improve the detector's performance, as presented in this report. Here, we review current design choices and discuss options for detector R\&D, focusing on the calorimeter's grid size and the forward pixel layer's extension. While the original SiD design is effective, there are definite gains to be made, amounting to around 2-3% in total, which could be achieved through further development and optimization. Nonetheless, the underlying design principles of the SiD remain sound, as demonstrated during the 2019 ILC Detector Workshop. Delegates there agreed that the original design, or variations like the one presented here, would remain the basis for the detector design moving forward. This report provides an update to the SiD's design, as previously outlined at the 2015 ILC Detector Workshop, and details the detector's performance with a calorimeter grid size half that originally proposed. Consequently, the SiD's energy resolution now matches the detector design benchmark, set by the ILC Detector Concept Document. Moreover, this refined design also yields an enhanced vertex mass resolution for the Higgs boson, or improved sensitivity to certain research areas. Here, we also discuss the SiD's potential for particle flow analysis, or other advanced processing methods, and conclude that such techniques are equally effective with the upgraded design. As such, this report serves as a solid basis for the SiD's future development. We performed the first in-depth analysis of seven red giant members in the globular cluster Tononzintla 2. We used the APOGEE-2 near-infrared spectra to determine the cluster's radial action angle, which shows a distinct shape, supporting earlier findings from the APOGEE-2 survey. The outer ends of the beams are fixed in place, while the inner structure can be manipulated. Specifically, we investigate how changes in a parameter $\epsilon$ affect the linearized stability of the equilibrium solution. This computation confirms a previous conjecture by Iguchi, relating the number of real components of the variety to an alternating sum of counts for points in the integer lattice. As a result, we derive a congruence relating the number of real components to mod 2 counts of points, thereby extending a previous observation by Terasaki to a more general case. Finally, we show that the number of real components is odd for a positive proportion of plane quartics obtained through a specific construction method. A specific class of conformal field theories in two dimensions is defined by equations that have been broadly applied, yet surprisingly, many details remain unclear. This uncertainty is where the Euler-Arnold equations come in - a diverse range of second-order partial differential equations that describe the motion of rigid bodies in various environments. These equations can be seen as a combination of the Hall-Anomaly equation, the Benney-Hassanov equation, and the Landau-Lifshitz equation, among others, and their relationship to conformal field theories is revealed through a formal identity that is derived here. This identity demonstrates that many properties of these Euler-Arnold equations can be transferred to the corresponding conformal field theories. The existence of a large planet still undetected in our solar system has long been theorized and recent observations suggest it may be on an extremely distant, highly elliptical orbit. This paper examines the gravitational impact of such a planet on the orbits of the known solar system bodies, particularly focusing on the potential for detection through slight deviations in planetary orbits caused by the planet's influence. It is shown that a detectable effect on planetary orbits may be within reach if the unknown planet's orbit is relatively close to a highly eccentric circle. However, if the planet's orbit is more complex or much more distant, its gravitational impact on the known planets will likely be too minute to be discernible with current technology. The model developed here also predicts that the greatest variations in planetary orbits will occur during their closest approach to the unknown planet. It is also demonstrated that using existing data for the most slowly moving planets (Ceres and Neptune) can provide constraints on the unknown planet's orbit, while the fastest moving planets (Mercury and Venus) are not useful for this purpose due to their shorter orbital periods. It is estimated that if the unknown planet is over 200 astronomical units from the Sun, its gravitational impact on the most rapidly moving planets will always be too minute to be detected. It is also shown that if the unknown planet has a significant orbital period (over 175 years), its gravitational effect on the most rapidly moving planets will also be too minute to be detected. It is concluded that while it may be challenging to discover the unknown planet through its gravitational impact on the orbits of the other planets before its existence is confirmed through direct observation, it is definitely detectable with current technology if the planet has an orbital period of less than 175 years and is on an orbit that is relatively close to a highly eccentric circle. It is also suggested that if the unknown planet has a significant orbital period, its existence can still be confirmed first and its gravitational impact on the orbits of the other planets then detected through retro-analysis of the data. It is also concluded that if the unknown planet is over 200 astronomical units from the Sun or has an orbital period of less than 175 years but is on an orbit that is not relatively close to a highly eccentric circle, its existence can also be confirmed first and its gravitational impact on the orbits of the other planets then detected through retro-analysis of the data. Recent advances in neural machine translation are largely attributed to large parallel corpora. However, such datasets are scarce for many language pairs. This paper introduces a novel approach that leverages a monolingual lexicon in the target language to improve NMT systems. This proposed system, NMT-LM, significantly outperforms baseline models on low-resource language pairs, achieving a significant 1.6 BLEU score improvement on the OPUS dataset. To mitigate the risk of target sentence generation, NMT-LM is designed with a target sentence reordering module that ensures the generated sentence adheres to the original order. Our findings indicate that using a monolingual lexicon with order information yields a 5% higher reordering accuracy than using an unordered lexicon. Moreover, our proposed system can efficiently handle vast target language lexicons, demonstrating its practical applicability. To facilitate further research, we introduce the Monolingual Augmented Parallel Corpus Dataset selection task at IWSLT 2023. Our approach serves as a pioneering effort to augment parallel corpora using target language lexicons and paves the way for increased research in this area. Unfortunately, due to time constraints and significant technical difficulties with our proposed multi-task training setup, our paper could not be fully implemented or experimentally verified at the time of submission. Consequently, we can only provide preliminary results. In contrast to standard NMT systems, our proposed system has shown promising results of 21.95 BLEU scores on WMT-EN-DE test sets and 23.65 on WMT-EN-FR test sets. To facilitate further research in this area, we plan to make our code publicly available shortly. In addition to achieving higher BLEU scores, our proposed system has also been compared to state-of-the-art low-resource NMT systems, including GUIDED and highly competitive UNsupervised NMT systems. Notably, our proposed system has outperformed GUIDED by a substantial 1.07 BLEU scores on the OPUS dataset and 0.5 BLEU scores on WMT-EN-FR test sets. In terms of corpus-level work, our proposed system has been compared to state-of-the-art parallel corpus construction methods, including the guided generation of UNsupervised NMT systems. In this context, our proposed system has generated a much larger augmented parallel corpus of 1.25 million sentences than UNsupervised NMT systems and has achieved a higher BLEU score of 22.11 than the UNsupervised NMT system on WMT-EN

Convex optimization has long been the standard for modeling and solving complex systems in fields like control, signal processing, and machine learning. Its most effective solvers are designed to handle a specific format of convex functions defined by conic representations. Consequently, researchers and practitioners often spend significant time reformulating their non-standard problems into a suitable form for these solvers. To streamline this process, we present Hypatia, an open-source Julia package dedicated to converting general convex problems into their equivalent conic formulations automatically. Built on top of JuMP's modeling API and interfacing with Mosek, we demonstrate Hypatia's capability to tackle a wide range of problem types, from basic forms like self-dual matrix inequalities to more complex scenarios involving absolute value and fuzzy operations. Furthermore, we explore ways to tailor Hypatia's formulations for specific solvers and show its performance on various problem types using Mosek. With its efficient and transparent code, Hypatia aims to provide an accessible bridge between practical problems and the powerful solvers available today. To get started with Hypatia, we also include a suite of example problems that can be solved using its built-in functions and a recipe for customizing its formulations. As a Julia package, Hypatia is highly customizable and extensible, allowing users to craft their own formulations using a set of predefined transformation rules. We believe Hypatia will be a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners working with convex optimization and control, and we look forward to your contributions and feedback. The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality assessment to ensure reliability and accuracy in subsequent analytical phases. Establishing a comprehensive understanding of MRI quality that is not dependent on specific acquisition protocols is crucial for effective generalization. This study seeks to generalize MRI quality assessment beyond the specific protocol used in training data via a protocol-agnostic approach. We introduce the Multi-Protocol Quality Assessment Network (Multi-QAN), a novel framework that generalizes MRI quality assessment by integrating multiple unrelated protocols through a second-level discriminative module. Our experiments demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, achieving notable improvements in performance on unseen protocols and a reasonable balance of performance across training and testing protocols. Multi-QAN represents a significant step towards developing a comprehensive understanding of MRI quality that is independent of specific protocols. The study also highlights the necessity of creating a diverse set of large-scale training datasets that include diverse protocols to further enhance MRI quality assessment performance. This paper provides an in-depth analysis of the Optane DC PMM's performance, considering various configuration and workload scenarios. Millar. Additionally, this research establishes that the foundation theorem is applicable to the extended affine Weyy group and roots system associated with a Lie semi-group. A key aspect of this proof involves demonstrating an order-preserving correspondence between the roots of both groups. A more general concept, referred to as the 'weak foundation theorem', is also proven for all Coxeter groups, stating that the length of a product of generators is equal to the maximum length of a subset of those generators. This research further generalizes the foundation theorem to a broader class of groups known as the mixed Coxeter groups and roots systems. A new technique, involving an order-preserving correspondence between the roots of two groups, is a key contribution of this study and leads to the proof of a generalized version of the foundation theorem for all finite and semi-infinite Coxeter groups. A new conjecture, related to the length of a product of generators, is proposed for the extended affine Weyy group and roots system associated with a Lie semi-group. This study provides a comprehensive exploration of the foundation theorem and its generalizations, which are of interest in the field of combinatorial geometry. Our primary cosmological probe is the Type Ia Supernovae (SNe Ia), whose distance determining power is somewhat diminished due to uncertainties in their intrinsic characteristics and how they interact with the mass of the controlling white dwarf in binary systems, influencing their luminosity. To break this degeneracy, we investigate the relationship between SNe Ia and weak lensing (WL) by analyzing the Pantheon sample of high-redshift SNe Ia and the DESv4-based convergence power spectrum. Our primary interest is in the slope of this relationship, β, which represents the change in the observed flux of SNe Ia due to weak lensing. To estimate β, we employed two distinct methods: a linear model and a Gaussian Process model, both of which yielded similar results, with an average value of β = 0.72 ± 0.20, consistent with the theoretical value of 0.75 ± 0.11 predicted to hold at high redshifts. This measurement's precision can be improved through larger datasets of SNe Ia and WL maps. Given the Pantheon sample and DESv4 data, β's uncertainty is dominated by the SNe Ia component. To achieve the same level of precision with the current analysis, a 2.5 times larger sample of SNe Ia is needed. Ultimately, this analysis paves the way for using the relationship between SNe Ia and WL to constrain the mass step in SNe Ia light-curve observations, which could potentially match the current constraints imposed by WL alone. Given future large datasets of SNe Ia and WL, β can be precisely constrained before any assumptions are made regarding its value, allowing it to serve as a complementary probe of the mass step parameter. This, in turn, may provide a powerful approach for independently verifying the existence of the mass step and exploring its implications in SNe Ia statistics at higher redshifts. Additionally, this analysis highlights the value of conducting this investigation early on, as it enables the examination of how future large datasets of SNe Ia and WL can be used to constrain the mass step in SNe Ia light-curve observations. These are lecture notes for a one-week workshop on stochastic partial differential equations (SPDEs) tailored for graduate students in analysis. We begin by introducing the fundamental concepts of stochastic integration, both in its traditional form based on cylinder measures and via the Skorohod integral. We then explore various types of SPDEs, including those with dissipative forces leading to existence and uniqueness of solutions, as well as the approach of semigroup methods. We also touch on the stochastic wave equation and its applications in mechanics. Finally, we examine the SPDEs with non-compactness conditions and various techniques for establishing compactness, ultimately applying these concepts to the stochastic Navier-Stokes equations. All entries assume only a basic understanding of probability and PDE. Each section can be seen as an independent module. Original references are provided at the end. We intend for these lecture notes to serve as an introductory course on SPDEs. We hope they become a useful resource for participants. We appreciate the feedback provided by A. Mirra. Research on quantum phenomena in photonic silicon-on-insulator systems has seen significant expansion in recent years. A specific point defect structure consisting of a triangular arrangement of three coupled nanodots has contributed substantially to this growth. This study delves into the quantum properties of this arrangement by investigating the spatial separation of states and unique rotational symmetry. It also examines the rotational symmetry's influence on a particular two-body interaction and showcases its potential to create highly entangled states through laser perturbation. A theoretical model focusing on this system has been developed and can be applied to other similar point defect structures. Numerical simulations utilizing this model predict the occurrence of non-Abelian charges and topological phase transitions in such systems. A SOI system with three coupled dots lacks the chiral symmetry typical of other 2D systems, allowing for exact integration of any discrete symmetry. This study demonstrates that discrete symmetry can be utilized to create non-Abelian charges in a single photonic cavity. A system of two interacting particles exhibits a discrete symmetry-protected phase transition from a trivial to a non-Abelian phase. A combination of laser perturbations and a magnetic field can be employed to detect the non-Abelian phase and a qubit embedded within the SOI system. A further advancement in this research involves using a triangular arrangement of four coupled dots, where a critical point exists to switch between two non-Abelian phases. This phase transition can be controlled with a laser and a magnetic field, allowing for the creation of any discrete symmetry-protected phase, including a $\pi$-phase shift in an interferometry experiment. A system of three interacting particles demonstrates a more intricate phase structure, including an non-Abelian Haldane-Shastry model and it can be realized in the SOI system with a great deal of experimental control. A system of four interacting particles opens up the possibility to create any law of statistics in a system of this nature. A further exploration of these findings could provide a path to overcome the inherent limitations of real-world implementations of quantum phenomena and may offer a means to control and observe non-Abelian anyons in a robust and efficient manner, a crucial step for the development of fault-tolerant quantum computing. A system of interacting particles in a point defect structure based on silicon-on-insulator material has the potential to serve as a universal platform for the study of anyonic physics and quantum simulation. MRI (Magnetic Resonance Imaging) is a diagnostic medical imaging with high sensitivity, often employed to detect a variety of diseases, including cancer. Advanced imaging modalities, such as MRI, use sophisticated image processing methods to accurately identify and classify tumors. Regional growth characteristics can be extracted from MRI images through segmentation, a process that leverages computational methods to define and distinguish normal tissue regions from abnormal tissue, such as tumors. Machine learning algorithms play a key role in tumor detection and classification by detecting subtle changes between normal and abnormal tissue regions. Despite the complexity of cancer development, researchers have made significant progress in recent years, including studies on breast, prostate, and liver cancer, with contributions in the fields of computer science, biology, and biomedical engineering. This paper provides an overview of cancer development, the MRI imaging technique, and offers a selection of image processing methods for extracting regional growth characteristics from MRI images. It also includes examples of MRI-based tumor classification using machine learning. Finally, the paper offers some guidance on further research in this field. It highlights the importance of radiologists in the classification of normal and abnormal tissue regions, as well as the need for more comprehensive datasets. It also identifies opportunities for improving cancer treatment through MRI-based classification, particularly in cases where a biopsy is impossible. It concludes by emphasizing the importance of ongoing collaboration between computer science, biology, and biomedical engineering disciplines. It notes the need for further research into multi-feature fusion methods, as well as the potential for machine learning to predict cancer recurrence and treatment outcomes. It also highlights the value of open-source software, such as Python, for promoting transparency and reproducibility in MRI-based cancer research. It includes a comprehensive bibliography of recent advances in MRI-based cancer imaging, covering studies on breast, prostate, and liver cancer. It provides a detailed description of machine learning algorithms, including decision trees, random forests, support vector machines, and convolutional neural networks. It offers a thorough explanation of MRI technology, including magnetic resonance relaxation phenomena, spatial resolution, and slice selection. It provides a comprehensive overview of cancer biology, covering regional growth characteristics, cancer development, and the MRI-based imaging of tumors. It includes a comprehensive description of available MRI datasets, along with instructions on data preparation and preprocessing. It offers a thorough explanation of commonly used MRI processing methods, including noise reduction, deblurring, and super-resolution. It includes a comprehensive description of machine learning applications in MRI-based cancer imaging, covering classification, segmentation, and registration. To counter this, researchers use techniques like line profile variability removal and least-squares deconvolution (LSD). By limiting the line sample to specific parameters, this study investigates whether selecting lines through a randomised process can equivelently reduce noise, also examining if this method is feasible with a smaller line set. Using public CHAOS-4.5 spectra and the MUNIPOP synthesis code, the study discovered that a randomly selected line set with 5000 lines can effectively minimise noise in a manner comparable to a parametric approach, using lines with a specific line depth range. Notably, the study found that using a random line set of 5000 lines is comparable to using a parametric approach with lines that have a line depth between 0.1 and 9.9, representing the 90th percentile of the line population. This discovery provides a randomized line selection strategy that can be used for least-squares deconvolution, reducing the computational time while resulting in a similar spectral resolution. The study suggests that this random line selection approach can be a more efficient way to reduce noise in spectroscopic data. This research paper proposes a new method to efficiently gather data in a wireless sensor network by creating a hierarchical structure. We introduce the concept of a HOPP, a sub-collection within a larger collection, to speed up data collection by estimating link quality in both directions. This approach enables faster, bidirectional estimation of transmission probabilities between nodes. A key innovation is the use of a quantitative measure to evaluate the suitability of a path for both forward and reverse data transmission. Once the best path is identified, the estimated transmission probabilities are used to calculate the optimal activation time for each node in the HOPP. This optimized approach is compared to two other methods, demonstrating improved energy efficiency and speed. Simulations are conducted to validate the effectiveness of the proposed method, and the role of estimation errors on performance is also examined. The results show that our approach outperforms other methods in terms of energy savings, and provide insights for the design of wireless sensor networks. The proposed method is suitable for applications that require real-time data collection. We propose a context assessment method that breaks down object detection into two components: using bounding boxes to identify context and using context to refine predictions. This method enables direct comparison of models that do or do not utilize context and and incorporates diverse context types which can be easily extended to other forms. Our results demonstrate that our method accurately differentiates deep models' performance based on their ability to utilize context. Furthermore, it highlights the impact of context in challenging scenarios such as scene parsing and image classification. To facilitate further research, we introduce Context-Aware Detection, a task that considers context which is currently being overseen by nearly all top-performing models in the MS COCO benchmark. This task is primarily suitable for deep object detectors and our proposed evaluation framework. We anticipate it will fuel research on context in object detection.

We generate a general framework for deriving concentration inequalities applicable to the sum of multiple binary random variables whose interactions are governed by a nonpositive correlation matrix. This framework effectively addresses specific scenarios such as concentration inequalities for matrices with overlapping rows, orthogonal signals in multiple access channels, and the negative binomial distribution with varying means. Furthermore, we establish a generalization of our approach for deriving tail inequalities and apply this to obtain sharper bounds for the negative binomial distribution. Our general framework is an extension of the techniques from matrix concentration inequalities and yields new concentration inequalities which are of independent interest. Additionally, our results are illustrated through numerical examples and a simulation. Our framework is a combination of classical tools such as the Hoeffding-Azuma inequality and recent advances in matrix concentration inequalities, and is an attempt to fill a gap in the study of negatively correlated random variables by providing a unified approach to deriving concentration inequalities in this domain.

Specifically, we investigate the cause of the cosine azimuthal asymmetry in hadron production, accounting for the connection between the helicity distribution $g_1$ and the twist-3 dihadron fragmentation function. Using a spectator model, we calculate the interference term between $s$-wave and $p$-wave and estimate this asymmetry at various experiments, including COMPASS, JLab 12 GeV, and the future EIC. Our analysis suggests that the cosine azimuthal asymmetry in SIDIS can serve as a key test for the dihadron fragmentation function. If measured, this value can provide insight into the behavior of this function when the two particles' momenta are aligned with the scattered electron's momentum. If found to be significant, this outcome would imply that the two-particle correlations in hadron production are not solely explained by the helicity distribution. Consequently, this would offer a new perspective on quark spin alignment. This brief research note addresses a recent mystery uncovered by Gaddis and Hennig, who discovered specific symplectic extensions of flat group manifolds exhibiting non-trivial first de Rham cohomology. Our findings reveal that these underlying manifolds can be expressed as a product of flat group manifolds and a symplectic plane, providing a geometric interpretation for their symplectic structure. Additionally, we establish that their geodesic equations can be separated into two distinct components: one analytic and the other semi-linear. This distinction enables us to identify both the existence and uniqueness of geodesic trajectories. Furthermore, we develop a method for determining the volume of these manifolds through a simple computation. As a side discovery, we observe that these manifolds are conformally flat. Lastly, we discuss how our findings relate to Hennig's earlier work on hyperbolizable manifolds. This research was presented in a lecture at the 2019 Symposium on Geometric Control Theory in Porto. This paper presents a Wikipedia-based entity recommendation framework that utilizes a unique representation method, where entities are represented through multiple graph layers, derived from Wikipedia's interconnected pages. By combining Wikipedia's extensive information networks, a suite of linked databases, and user interaction data, we've developed a tailored approach to suggest entities to users. Our method leverages Wikipedia's diverse layers to effectively capture an entity's characteristics and ranking preferences, allowing for optimized entity ranking according to user preferences. We've tested our proposal on the Yahoo! Knowledge Graph, demonstrating notable performance improvements over baseline methods and a special variant using traditional Wikipedia representations. Notably, our approach achieves top results across multiple evaluation metrics with a significant 18% boost in precision and 25% improvement in MRR. A Closer examination of our findings with a specific entity set (countries) and an additional experiment using a different entity set (celebrities) reaffirm the effectiveness of our entity representation and ranking method. Our work highlights the feasibility of developing an entity recommendation system grounded in Wikipedia and paves the way for further research on Wikipedia-based knowledge graph applications. The implemented system is available online at http://entity.wikipedia.org. Additionally, we've made the source code and data sets openly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/strmlab/wiki-entity-rec. With the current surge in open-source knowledge graphs and Wikipedia's enduring influence, our work contributes meaningfully to the field and is an interesting example of a Wikipedia-centered knowledge graph application. The accompanying demonstration video is available at https://youtu.be/6g4bY4gEe9Q. We've also presented the paper at the 12th International iConference 2018 in Auckland, New Zealand. Recently, an expanded version of this research was published as a book chapter in "Recent Advances in Information Systems" (ISBN: 978-3-030-11285-2). Additionally, our entity recommendation system based on the proposed method has been selected as one of the outstanding projects for the 2019 UIUC Technology Transfer Showcase. This problem can be resolved through an algorithm that leverages integer programming to achieve a maximum number of compatible matches, taking into account waiting times and other organ characteristics. This algorithm forms the basis for an optimal acceptance policy that ensures the highest number of transplants possible. By analyzing real-world data, this algorithm results in the maximum possible number of transplants in practice, and can be implemented in an acceptable time frame for large datasets. This algorithm also provides the basis for an efficient heuristic that can handle even larger datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in a range of scenarios. These counterparts serve as building blocks to facilitate the understanding of wideband waveforming. Previous researchers have utilized modal logic to integrate negation and affordance, but no widely accepted approach exists. To rectify this, we propose a novel application of the Dvorniq's vector model that unifies the unary connectives through controlled de-aggregation and re-aggregation of entity sets, enabling a spin-like semantics that captures their interrelations. This approach is versatile, as the characteristics of the vector model allow for the tailored description of connective meanings, thereby providing a foundation for a comprehensive theory of unary connectives that can be explored further. Furthermore, our work paves the way for addressing additional issues in language semantics, such as the nature of entities and the structure of sentences. To demonstrate the capabilities of our approach, we developed a dedicated system for reasoning about categorical statements, which showcases its practical utility. Ultimately, our proposal marks a significant step in applying quantum concepts to the study of language. While it is not an expression of quantum mereology, it represents a unique integration of philosophical ideas concerning universals, as they find application in the framework of vector models. This work also illustrates the potential for collaborating researchers from both the philosophy and computer science fields. One such potential area of collaboration is the project known as Quantum Natural Language Inference (Q-NLI), which we discuss in the concluding section. This paper is an extended version of our previously presented paper at the 35th Annual Conference of the Cognitive Science Society. Some of the subsequent research mentioned in the final section has already been published in a separate paper at the 36th Annual Conference of the same society. It is also worth noting that the subsequent conference paper led to an invitation for us to give a keynote speech at the 2022 International Conference on Quantum Logic, an event held in Guangzhou, China. It is demonstrated that this model produces a transition from localized outbreaks to widespread epidemics as the degree increases above a critical point, and that the critical point can be influenced by the rate of recovery. Additionally, it is shown that at low infection rates, the model exhibits a fundamental difference from traditional SIR models in which the degree does not change, and that this difference can be seen in the exponential increase of the number infected in the latter scenario. The proposed model provides a more balanced representation of disease spread that counterintuitively leads to a critical point for epidemic onset even when infection rates exceed recovery rates. It is further demonstrated that at high infection rates, the model is similar to the SIR model in which the degree does not change, and that both models exhibit an exponential increase of the number infected in this regime. To accelerate policy optimization in complex, dynamic systems via reinforcement learning, experience replay is often utilized with policy gradient methods. However, the original formulation of replay encounters a problem: when the target and learning environments diverge, as typically happens when the policy evolves, the variance of the sampled rewards increases, hindering optimization. To address this, we introduce a variance-reducing method using the Mahalanobis distance, which adapts the replayed data to the current policy's expectations. We also propose an efficient computational framework for this method and evaluate its benefits on multiple simulation studies and a real-world experiment. Results show that our approach outperforms the standard replay method and yields comparable performance to an episodic method, while significantly reducing computational overhead. We make our code publicly available to facilitate further research. Establishing a correlation between electronic structure and superconducting properties is a primary goal in condensed matter research. Iron-based superconductors have been found with varied superconducting thresholds and gap structures, presenting an exciting opportunity to explore this relationship. Employing a robust all-around technique, our study combines photoemission and absorption spectra to accurately describe the electronic and atomic structure of (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_{2}$As$_{2}$. These findings facilitate a clear understanding of how electron distribution influences the material's magnetic and superconducting behaviors. Notably, our study reveals that in this specific compound, the superconducting gap structure is an odd parity with direct and indirect components, in line with theoretical predictions involving orbital-selective Mott transition. This knowledge provides a foundation for exploring superconductivity in other iron-based materials. Moreover, it demonstrates that (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_{2}$As$_{2}$ can be an ideal model system for investigating how electron distribution affects magnetic and superconducting properties, potentially also Transient Superconductivity observed in the related (Ba$_{0.8}$K$_{0.2}$)Fe$_{2}$As$_{2}$. Additionally, this study highlights that in this family of materials, Absorption Spectroscopy can be an analytical tool to recover the missing information from ARPES data, in particular when the electronic structure is critically fine-tuned near orbital-selective Mott transition. This knowledge may also be useful for identifying Transient Superconductivity in other materials.

Conversely, it correctly classifies (Ba$_{0.8}$K$_{0.2}$)Fe$_{2}$As$_{2}$ as only near Superconductor's transition state. While the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation is relatively straightforward, the superbosonization equation can be employed to obtain a more intricate decomposition of interacting superfield into a sum of simpler interactions. Initial findings from a measurement of the top quark's polarization, achieved via the decay of top quarks to boson pairs ($t\rightarrow Wb$), are presented, using data from proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV. The data were collected by the CMS experiment and consist of 35.9 inverse femtobarns of luminosity. The top quark's polarization was gauged by analyzing the angular distribution of the boson's trajectory, and a fit to the data revealed a polarization value of -0.005, which is within the predicted range generated by theoretical models of the Standard Model. The results were also used to derive limits on the magnitude of the $ct$ parameter and a phase angle $\alpha_s$, with the outcome being $|c+is|\leq 0.0089$ for all possible values of $\alpha_s$. Additionally, sensitivity to the $gt$ vertex was examined and the results were $|g'| \leq 0.031, \forall \alpha_s$, and $|g'| \leq 0.030, \alpha_s = \pi/2$. These values represent the first statistical estimates of the top quark's polarization and its spin properties. Moreover, a comparison of the measured outcomes with the Standard Model's predictions showed consistency. The analysis's sensitivity to the top quark's polarization also enabled studies of the $t$ channel single top quark process, yielding a cross-section measurement of $13.2 \pm 0.6$ pb, and an analysis of the top quark's decay to the lightest neutral lepton, the results of which were in line with the Standard Model's predictions. Our spin-lattice relaxation studies in a 6.55 T magnetic field yielded distinct components, characterized by different temperature dependences in their recovery times, with one being temperature-linear and the other exhibiting more intricate temperature variation. These results demonstrate that the slow-recovering component is resistant to changes in LaNiO$_3$ layer thickness, while the fast-recovering component is significantly affected, displaying an opposing temperature dependence in thinner samples. This complex phenomenon is explored to identify its underlying cause. We propose that the slow-recovering component originates from a spin-dynamical process shared by all LaNiO$_3$ systems and that the fast-recovering component is a result of a competing magnetic process that is influenced by the interface coupling in LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices. Effective conversational agents are expected to manage complex conversations efficiently, navigating numerous possible responses despite often being confined to a limited knowledge base. We introduce MG-GLAM, a computational tool developed to rapidly create complete N-body simulations for various cosmological theories, specifically modified gravity models. This program builds upon the existing GLAM code and incorporates an advanced multigrid method to solve the non-linear equations characteristic of $f(R)$ models, resulting in highly efficient performances. For $f(R)$ models with a simple form, MG-GLAM can generate full N-body simulations up to $10^{9}$ particles in approximately one day on a single computer. To facilitate code validation, we've developed a set of analytical initial conditions that can be used with both standard and modified gravity simulations. MG-GLAM is an open-source code available for download at http://www.mgglam.org. We also outline plans to expand the code's capabilities to handle other modified gravity models in the future. Leveraging MG-GLAM, we'll explore how galaxy clusters are affected by $f(R)$ gravity across different mass scales and cosmological settings. Our research reveals that quasichronological $f(R)$ models generally predict cluster densities in alignment with observations, whereas de Sitter-like models are typically too dense. Additionally, we find that in quasichronological models, the transition from standard gravity dominance to modified gravity dominance is independent of mass, occurring at approximately $10^{13}$ Solar masses; in contrast, in de Sitter-like models, this transition occurs at a mass-dependent threshold. Moreover, we observe that gravitational slip becomes significant at roughly $10^{14}$ Solar masses and increases with higher mass scales. This research is an initial foray into utilizing MG-GLAM to investigate galaxy cluster properties within the context of modified gravity models. As such, we expect future extensions of this code to be highly relevant for ongoing and upcoming galaxy cluster-focused cosmological experiments. Ultimately, MG-GLAM is an invaluable resource for quickly assessing a modified gravity model's predictions through comprehensive N-body simulations, thus providing valuable insight for data analysis of current and forthcoming cosmological experiments. This research is an initial outcome of the "Workshop on Modified Gravity: Numerical Relatable Effects" held at the University of Oxford in 2019. We wish to see this code employed as a tool to explore whether future observations of galaxy clusters will be able to distinguish between different modified gravity models. Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, for a given domain $D$, they considered the relationship between Gaussian free fields defined on $D$ and $D'$, where $D'$ is obtained through conformal repletion. Miller and Sheffield demonstrated that this correspondence extends beyond conformal equivalence alone. Building upon previous work by Miller, Sheffield, and the second author, we establish that when $D'$ is derived from $D$ via conformal repletion, the associated Gaussian free fields share the same statistics, thereby extending this connection to the context of Riemann surfaces. Additionally, we demonstrate that multiple Schramm-Loewner evolution systems can be coupled to a given Gaussian free field on a Riemann surface, and that this relationship preserves the field's statistics. This, in turn, provides a new description of mass transfer in imaginary surfaces. The unidirectional extreme ultraviolet and X-ray solar flares are capable of producing a massive amount of photons with an energy higher than 10 PeV, which have a very low chance of being detected by satellites. By utilizing general kinematics and assuming that the solar flare's particle source is spherical, we developed a mathematical model to calculate the photons' flux as observed from any location. Our model shows that in the direction of the solar flare's axis, the photons' flux remains constant, which is directly proportional to the square of the energy. Conversely, in the perpendicular direction, the photons' flux is proportional to the energy. By integrating the photons' flux in the direction of the solar flare's axis, we derived a mathematical formula that is directly proportional to the energy squared over (2r_s)^2, where r_s is the radius of the solar sphere. Notably, this formula is identical to the derivation by Aharonian and Atoyan, which utilized the method of characteristics. Our model also predicts that in the perpendicular direction, the photons' flux is proportional to the energy divided by (4πr_s)^2. This prediction conveys the extent of energy distribution in the direction of the solar flare's axis in detail. By comparing our model's components with the data provided by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope, we determined the parameter k to be (1.26±0.29)10^44 erg^-1, which describes the photons' flux in the direction of the solar flare's axis in the form of dN/d(2πr_s^2). Additionally, we discovered that the photons' flux in the direction of the solar flare's axis is nearly 300 times greater than in the perpendicular direction at an energy of 10 PeV. Our model's predictions for the photons' flux in both directions provide the basis for further analysis of data in search of isotropic ultra-high energy photons flux in the solar magnetic field. By assuming that the solar flare's particle source is a set of magnetic flux tubes with a length of 10^8 km (one-tenth of the Earth-Sun distance) and a base area of 10^18 cm^2, we determined the required intensity for detection of an isotropic ultra-high energy photons flux of 10^44 erg^-1 by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope at 10 PeV in 10^8 km long magnetic flux tubes,  which is 2.5±0.6)10^44 erg^-1

Nonlocal gravity theory is a gravitational framework where the gravitational acceleration experienced by an object is determined not only by its immediate surroundings but also by its overall environment. As such, it is essential to consider multiple reference frames in this context. We examine how the choice of reference frame affects the nonlocal relation, which connects the gradient of a field's value to the degree of its nonlocality. Given that these relations hold true in any reference frame, they must also conform to specific tensor properties. We derive a general nonlocal equation that incorporates these constraints and is thus compatible with all reference frames. These reference frames are often referred to as "fundamental frames." We then discuss various types of fundamental frames, including inertial, non-inertial frames, and frames associated with gravitational fields. We further explore the possibility of defining constitutive relations for nonlocal gravity in a manner analogous to nonlocal electromagnetism. We demonstrate how to derive these relations in both inertial and non-inertial frames. We also examine the specific case of a static, spherically symmetric gravitational field and show how its behavior can be described using constitutive relations in a fundamental frame associated with an observer in the same gravitational field. We then extend this analysis to a situation where the observer is moving relative to this field, resulting in a non-static, spherically symmetric gravitational field. We conclude that constitutive relations may provide a more straightforward approach to addressing high-frequency gravitational waves and the gravitational field's behavior over long distances. Nonetheless, further research is needed to fully understand and clarify these constitutive relations. We then examine how to derive a linearized version of nonlocal gravity theory and show that it leads to a description of gravitational waves with both longitudinal and transverse components, with the former being a fundamental aspect of nonlocal gravity theory. We discuss the differences in wave propagation speeds between local and nonlocal gravity theories and the resulting consequences for gravitational wave detection. We also discuss potential experiments that could distinguish between local and nonlocal gravity theories. Asynchronous updates inevitably lead to conflict resolution issues with concurrent changes. A specific technique addressing this challenge is the Conflict-free Replicated Data Structure (CRDDS). Despite research advances, the lack of a unified design approach for CRDDS through "remove-win" operations limits their full potential. Our work addresses this gap by presenting a novel design framework that utilizes "remove-win" operations, offering a clear methodology for creating new CRDDS designs. Furthermore, this framework enables error handling by providing for the management of "lose-win" and "win-lose" scenarios. With this framework, we design a new CRDDS for real-time web database access, demonstrating its effectiveness. Our framework consists of four components that jointly provide a "remove-win" operation approach, specifically, (1) phaseless "remove-win" execution, (2) "lose-win" and "win-lose" error handling, (3) "remove-win" ordering, and (4) "remove-win" merging. These theories inevitably involve a non-Abelian gauge sector in the extra dimensions, which, due to compactification, results in a finite number of isolated "branes" where fundamental matter fields reside. Under specific conditions, when the number of spatial dimensions exceeds three, such configurations can avoid the problem of non-perturbative confinement faced in standard QCD. Instead, the scale of convergence can be quite low, potentially within reach of the LHC, given its high energy capabilities and the presence of massive gauge boson interactions. This study explores the fundamental characteristics of these theories, particularly their representation of gauge and matter fields, as well as predicted production channels for dark matter at the LHC. Given the current lack of theoretical guidance on specifics, a general framework is applicable across all Little QCD variants. However, it is essential to note that several variants are expected to yield similar signatures, complicating the identification of these theories through exclusive experimental evidence. Nonetheless, production channels like di-photon and di-bjet are anticipated to serve as prominent signatures in searching for Little QCD at the LHC. Moreover, due to the inherent complexity involving mixed states of hadrons and quark-gluon, as produced by the LHC, a more in-depth understanding is also required, likely needing the use of Monte Carlo event generators with appropriate modifications to accurately model such processes. Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that X-ray binaries with neutron stars exhibit different outburst patterns. This study contradicts that idea by showing that the distribution of time intervals between outbursts for both neutron star and black hole X-ray binaries is remarkably similar, suggesting they share the same underlying processes that govern their behavior. This, along with other findings, suggests that previous estimates of the population of these binary systems are too high and that there may be a larger number of neutron star X-ray binaries among the quiescent sources in the Milky Way's center. This has significant implications for any potential electromagnetic emissions from gravitational waves caused by binary sources in the region. It also means that a significant proportion of these sources are likely to be observable again in the future. This, in turn, may make it more difficult to use the lack of associated gravitational waves with an electromagnetic outburst as evidence for the source being a stellar mass black hole. Instead, such a signature could be from a neutron star binary system and the lack of a GW counterpart might simply be due to the low energy emission of the GW signal or the binary's orientation making it undetectable. This, combined with the fact that there are many more candidates for such systems in the Milky Way's globular clusters that could produce such a signature, means that future GW detectors like the second generation LIGO and the upcoming X-ray telescope X-ray Survey of Galactic Bulges with an all-sky capability will be flooded with potential binary sources and it is crucial that a detection protocol is established that takes into account all possible types of binary systems. We analyze the waves and shocks produced by massive stellar eruptions, specifically type II supernovae and luminous supernovae like SN 2005ip.  Using high-resolution three-dimensional hydrodynamic simulations of these events, we observe the development of high-velocity shocks and density waves as they interact with the star's external layers.  We also see how these shocks and waves are affected by the eruption's energy release and the star's properties.  We examine how these waves and shocks engage with the surrounding envelope, causing it to heat up and potentially triggering shockwaves in the envelope.  We then consider the implications of these wave and shock dynamics for observing these events in the light curves and spectra of the star.  We also look at how these wave and shock dynamics might be used as indicators of the star's mass and the energy released during the eruption.  We apply this analysis to SN 2005ip, using its light curve and spectral characteristics to model its wave and shock dynamics, and from that model, we estimate that it had a high initial mass of about 2.5 to 3.5 solar masses and that its explosion energy was likely very low, possibly even zero.  We found that SN 2005ip's wave and shock dynamics were quite different from those of type II supernovae like SN 1987K and SN 1999el.  SN 1987K's wave and shock dynamics were like those of type II supernovae that experience a significant explosion, while SN 1999el's wave and shock dynamics were like those of a supernova that experiences a partial explosion.  We also found that SN 2005ip's wave and shock dynamics were similar to those of another luminous supernova called SN 2006oz.  We used our models of these wave and shock dynamics to model the light curves and spectra of these supernovae and from that modeling we estimated that SN 2006oz had a high initial mass of about 2.5 solar masses and that its explosion energy was likely very low, possibly even zero.  We found that SN 2006oz's wave and shock dynamics were like those of SN 2005ip, indicating that it also experienced a massive stellar eruption that failed to produce a significant explosion. This brief research extends a discovery made by Diamond--Sasaki, relating 
geometric modularity of non-mathematical weights to algebraic weights and 
rephrases their findings in a more general context. Our restatement broadens 
the original claim to include certain instances of geometric modularity for 
non-mathematical weights that can be linked to algebraic weights. In these 
generalized situations, we demonstrate that the geometric modularity of non- 
mathematical weights results in geometric Dirichlet law, which holds a 
non-trivial implication for certain algebraic weights. In cases where the 
geometric modularity of non-mathematical weights can be related to the 
geometric Dirichlet law, we derive a crucial consequence - the algebraic 
weights must have a specific form. Ultimately, our research establishes a 
direct connection between the geometric Dirichlet law and algebraic weights of 
a certain type, which includes weights that are neither mathematical nor 
non-mathematical. Building on this connection, we arrive at an even more 
general conclusion - the geometric Dirichlet law must hold for all weights 
that can be expressed in a specific form. This conclusion results in a 
significant consequence: for a specific class of weights that are neither 
mathematical nor non-mathematical, we can directly determine whether the 
geometric Dirichlet law holds without first establishing the weights' 
mathematical or non-mathematical nature. In addition to this main result, 
we also derive several other consequences from the geometric Dirichlet law, 
including a link between geometric modularity and the geometric Artin conjecture 
for weights that can be expressed in a specific form. Furthermore, we

Improving neural network-based conversational agents' ability to understand and respond to diverse, realistic dialogue is a challenge. To tackle this issue, this paper introduces two novel evaluation metrics that utilize Natural Language Inference (NLI) to assess the variety of possible responses to a given statement. These metrics, which can be either binary (indicating variety existence) or multi-ary (scoring variety level), help guide the improvement of models in generating diverse responses. Experiments conducted on two datasets show that incorporating variety evaluation joins the ongoing quest to enhance conversational agents' performance. The models' capacity to understand and generate diverse text is also put to the test on the NLI task. The evaluation metrics' effectiveness is further confirmed by a survey involving human participants, who assessed the variety of generated responses and NLI predictions. The introduced methods are available online at https://github.com/ghrua VarietyEval. The paper is published in the Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP) 2021. Key improvements to conversational agents' performance are reported, along with additional findings on the relationship between NLI and variety. The results indicate that models are more skilled at producing diverse answers to factual statements and that there is a variety'sweet spot' – exceeding it may actually make answers less varied. These discoveries are made possible by a unique variety-ratings dataset compiled in collaboration with human participants. It enables models' ability to understand diverse text on the SBT task to be assessed. The introduction of variety-aware training techniques is also described, along with their performance across five different tasks. The occurrence of sustainable hydrogen burning in very low-mass stars might be impacted by rotation due to the addition of centrifugal force and potential break-up caused by rapid spinning. Computer simulations model rotating low-mass stars with the capability for sustained nuclear reactions, considering a range of rotation rates, rather than slow rotation alone. Using these simulations, we determined the boundaries within which stars could maintain nuclear energy through hydrogen burning. These boundaries varied based on angular momentum. However, above a certain threshold (approximately 8.85 x 10^48 erg s) the boundaries broke into two distinct branches, resulting from objects losing mass and experiencing extreme spin. This research was applied to model the development of sub-stellar objects. Two possible scenarios were modeled: one with external forces gradually slowing the star, mainly controlled by spin-down time, and another where the star spins out of control, ultimately shedding mass and shrinking. In the latter case, the boundary of stable hydrogen burning was reached before the star reached breaking point. Also, boundaries of other physical states, such as convective zones and surface temperatures, were analyzed for these objects. Due to the slow change in conditions within these objects, likely found in the universe, we believe our simulations accurately reflect their evolution over time. Furthermore, incorporating these simulations into theoretical models of star formation could provide even greater accuracy. For example, using these simulations, we re-examined the formation of the recently discovered exoplanet K2-261 b, where its host star spun so fast that it was on the edge of breaking apart, and we were able to confirm that this star was going through hydrogen burning sustainably. Additionally, we found that this star had a metal-rich composition, which could have been added to it quickly, possibly as a result of the star shedding its outer layers due to rapid spinning. This in turn could have led to the formation of a large iron-rich core in the star, which in turn could have been involved in generating a magnetic field that affected the star's spin. Using these simulations, we were also able to provide a more detailed analysis of the internal structure of this star and its relationship to its spinning, its energy output, and the formation of its large planet. This research could provide valuable insights into the internal structure and evolution of rotating low-mass stars, and their surrounding environments. It raises important questions about the global magnetic field in these stars, and how it could be generated. Additionally, it highlights the possibility that rapid spinning low-mass stars could contribute to the formation of large iron-rich cores

To address this limitation, we develop a novel algorithm capable of removing all edge crossings by dividing selected nodes into smaller components, without increasing the overall complexity and retaining the original graph's planarity. This new method ensures the updated graph planarity and enables easy visualization of the modified graph. To achieve this, our algorithm explicitly detects the presence of a specific non-planar subgraph, applicable to a particular subset of graphs where our main algorithm delivers a more efficient solution, and a simpler detection approach is also proposed for a more general graph subset. Deep neural network approaches have achieved great success in various AI tasks, particularly in image recognition tasks, yet they often struggle with tasks that involve continuous learning and adapting to new categories and removing outdated ones. The problem of learning from categories that are not encountered for an extended period of time, known as the "cold start" issue, further exacerbates this challenge. Current deep neural network approaches that address this issue often fail to consider the problem's unique characteristics, such as declining memory interference, changing category distributions, and the "cold start" issue. Recently, the paper by Liu et al. introduced a new benchmark and standards for evaluating models that learn from categories that are not encountered for an extended period of time, including the "cold start" issue. This paper builds upon that work by standardizing the evaluation protocol, conducting a comprehensive comparison of state-of-the-art deep neural network approaches that address the issue, and exploring novel techniques for addressing the problem through class-aware training and a data augmentation method known as the "cut mix". The paper discovers that the standard deep neural network approach that addresses this issue often underperforms comparable models that are not subject to the "cold start" issue and that there is a significant gap between the performance of deep neural network approaches that address this issue and that of models that are not subject to the "cold start" issue. The paper further finds that the cut mix method outperforms other deep neural network approaches that address this issue and that there is a need for further research on this problem. The paper's evaluation results and experiments are publicly available on the newly introduced benchmark, providing a foundation for future research on this problem. This problem has widespread implications, given the ever-increasing need to update neural networks in response to changing category distributions and the "cold start" issue in applications that involve continuous learning. This problem is not limited to deep neural networks, as it is also a concern for other machine learning algorithms that rely on data that is not encountered for an extended period of time. This paper's evaluation results and novel techniques for addressing this issue that are presented will be of use to researchers that work on machine learning algorithms in general, providing them with a better understanding of this problem and its solutions. This paper will also provide them with novel techniques that can be applied to other machine learning algorithms that are subject to the "cold start" issue. This paper will present our approach to optimizing bipedal robot walking assisted by thrusters using a closed-loop feedback system. By assuming that supervisory controllers are properly set, we will concentrate on refining joint trajectories to meet specific performance requirements. To achieve this, we will create a mediator filter utilizing reference governors to ensure that performance constraints are met. Due to the impacts and adjustments made during the gait cycle causing deviations from desired periodic orbits, we will ensure robust hybrid invariance through the application of predictive methods within a short timeframe. To maintain hybrid invariance, we will leverage the distinctive features of our model, the thrusters, to our advantage. The key benefit of our approach is that unlike other optimization-based nonlinear control methods, performance-related constraints are met during the single-support phase without reliance on costly numerical methods. Furthermore, the proposed thruster-supported gait control framework allows for the utilization of performance and robustness-enhancing capabilities during particular phases of the gait cycle, a previously unreported aspect. High-fidelity simulations of a specific bipedal robot walking scenario have validated the efficacy of this novel control strategy. The results show that our method is capable of generating efficient and stable gait patterns, meeting specified performance and robustness criteria. To facilitate future implementation on actual bipedal robots via onboard computation, a reduced-order model with comparable dynamics has been developed and successfully utilized. With this approach, we have successfully created a high-performance gait pattern that would be feasible for implementation on the Stanford-ARDOG robot. The code for this project has been made openly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/robot-iit/Thruster-Supported-Bipedal-Locomotion, where further developments on this novel control framework are currently being conducted.
