This research focuses on the performance evaluation and creation of a performance model for real-time video transcoding using a variety of cloud services. Real-time video processing requires significant computational resources and, to ensure quality, real-time transcoding is necessary across different video formats and bitrates. This process can be efficiently outsourced to cloud services for data center-based implementations. However, to effectively design and optimize such deployments for real-time performance, understanding the processing capabilities and bottlenecks of cloud services is crucial. Based on experimental data collected from multiple cloud services, we developed a performance model that characterizes the processing capabilities of cloud services and identifies performance bottlenecks. This model can predict output bitrate for given cloud configurations and workload conditions. It also highlights the variability of cloud performance, the impact of cloud heterogeneity on processing capabilities, and the occurrence of system bottlenecks that can limit output quality. These findings provide valuable insights for cloud-based deployments of real-time applications and offer a framework for evaluating and optimizing system performance across different cloud services. This research used Amazon EC2 cloud services, but the principles are also applicable to OpenStack cloud platforms. To demonstrate this, a performance model for OpenStack cloud services has been presented as an extension of the initial model. This research has important implications for the creation of reliable and efficient cloud-based systems that depend on real-time video processing and transcoding. A performance model such as the one proposed can facilitate implicit quality variations, due to cloud system bottlenecks, and enable the development of more effective quality assurance strategies in such systems. Furthermore, this model can serve as a precursor for more sophisticated models that capture additional system behaviors, such as system energy consumption, reliability, and user experience. This research has been theoretically validated through numerical modeling, but it also included an experimental validation phase where the performance model was put to the test using actual cloud services. The model was shown to accurately predict its observations, further cementing its validity. To facilitate widespread adoption of this model, a prototype implementation has been created and made available for public use. We have derived a semi-analytical formula for the dynamic density-density correlation of massless Dirac electrons in doped graphene, which is applicable at finite temperatures. This finding is key to understanding the thermal screening of interactions among Dirac electrons and we leverage it to calculate the thermal capacity and compressibility of doped graphene. Notably, at very low temperatures, the heat capacity displays a linear temperature dependence characteristic of normal Fermi liquids, with the coefficient controlled by the velocity of charge carriers in the material. Conversely, the compressibility is independent of temperature and is instead dictated by the fine structure constant and the velocity of charge carriers. Interestingly, when the temperature approaches the quantum oscillation limit set by the chemical broadening parameter, a thermal activation term becomes evident in the heat capacity, arising from the thermal activation of Dirac electrons across their chemical potential barrier. This induced anisotropy can be probed through infrared spectroscopy, with the onset defined by the ratio of temperature to chemical broadening parameter. Ultimately, our results imply that the heat capacity of doped graphene can be tuned via chemical means over broad ranges of energy, making it a compelling model system for studying the interplay between interaction strength and heat capacity in two-dimensional materials. Depletion of low-energy excitations due to dielectric screening also leaves its imprint on the heat capacity at finite temperatures, with a corresponding correction term displayed for absorption spectra that can be probed through infrared spectroscopy. This additional contribution arises from the thermal release of charge carriers from the Dirac sea and their subsequent scattering on each other, with resulting resonant peaks appearing in the absorption spectrum when the infrared photon energy equals an odd number of times the quantum oscillation energy. A numerical regime map is provided to guide experimental and theoretical examination of this phenomenon. The heat capacity formula also reveals that the thermal activation term can be adjusted through chemical doping, potentially aligning it with the frequency range of new infrared and X-ray free-electron lasers now being developed. As a result, we anticipate that our theoretical predictions will provide a valuable basis for a new generation of experimental and theoretical studies of doped graphene and will help identify the most suitable chemical conditions required of this material. In turn, this will facilitate a deeper understanding of the electronic structure of this material, with potential to generalize this knowledge to other two-dimensional Dirac materials. In the case of graphene, this knowledge can be tested through a combination of experimental and theoretical approaches, with potential breakthroughs to come from incorporating additional atoms into this material. For speech synthesis, selecting the optimal acoustic features is crucial, and our research suggests using a combination of both spectral and prosodic features for better results. We propose MaskedSpeech, a context-aware speech production model that integrates masking strategy with speech synthesis objectives. During training, a masking strategy layer automatically determines the feature type needed for each frame, blending the spectral and prosodic features accordingly. This forces the model to focus on missing information, leading to enhanced result quality. Experimentally, MaskedSpeech showed significant improvements over baseline models, as measured by mean opinion score (MOS) and semantic ratings. Notably, our model achieved an unsupervised speech synthesis objective score of 4.243, outperforming state-of-the-art models like Fastspeech2 and FastSpeech3. The code and model are available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghruv/MaskedSpeech. Additionally, pre-trained models for various speech synthesis tasks can be found at https://github.com/ghruv/MaskedSpeech-PretrainedModels. These improvements provide a foundation for future research on speech synthesis and feature analysis. As the model's name suggests, it represents a significant step in the development of context-aware speech production models. Although our results are tailored to English language synthesis, the model's principles are equally applicable to other linguistic contexts. As such, MaskedSpeech can serve as a versatile framework for various speech synthesis tasks. As the field of speech synthesis continues to evolve, it is essential to strike a balance between system complexity and performance. For this reason, it is not uncommon for contemporary speech synthesis models to employ multi-stage architectures comprising sequential connection units. Such systems are now the norm, with each stage representing a separate syntactic phrase. Consequently, optimizing each unit individually has become a key research focus. To this end, our proposed model leverages a unique masking strategy layer that simplifies speech synthesis by integrating multiple features at once. We investigate a cyclic universe with matter-filled singularities where dark matter plays a crucial role, requiring its presence to avoid cosmological singularities and reconcile initial conditions with the laws of physics. A specific dark energy-like phenomenon is observed in this universe, attributed to the interaction between dark matter and gravitational fields at high energy densities. This interaction leads to dark matter's non-linear response to gravity, causing it to act like a form of dark energy when the universe's expansion is rapid. This results in a simplified dark matter dynamics picture, where dark matter's overdensities or underdensities in the universe are suppressed in comparison to the findings of the N-body simulations commonly used to model our universe. As a result, structure formation in this universe occurs more slowly, with larger scales developing at a rate similar to that of the universe's overall expansion. This leads to a distinct feature in the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest, characterized by a higher correlation scale than seen in the universe modelled by the Illustris simulation, potentially resolvable with an upcoming spectroscopic survey like CEERS. Structure formation at these scales is largely independent of cosmic variance, making it a useful probe of the fundamental properties of dark matter. A more sensitive telescope like James Webb will be able to provide conclusive evidence of this model by observing just a small section of the sky. This study provides a detailed examination of contextualized models in detecting
arbitrary semantic alterations in text. We convened a diverse group of human
judges who applied the name "SemAlter" to this task. Unlike previous studies,
SemAlter isn't focused on identifying specific types of
disinformation--truthfulness, deception, factual accuracy, or offensive content.
Rather, SemAlter equates to determining whether two pieces of text have the same
meaning. Human assessors evaluated 800 text pairs as part of our endeavor, and
our top-performing contextualized model achieved an impressive F1 score of 73% in
our rigorous evaluation framework. Notably, 0.26 or nearly a quarter of the text
pairs that human judges deemed semantically equivalent were actually identified as
not equivalent by the model. We believe this discrepancy may result from the
model's tendency to rely heavily on surface features rather than engaging in
deeper semantic analysis. Moreover, certain types of alterations, such as those
involving changes to the text's emotional tone, seem inherently difficult for the
model to detect. These findings suggest that contextualized models like BERT
excels at SemAlter, yet there's still room for further improvement, likely by
incorporating additional structural aspects of language. Additionally, more complex
forms of semantic alterations remain an open challenge for future research. We
publicly release the evaluations conducted by human judges along with the contextualized
models they assessed, with full details available at our website. We anticipate

language models. These models, which incorporate automatic evaluation via
human judges, can serve as a foundation for addressing other critical language

In various image processing tasks, including video compressed sensing and color image demosaicing, images must be separated from compressed or distorted mixtures. To achieve this, a separation code with a maximum a posteriori estimator was proposed, utilizing assumptions about natural image characteristics. Research was conducted to enhance this separation code, addressing potential drawbacks mentioned in a previous study. Specifically, modifications were made to handle illuminated areas in compressed video frames and remove assumptions about natural image gradients. A computational algorithm with reduced complexity was also introduced. Experimental results indicate that the enhanced code outperforms the original code, producing superior PSNR values for video compressed sensing and comparable performance for color image demosaicing. Interestingly, the study reveals that the original code can still produce high-quality results for certain demosaicing tasks. Furthermore, the findings suggest that the simplified algorithm is almost as effective as the full algorithm, providing further evidence for the code's efficiency. Overall, the research demonstrates the code's effectiveness and potential for further improvement. Additionally, a publicly available source code is made available for reproducibility purposes. Investigated scenarios include compressed video recovery, color image demosaicing, and a challenging compressed video reconstruction scenario. To facilitate future research, further code enhancements are proposed, primarily related to edge preservation and gradient field optimization. These proposed modifications could be useful for other image processing tasks that involve source separation. In addition to code enhancements, a discussion is presented on the role of priors in image processing, emphasizing the importance of balanced prior terms that avoid over-suppression of image details. This perspective on prior terms can provide valuable insights for researchers in the field. Experimental results and associated data visualizations are also included in the supplementary material. A correction to the previous study's equation (1) is identified and the associated code modification is validated. This response is incorporated into the main text. Overall, the research provides code enhancements, proposes future research directions, and offers insights on image processing that can be beneficial for the research community. Building upon Aberdeen's underground laboratory, primarily utilized for hosting sensitive rare event search and neutrino physics experiments, requires careful consideration of external radiation background sources. Neutrons produced by cosmic ray spallation play a significant role in contributing to this background. To better understand and characterize these neutrons, a dedicated detection system is needed. This paper presents the design of such a device consisting of a horizontal water tank filled with 20 metric tons of pure water, surrounded by six 2.5 meter-long plastic scintillator modules functioning as a neutron moderator and detector of the produced gammas and secondary neutrons. This device will significantly contribute to developing tools necessary for optimizing the choice of locations and depths for hosting sensitive rare event search and neutrino physics experiments beneath Aberdeen's tunnel laboratory. Furthermore, it has the capability to be modified for retrieving data that can be utilized in conjunction with simulations, thus making it a valuable device for any deep underground laboratory setting. We also discuss the prototype's initial testing results obtained from observing spontaneous neutron decay events in the Aberdeen tunnel laboratory. This device is currently operational and collecting statistical data, which will be pivotal in obtaining a quantitative understanding of Aberdeen's tunnel laboratory's background noise. We anticipate that with further data analysis, it will be feasible to activate the sensitivity of detection system at a level comparable to that of detection systems employed in facilities like SNOLAB. This paper investigates the normalized ground state solution for the given equation $\Delta^2u=\lambda u+\frac{1}{\beta+1}|u|^\beta u$, where $\lambda$ is a normalization parameter, and $\beta$ satisfies $0\leq\beta<1$. Due to the superlinear criticality, conventional variational methods are insufficient, thus we employ a different approach based on the spirit of the global normalized ground state links. By establishing a homotopy-type map and leveraging the geometry of the equation's Sobolev embedding, we demonstrate the existence of a normalized ground state solution for this biharmonic Choquard equation with exponential growth. Notably, this technique allows us to handle the subcritical case as well. Additionally, we investigate the asymptotic behavior of the solutions as $\lambda$ tends to zero or negative infinity, as well as obtain a quantitative estimate of the solutions' first eigenvalue. This research extends the previous works by Dang and Giannetti in 2021 and 2022 towards a broader criticality range.

  The main consequence of this research involves proving the existence of a normalized ground state solution for the given equation under the specified growth condition at infinity, thus generalizing the previous works by Dang and Giannetti in 2021 and 2022.

Multiple formal models can equivalently capture the infinite behavior of finite-state systems, including rational transductions, monadic second-order logic with one successor, and Streett and parity automata. While combinatorial specifications can be automatically converted into any of these models, their infinite automaton equivalents often lack inherent combinatory structure. We introduce a novel, structurally intuitive language that can express and combine components of finite-state systems and their infinite behaviors. This language allows us to translate combinatory specifications into equivalent automata with built-in structure, making our method more efficient and flexible than previous approaches. We demonstrate our method's effectiveness by applying it to a range of examples from the literature. Our technique uses a combination of automaton and logic operations to achieve its goals. We first introduce a method for converting our combinatory specifications into equivalent Streett automata and subsequently develop a translation between Streett and parity automata. We also establish a more complex equivalence between our language and combinatorial specifications involving nested recursion, which enables us to convert these specifications into equivalent parity automata. This solution to the combinatory specification problem for infinite words provides a fundamental solution to a related problem for finite words and further generalizes previous solutions to a broader class of specifications. Our approach also offers a practical solution to synthesizing systems from combinatory specifications. We experimentally evaluate our implementation's performance on a variety of examples and compare its efficiency to other state-of-the-art synthesis tools. Our technique is generally more efficient, although there are some cases where other methods may be superior. We believe our research contributes positively to the ongoing debate about the relative expressiveness of different models of finite-state systems. Our findings are all based on actual implementations and examples, rather than theoretical proofs. We hope our work will facilitate a wider discussion about the combinatory specifications and their relationships to various models of finite-state systems. Our research is primarily focused on system design, where systems are composed of multiple components that rely on each other's behaviors. However, our approach can also be applied to other areas, such as verifying the correctness of systems that involve recursive functions. We plan to continue exploring other aspects of combinatory specifications and our solution to the associated problem, while also expanding our technique to handle additional features and more complex specifications. One potential extension is to include recursion operators in our language, which would enable us to handle a broader class of specifications. We are also considering other conversion methods, such as converting our language to Büchi automata, which could provide a more straightforward solution to some of the associated problems.

Multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) have historically been difficult to interpret due to their opaque nature. Recent research has made progress in providing features similar to LDA/QDA by using MLPs. These efforts often employ periodic activations such as sine and cosine in a single hidden layer. However, the periodic activations used in these studies are not modulated by the inputs, thus limiting their ability to capture relevant data features. In response, we've developed a new method that uses input-modulated periodic activations within a hidden layer. This approach enables the network to learn more accurate and generalizable data features. In experiments using both synthetic and real-world datasets, our method consistently outperforms the standard MLP by achieving a lower error rate. Additionally, we found that the features learned using modulated periodic activations closely match the underlying structure of the data, while also exhibiting better generalization across different viewing angles, which is critical for applying such methods in high-stakes settings. A key limitation of our approach, however, is that it only works well when using small hidden layers, and we propose a new method to overcome this constraint by applying a secondary modulated periodic activation in the output layer. This layered strategy enables us to capture more complex data features and significantly improves our results on both synthetic and real-world datasets. A further analysis of our methods also reveals that they can provide features that are not only locally informative but also globally coherent. The rapid transmission of contagious diseases is frequently intensified by a single high-transmission event, a super-spreader occurrence. This study presents a stochastic Susceptible-Infected-Removed model that accounts for such events and incorporates epidemic outbreaks in closed and open population settings. A specific super-spreader event is represented by an exponential increase in infection rate, lasting a short period. We derived and analyzed the model's basic reproduction number (R0) by evaluating the ultimate fate of the stochastic model and its components. Specifically, we established that in isolated populations, the probability of sustained infection transmission is inversely related to the intensity and duration of the super-spreader event. In open populations, the probability of sustained transmission depends on both the intensity and duration of the super-spreader event and the mean population turnover rate. A numerical analysis of closed populations revealed that the critical interval for a high-transmission period is related to the square of the population size, consistent with previous findings by May and Anderson. We also examined non-exponential distribution scenarios and developed a closed-form expression for the critical super-spreader duration in closed populations under the assumption of a Weibull distribution. This study provides a theoretical framework for assessing the impact of a high-transmission event on the dynamics of epidemic transmission and can be applied to evaluate the effectiveness of interventions aimed at containing the spread of the disease. Furthermore, this research can be extended to model the transmission of infectious diseases in complex networks and social structures. Additionally, we investigated how the probability of a person attending a super-spreader event affects the transmission dynamics. A comprehensive analysis has been conducted to measure the radii of 7537 young stellar clusters in 29 galaxies across 0.8 million square kiloparsecs of the Coma supercluster. The study's findings reveal that the average radius of a cluster in a given galaxy correlates with the galaxy's mass, following a $R_{\rm cl} \propto M_{\rm gal}^{0.30\pm0.02}$ proportionality. This relationship holds true for galaxies with 10^9 to 10^11 solar masses and may be used to predict the size of low-mass galaxy clusters. Notably, a cluster's radius is independent of the host galaxy's star formation rate. Within a given galaxy, the size of a cluster correlates with the number of stellar members, following a $R_{\rm cl} \propto N^{0.15\pm0.01}$. This study provides a cluster radius catalog that can be utilized as weak lensing masks or to study the internal dynamics of clusters. Ultimately, these findings will be informative for modeling the size distribution of star clusters and the potential of star clusters to act as gravitational lenses. Additionally, they may offer insight into cluster dynamics and possible mergers between small galaxy clusters. The data presented can be accessed through the Astrophysics Data System under the label "Cluster Radii".

The framework consists of two stages: a retrieval stage and a modification stage.
In the retrieval stage, models are fine-tuned for related tasks to expand their internal memory with relevant examples, which helps them recall more effective information in the modification stage.
The modification stage involves using the retrieved examples to update the model's parameters, enabling it to perform better on the new task.

Optimizing hyperparameters in the private version of the stochastic gradient descent algorithm is a critical issue due to limited access to private datasets for hyperparameter tuning. The development of algorithms that simultaneously optimize model parameters and hyperparameters has shown promise but is impeded by the restriction on private data usage. To address this challenge, we present a novel algorithm, called Hyperparameter Tuning via Unbiased Samples (HTUNs), in this paper. HTUNs leverages an unrepresentative subset of sampled data without drawing from the private dataset. It employs the unbiased estimator from the sampled data to update hyperparameters, while utilizing the full dataset for model parameter updates. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that HTUNs can effectively optimize hyperparameters for the private version of the training process. The algorithm's performance is verifiable through comprehensive experiments conducted on both common hyperparameter tuning scenarios and the challenging task of unsupervised hyperparameter selection. Additionally, our research showcases the value of meta-learning in deep learning, especially when the topic is classification. This framework not only improves model interpretability but also provides a solution to the longstanding problem of establishing a connection between the loss function used in training a deep learning model and its generalizability. A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via relative rankings of experiences, offering a versatile and user-friendly way for humans to engage with agents. However, the existing methods based on human rankings across entire state spaces are impractically time-consuming for large environments. To overcome this limitation, we present ACR (Auxiliary Target for Cluster Ranking), a new framework that divides the state space into manageable clusters based on visual features and seeks the optimal cluster assignment that aligns with human preferences. To achieve this, ACR utilizes both self-supervised and human-provided data to identify clusters and map states to them. By reducing the scope of human input to cluster rankings rather than full state rankings, our approach significantly cuts down on the required human labeling, enabling efficient, near-real-time human-in-the-loop learning across complex environments. Notably, our results on the OpenAIGameControls dataset demonstrate that ACR's cluster-based strategy not only accelerates learning but also yields policies with improved performance. Moreover, our research on real-world human subjects at the Amazon Mechanical Turk further confirms that humans can efficiently provide high-quality feedback with our cluster-based ranking interface. Additionally, our research also uncovers an intriguing efficient learning regime with only a single human round after an initial self-supervised unstructured learning phase. Nonetheless, this algorithm demands multiple fragile resources, including high-quality random number generation, distinct classical data storage, and distinct qubits for input and output. We have developed NISQ-HHL, a hybrid HHL algorithm designed to function on noisy, intermediate-scale quantum hardware. We introduce a novel variation of NISQ-HHL, incorporating a hybrid variation of the HHL algorithm that includes classical Monte Carlo simulations to enhance performance on such hardware, resulting in improved execution time and reduced quantum bytecode size. This implementation is presented through a linear system solving application involving portfolio optimization in financial settings, where we demonstrate its efficiency on a range of classical and quantum hardware. Notably, NISQ-HHL outperforms classical Monte Carlo methods in multiple scenarios. The source code of our project is available on GitHub at https://github.com/QSharpUSNS/NISQHHL. Additionally, a tutorial on incorporating hybrid HHL into portfolio optimization can be found at https://quantumtutorials.org/nisqhhlpot/. We have also introduced a new five-valued metric for evaluating the performance of quantum classifiers at https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.08657, and we anticipate exploring its integration with NISQ-HHL in a forthcoming study. We have further investigated the application of NISQ-HHL to matrix diagonalization, a crucial subroutine with numerous uses, and a prototype of this algorithm is currently being executed across multiple quantum simulators. We have also established a community forum for discussing hybrid quantum algorithms at https://discord.gg/hZ4K43X. We have collaborated with industry leaders, such as Microsoft, Google, and IBM, to gather feedback on our work, and we have presented our research at various conferences, including the 2022 AQS conference and the 2022 QNAT conference. This paper introduces a novel multi-modal learning method that utilizes a bidirectional attention mechanism. This approach prevents the disparity between speech and language models caused by different numbers of training examples and enables the network to automatically select relevant audio features for improved performance. Experimental evaluations on the Librispeech corpus demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, yielding a 4.3% improvement in word error rate compared to the baseline model. Furthermore, our method achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art models using only a fraction of the training data (960 hours vs 480 hours). The proposed architecture is simple, easy to implement, and compatible with various ASR models, making it a promising solution for multi-modal learning in ASR. Experimental results on the Common Voice corpus are also presented in the supplementary material. This work is an extended version of our previous research presented at the 2019 Interspeech conference. To address these issues, a revised version of our method has been introduced and named Bidirectional Multi-Modal Learning using Attention mechanism, subsequently published as a conference paper at the 2020 Interspeech conference. Quantum chromodynamics enables the representation of hadronic processes on the basis of an interacting quark-gluon plasma.  Within the scope of perturbative QCD, long-distance properties of heavy mesons can be described by light-like correlations, or 'light-cone correlations.  These correlations are directly measurable in deep inelastic scattering and positron infrared finiteness.  Our study focuses on the interpretation of DIS data through the examination of light-cone correlations in place of traditional structure functions.  We also examine the systematics of these correlations and their impact on the description of the Breit-Feynman picture in the infinite momentum limit.  Our analysis indicates that the positron infrared finiteness in DIS results from the interaction of quark and gluon fluids in the infinite momentum limit, offering a new perspective on the positron IR finiteness in DIS.  We further show that the positron infrared divergence in light-cone gauge can be circumvented by introducing a cassical approximation for soft processes, which simultaneously explains the positron infrared finiteness in DIS and the emergence of parton distribution functions in e+e- annihilation through the conversion of quark-gluon plasma into partons.  Our analysis also reveals the nontrivial relationship between the light-cone wave function of a heavy meson and the parton distribution function in e+e- annihilation, paving the way for an understanding of heavy meson semileptonic decays within this framework.  We anticipate that this new perspective on the interpretation of DIS data and the nature of quark-gluon plasma in the infinite momentum limit will be valuable for exploring connections between particle and nuclear physics.  We propose a new experimental test at an future electron-ion or ion-ion collider that would allow for the direct measurement of the light-cone wave function of a heavy meson, providing crucial evidence for the existence of quark-gluon plasma in the infinite momentum limit and shedding new light on the nature of heavy meson semileptonic decays.  We also examine potential for new discoveries at a future $12$ GeV version of the JLab electron-ion/collision facility that could significantly impact our understanding of the interplay between particle and nuclear physics.  We conclude by outlining a research pathway that could address fundamental open questions in the physics of light-cone correlations, parton distribution functions, heavy meson semileptonic decays and the nature of quark-gluon plasma in the infinite momentum limit. Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or shortened scan times. Deep-learning models have made significant advancements in enhancing PET images by translating low-quality PET scans with associated MRI data to high-quality PET images, particularly with significantly reduced doses. Nonetheless, such deep learning approaches have primarily focused on utilizing training datasets similar to their test data, neglecting performance evaluation for new acquisitions outside of their distribution. We introduce a novel neural network framework that incorporates the physics underlying the PET imaging process and estimates output uncertainty to address these limitations. This new uncertainty-aware neural network framework can utilize low-dose PET scans and accompanying MRI data to generate high-quality PET images at standard doses, thus enhancing robustness when dealing with various acquisitions outside of its trained data range. This new model has been successfully validated using a realistic simulation-based dataset for brain scans, where it significantly outperformed existing models in reconstructing PET images from various out-of-distribution PET-MRI pairs. It notably produced images from unseen MRI protocols, such as RASTL and BERT, which it had not been trained on. This research provides a starting point for developing deep learning models capable of handling a wide range of PET-MRI pairs, thus paving the way for creating protocols adapted to individual subjects without the need for extensive training data. This protocol-adapted model has been made available for downloading at this website: https://sites.google.com/ualberta.ca/pet-codelibrary/home. It has also been incorporated into an open-source PET reconstruction software package called TichoRecon, also available for download at this website: https://github.com/USAHRT/TichoRecon. The proliferation of internet-based services has transformed how users interact with technology and each other, generating vast amounts of data that are increasingly sensitive in nature. These data, now being extensively collected and detailed, pose significant concerns regarding individual privacy. The current approach to addressing privacy issues is often viewed as unappealingly restrictive and complicated, leading many to adopt a common misconception that privacy is an exceptional rather than an inherent component of modern life. To better understand the perspectives of ordinary people on these issues, a novel method involving a set of relaxed deontic logic principles is introduced. This method enables the formal representation of users' opinions on topics such as privacy, customization, and related concerns. Our results reveal the prevalence of privacy concerns among nearly all participants, alongside a notable disparity in how men and women perceive issues of customization. Furthermore, our research highlights the significance of perceiving privacy as an integrated component of modern life rather than an exception. Additionally, we found that among young adults, personalized recommendations are widely admired, but with a crucial limitation: they must be accurate. Our research offers valuable insights for designers of data-driven systems, with implications for the development of more user-centered technologies that prioritize both customization and privacy. A new approach to tailoring services is proposed, one that strikes a balance between providing accurate recommendations and respecting users' desire for autonomy. Our findings also highlight the need for clear, uncomplicated language in informing users about data collection and usage practices. To achieve this, we propose a novel method for communicating data-related information in a straightforward and appealing way. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in increasing users' understanding and comfort with data collection and related issues. This research provides a foundation for exploring additional aspects of customization and privacy, including users' attitudes towards data sharing, personalization algorithms, and technology-induced biases. With the rapid evolution of technology and changing user perspectives, it is essential to establish a continuous research cycle that monitors and reassesses these views. By doing so, we can contribute to creating data-driven technologies that prioritize both customization and privacy, two components that are inherently interconnected. Our research is an attempt to initiate this type of cycle. To facilitate this process, we are publicly releasing our formal representations of user opinions, along with our methodology, to serve as a starting point for a broader investigation into these matters. A renowned linguistic analysis known as centering theory (CT) posits that spoken language is most coherently understood when structured around recurring 'centers of attention'. This paper delves into the current state of coreference resolution (CR) by examining the implications of modern CR models in relation to CT principles. Through a comprehensive examination of leading CR models and their evaluations, the authors seek to identify any correlations between the performance of these models and their adherence to CT. Coreference resolution can be seen as an extension of centering, as both share the goal of identifying relationships within a text. Unlike centering, which focuses on coherent structures, coreference resolution focuses on specific links. Nonetheless, coherent structures emerge from combining all connections, including core references. Given this interconnectedness, it is not surprising that systems exhibiting strong centering performance also perform well on coreference tasks. Further analysis reveals that while almost all coreference systems with high scores exhibit good centering performance, the converse is not true. Some centering systems with high scores lag behind in coreference tasks due to limitations in capturing diversity, a crucial aspect of coreference resolution. Moreover, coreference solutions have been achieved abscent of any centering-based components, indicating that coreference is a more complex task than centering. These findings provide valuable insights for both the CT and CR communities, highlighting the necessity for further centering-based coreference models that can capture diversity and the exploration of coreference tasks through the lens of CT. In doing so, this work constitutes a ground-breaking integration of CT and CR. The evaluation of coreference systems in conjunction with centering metrics has implications for the evaluation of coreference systems as well as potential avenues for ensembling and hyperparameter selection methods. Furthermore, this work raises questions regarding the coherence of coherent paraphrases, an area that merits future investigation. This paper also extends the standard coreference resolution task by incorporating centering-oriented supervision, leading to improved performance on both coreference and centering tasks. This approach, though not broadly applicable due to the rare nature of centered clauses in typical coreference datasets, may be of use in processing texts with prevalent recursive structures. Additionally, this work demonstrates the difficulty of replicating prior centering research due to the existing gap in coreference datasets and highlights the necessity for more nuanced measures of centering that can capture diversity. On the other hand, it also shows that coreference systems based on neural models can succeed without any centering-based components, providing valuable insights for both the CT and CR communities. Quantum complexity theory seeks to understand an isolated system's degrees of freedom over time. Various proposals quantify this using operator growth metrics, which measure the system's informational depth. Krylov complexity, a specific operator growth theory, proposes that the number of linearly independent basis vectors remains constant, regardless of the system's size. This work investigates the relationship between Krylov complexity and other operator growth models, such as the standard operator growth model inspired by BBPZ, and examines whether they are intimately connected, with a focus on systems that can be described by a non-degenerate Hamiltonian. For an initial time period, all models exhibit similar behavior, but ultimately, their differences become apparent, often resulting in one surpassing the others. Nonetheless, neither is ever surpassed by the other for as long as the system remains in an exponential decay phase. This work also sheds light on the underlying reasons for these behaviors in multiple operator growth models. Moreover, it presents a simpler, yet robust, proof of the exponential scaling of Krylov complexity in systems that are not necessarily integrable. Additionally, this work demonstrates that the standard operator growth model inspired by BBPZ outperforms Krylov complexity in systems that have undergone a quantum critical transition, as evidenced by power-law scaling in both the spin-1/2 XXZ chain and the anisotropic Heisenberg chain. In these cases, the complexity may initially decline before eventually increasing in a manner consistent with a specific universal exponent. This work also explores the relationship between operator growth models and other system properties, such as entanglement dynamics, with a focus on uncovering whether a universal complexity scale exists across all systems. This uncovering reveals that systems that exhibit exponential complexity also exhibit exponential entanglement, whereas systems that exhibit power-law complexity are associated with power-law entanglement. This distinction holds for both Hamiltonians that degrade and those that remain non-degenerate. This work further establishes that the standard operator growth model inspired by BBPZ is more robust in capturing the associated universal complexity scale than Krylov complexity, particularly in systems that undergo a quantum critical transition. Nonetheless, Krylov complexity continues to provide a more intricate understanding of the complex dynamics underlying these systems. Lastly, this work also contemplates the potential for further research into operator growth models, with a focus on identifying whether the associated universal complexity scale is a more general phenomenon that arises from the inherent properties of an open system's closed subspace. Network-based services provide significant income to service operators, which they regulate through Service Level Agreements (SLAs). These agreements define predictable performance parameters for applications transmitted over the network. Ensuring the adherence to these agreements is crucial not only to maintain customer satisfaction but also to prevent the deterioration of network reputation, which could ultimately threaten revenue generation. This paper introduces an innovative method for SLA monitoring based on peer-to-peer technology. A decentralized system is proposed, comprising individual monitoring units located within network nodes, which collect local measurement data and identify local breach occurrences. These detection results are then shared among neighboring units through a peer-to-peer network, formed from the underlying communication links. As a result, the entire system becomes aware of all instances of SLA non-compliance across its scope. A numerical study is presented to assess the precision and efficiency of this approach, as well as the impact of key system parameters on its operation. Additionally, guidelines are offered to optimize the design of a decentralized SLA monitoring system. A real-world implementation scenario is also described to further illustrate the effectiveness of this system in monitoring network SLA violations. A key limitation of this method is the reliance on units' accurate classification of breach occurrences, which could lead to false positives or negatives. Future work is suggested to address this issue through the enhancement of individual monitoring units using machine learning techniques. A key open issue in this research area is the identification of optimal system parameter settings, which is currently achieved through a trial-and-error approach but could benefit from a more systematic method. Another significant research opportunity arises from the integration of this system with network SLA management tools to facilitate proactive remedial actions in cases of detected breach occurrences. Finally, integrating this system with machine learning algorithms to enhance the accuracy of units' classification of breach occurrences is another promising research path. This could be achieved through a collaborative approach, which could lead to a significant reduction in false positives and negatives. Furthermore, integrating this system with machine learning algorithms to enable units to classify breach occurrences based on their prediction of future network behavior could further enhance its performance. This could result in the early detection of persistent breaches and reduce the system's reliance on fixed statistical thresholds. The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically constrains the maximum beam current that can be achieved, especially for energy recovery linacs with multiple passes where a small amount of charge can generate a large beam current. Studies have highlighted the impact of filling design and machine geometry on beam breakup instability in multi-pass energy recovery linacs. This paper delves deeper into this understanding by examining how filling design influences beam breakup instability and presents strategies for optimizing machine geometry to delay the onset of beam breakup instability. Numerical simulations were conducted for a 3 GeV energy recovery linac with multiple passes and different filling designs, showing that beam breakup instability can be managed by selecting an appropriate fill length that balances the regeneration process and machine impedance. Furthermore, increasing the gap voltage in an RF cavity is an effective way to further suppress beam breakup instability. This research provides a theoretical basis for evaluating beam breakup instability in multi-pass energy recovery linacs and offers a tool for optimizing machine geometry and RF cavity voltage to delay the onset of beam breakup instability, enabling the operation of these machines at full capacity. This paper will describe this design in detail and present its implementation on the 3 GeV energy recovery linac at the STF facility in the University of Wisconsin-Madison. Measurements conducted on this machine demonstrate the practical effectiveness of this design in suppressing beam breakup instability. This paper will also discuss a design flaw in the RF cavity that led to beam breakup instability in the University of Wisconsin-Madison's energy recovery linac and showed that while increasing the gap voltage can delay the onset of beam breakup instability, it may not be sufficient when there is a design flaw in the machine. This paper will conclude with some consideration on future research that could provide a comprehensive understanding of beam breakup instability in multi-pass energy recovery linacs. This understanding could enable the design of machines that operate at full current capacity in programs like future free-electron lasers and high-brightness proton sources for next-generation colliders. This paper will also discuss the status of existing research on beam breakup instability at the University of Wisconsin-Madison's energy recovery linac and the plans for future research on this topic. To determine the parameters for neutrino oscillation, cutting-edge experiments employing long-baseline neutrino detection systems are crucial. Neutrino-protein interactions can be misleading and contaminate data, thus it is essential to establish comprehensive neutron interaction spectra with geologically derived materials, in order to enhance detection system performance. We present the results of a comprehensive neutron flux measurement, obtained by detecting the products of neutron interaction with a 10-inch scintillator sensor featuring a novel 3D design and minimal pulse-shape analysis, allowing for precise identification of stopping non-relativistic neutrons within a 1.4 GHz bandwidth. This measurement was accurate within ±17%, or better, for neutron energies greater than 1 MeV. It achieved the most precise measurement of the 12.8 barn neutron cross-section at 1 MeV to date. We also demonstrated the capability of this detection system to distinguish between 1 MeV neutron energy and background, as well as identify the scattering of non-relativistic neutrons for energies below 1 MeV. This detection system can contribute to the development of more accurate neutrino interaction models. It has the potential to be adapted for use in large-scale detectors, such as those employed in long-baseline neutrino experiments. Furthermore, this detection system can detect the presence of low-energy neutrons, making it suitable for detecting cosmic muon neutrino interactions that result in the emission of a 0.25 eV antineutrino, such as those involving the conversion of a cosmic neutrino into a cosmic antineutrino in the presence of a 5.5 km distance, as required for the detection of neutrinoless quantum entanglement. Additionally, due to its ability to accurately determine the energy spectrum of neutron interaction with a 10-inch scintillator sensor, featuring a novel 3D design and minimal pulse-shape analysis, this detection system can potentially detect the presence of sterile neutrons, such as those that could result from the interaction of a 1 eV neutrino with a 5.5 km distance. Furthermore, we established that the novel 3D design of this detection system offers better than double the sensitivity of a similar system employing a 2D design. Imitation learning has emerged as a key approach for robot skill learning due to its user-friendly and straightforward solution for robot trajectory generation. Unlike unconstrained methods that overlook environmental and kinematic constraints, constrained imitation learning allows the transfer of human skills to unstructured settings. Current works in constrained imitation learning have addressed various constraints but have left the issue of nonlinear constraints unresolved. To tackle this, we introduce Extended Kernelized Movement Primitives (EKMP) which addresses multiple challenges in imitation learning, including nonlinear constraints. EKMP can learn from multiple demonstrations, adapt skills to various target points, avoid obstacles, and meet complex linear and nonlinear constraints. Our work also establishes connections to state-of-the-art motion planning methods, and we provide linear and quadratic programming examples using human-annotated zones to tackle complex constraints. EKMP outperformed state-of-the-art kernelized movement primitives in multiple scenarios, demonstrating its effectiveness in solving complex constraint problems. Our code is available at https://github.com/robotbrain2019/EKMP. EKMP has been accepted for publication in the IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA) 2023. A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R with the smallest number of elements that can do this is known as the minimum identifying set and the number of elements in this set is referred to as the graph's identifying number. In this study, we determine the identifying number for all basic graphical structures. Additionally, we establish a non-linear correlation between certain graphical H-amplifications and their corresponding H-trimmed identification numbers. Finally, we propose a generic approach to identify the minimum trimmed number for graphs with a high degree of symmetry. This approach is specifically applied to Cartesian products, d-dimensional hypercubes, and complete trees. However, for some instances, an exact answer couldn't be derived using this method. As such, we resort to a randomized algorithm based on a trimmed version of the metric dimension problem itself. This algorithm provides a solution that, while not optimal, is at least twice as accurate as the best possible trimmed value for a given graph. In some cases, this algorithm yields the exact answer, which implies it is correct for graphs with a small number of vertices. As part of this study, we also introduce the concept of a 1-trimmed metric dimension and prove it is an NP-complete problem. One of the graphical structures for which we determine the exact identifying number is a 1-trimmed version of a complete bipartite graph. This study provides an open question section to which potential answers are also provided in an appendix. In particular, it is shown that one of the randomized algorithm's parameters can be optimized more efficiently. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that many of the exact answers derived using the study's methods could also be obtained using a brute force approach, however this approach isn't feasible for larger graphs due to limitations of time and memory. Finally, it is proven that one of the graphical structures for which an exact answer was derived is actually an instance of a much simpler problem, which could have been solved much more efficiently. In the paper's conclusion, it is suggested that a genetic algorithm could be an effective way to solve some of its open questions. The Southern Atlantic rift system, extending from 3°S to 37°S latitude, developed as a linear intra-continental rift within the South American and African continental platforms.  It formed as a result of the separation of these continents during the Gondwana supercontinent's break-up in the Jurassic and Cretaceous periods.  Initial rifting in this region occurred between South America and Africa during the Jurassic, with subsequent sea-floor spreading beginning around 126 million years ago.  Estimates of continental separation vary by area along the rift, but generally placed between 128 million years ago in the south to around 90 million years ago in the north.  Studies have often analyzed magnetic lineations, seafloor spreading rates, and anatomic coefficients to determine rifting parameters, with results showing that rifting in this region occurred over a long period, sometimes incorporating extensional multi-phasal activity.  However, these studies have also demonstrated that rifting in the Southern Atlantic ended before continental separation, with initial rifting followed by post-separation continental break-up deformation in areas like South America.  This research analyzes movement patterns within the rift by calculating non-conformable block movements, reconstructing ancient landscapes, and estimating extensional and compressive rates.  Results indicate that rifting in the Southern Atlantic occurred over a long period, with initial extension followed by compression and subsequent extension in different areas, likely caused by thermal weakening of the mantle beneath a breaking continent. This connection arises from analyzing the structure of the EAHAlgebra, which is derived from the algebra of sections of line bundles on a toric Deligne-Mumford stack. By establishing an equivalence between the category of coherent sheaves on a blowup of a torus and the category of coherent sheaves on the original torus, we are able to express the EAHA as the symplectic mutation functor on the category of coherent sheaves on a blowup of an algebraic torus. This construction enables us to extend the category of coherent sheaves on a toric Deligne-Mumford stack by using symplectic mutations, resulting in a precise description of the derived category in terms of the EAHA. This relationship serves as a proof that the EAHA is a quotient of the ring of the algebraic torus's line bundles' sections. We also establish that the EAHA's representation theory is equivalent to the representation theory of the algebraic torus's line bundles' sections. This derivation relies on the algebraic description of the mutation functors, which expresses them as composition of pull-backs, push-forwards, and symplectic mutations of sheaves. This connection enables us to describe the action of the EAHA's generators on the category of coherent sheaves's objects by using the structure of these generators. This description relies on the explicit expression of the push-forwards and pull-backs' actions, which are derived from the structure of these functors. The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. Successful smart healthcare relies on training models using a large quantity of user data, but several key challenges arise: preventing breach of user privacy, addressing class imbalance due to individual data collection limitations, and overcoming gaps between training and deployment environments. This paper presents FedHealth, a pioneering framework for transfer learning in healthcare that mitigates these difficulties by protecting user confidentiality, tackling imbalance issues, and bridging the gap between training and deployment. FedHealth incorporates a hybrid framework that combines hard and soft methods for federated learning, a random walk approach for data imbalance issues, and a novel protocol for ensemble models. This framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through two benchmark datasets, indicating improvements over baseline models of up to 11.6% in accuracy. Furthermore, FedHealth facilitates easy integration with popular healthcare datasets, enabling easy reproducibility and expansion of the framework. A publicly accessible code repository is available at https://github.com/yousefbinaseh/FedHealth. This framework has far-reaching potential to develop private, data-driven healthcare solutions. This paper is the first of its kind to introduce a transfer learning framework for healthcare and boldly envisions a future where healthcare solutions are privately developed using a global pool of data. To investigate the impact on neutral kaon decay in the $K^0 \to \pi^0 e^n \nu_e$ channel, we develop a set of unitarity and renormalizable constraints for the relevant low-energy parameters.

Within the one-loop approximation, we calculate the influence of the anomalies on the neutral kaon mixing parameters $\epsilon$ and $\epsilon'/\epsilon$, finding that the anomalies could potentially increase $\epsilon$ by a factor of up to three and lower $\epsilon'/\epsilon$ by as much as a factor of ten.

However, the one-loop corrections also indicate that the anomalies could raise the $K^0$ meson lifetime by a significant amount, likely exceeding the observed $0.5\times 10^{-8}$ s threshold, and could also significantly lower the $B^0$ meson mixing parameter $\Delta \Gamma_{B^0}$.

To avoid these discrepancies, the new physics scale must be set at $1-10$ TeV, which could still be within the reach of upcoming $K$ and $B$ physics experiments. 

In contrast to many other new physics scenarios, the proposed vectorlike compositeness theory can concurrently explain the $K^0 \to \pi^0 e^n \nu_e$ anomaly, along with the $B$ meson mixing and $R_K$ anomalies observed in $K$ and $B$ meson systems respectively. 

This new physics scenario predicts the $B^0 \to K^0 \pi^0 \gamma$ decay to significantly exceed the predicted SM outcome, a signature that experiments should seek in order to further validate or invalidate the proposed theory.

Research on musical instrument recognition has made significant progress in recent years, yet a major limitation still exists when it comes to identifying unknown instruments. This challenge arises because many approaches, despite using advanced techniques like deep learning and robust features, often rely on being presented with images of known instruments to train. This isn't a practical solution for researchers who need to identify instruments based on a wide range of images, including those of instruments that have never been seen before. This problem is even more pronounced in cases where only a small number of examples are available for each type of instrument. This paper proposes a groundbreaking new method that addresses this issue by creating a hierarchical framework that groups similar instruments together and uses a novel technique to perform classification at both the overall category and specific instrument levels. Topological nodal lines, a newer class of topological phenomena, involve one-dimensional trajectories where points of zero energy converge. Topological nodal lines can be distinguished by a novel quantity, the nodal line invariant, which requires three-dimensional momentum space integration. A brain tumor affects every age group and has the highest mortality rate.  MRI technology is commonly used for tumor detection and diagnosis by radiologists, who must accurately identify the tumor type and area for proper treatment planning.  However, interpreting MRI scans can be challenging and time-consuming for radiologists.  Building on advances in computer-aided diagnosis powered by deep learning, this study presents a multi-task attention directed network (MAG-Net) that uses MRI images to classify and segment brain tumors in coronal, axial, and sagittal views.  The model is trained on the Figshare dataset containing images of three tumor types, meningioma, glioma, and pituitary tumors, and outperforms existing models through numerous trials while requiring the fewest parameters.  Notably, MAG-Net achieves state-of-the-art segmentation accuracy on the BRATS 2019 challenge and outperforms a leading classification model on the Figshare dataset.  The model's efficient use of attention mechanisms and sparse parameters makes it highly suitable for practical implementation in clinical settings.  The source code of this study is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/yoyo14314141/MAG-Net.  The model's parameter file is available on UML at https://umlgallery.cs.umass.edu/models/49. The model has been tested on a workstation with a NVIDIA Tesla V100 16GB graphics card and a server with four NVIDIA Tesla V100 16GB graphics cards. The model has been trained and ran on the University of Massachusetts Lowell's HPC cluster.  The collaboration of this study involved researchers from the University of Massachusetts Lowell, Nanjing University, Southeast University, and the University of Alberta.  The funding for this study was provided by the National Science Foundation, the National Natural Science Foundation of China, the Jiangsu Province Science and Technology Plan, and the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada. This equivalence paves the way for a more intuitive proof of the latter result. This study explores the connection between star formation rates and the mass of these star clusters, examining how adding massive star clusters affects this relationship. At low masses, the relationship follows a straight line as expected, but a notable turn in the curve occurs when mass exceeds approximately 10^10.6 Solar Masses. To understand this turn, we consider several factors including gas supply, star cluster mass spectrum, and cluster survival rate. Through a comprehensive statistical analysis, we identify that the mass of the central black hole plays a significant part in explaining this turn in the curve, particularly in governing the cluster mass spectrum. Additionally, we find that gas supply limits star formation at both low and high mass ranges, while the cluster survival rate has a significant impact at high mass ranges. This understanding offers valuable insights into the assembly of massive galaxies and the development of their central black holes. While they may not be as massive as their host galaxy's bulge, they do contribute significantly to the overall star cluster mass. If we exclude these nuclear star clusters from the analysis, the relationship shifts even more dramatically, exhibiting an even more pronounced turn at high mass ranges. It also raises implications regarding the origin of these clusters and their role in galaxy evolution. Using Dirac's time-dependent variational principle, we establish a simple H\'enon-Heiles model based on semiclassical mechanics. A two-body trial wavefunction in the form of Hatree-type is applied, leading to the derivation of an effective Hamiltonian in the context of Jackiw-Kerman theory. The calculations yield consistent results with the existing H\'enon-Heiles research, furthermore predicting the existence of stationary states displaying quantum fluctuations around mean positions, in alignment with classical prediction of symplectic integrals. Notably, we demonstrate that in the region of motion where classical trajectories are unstable, microscopically described by the Jackiw-Kerman approach, stationary states can still be found, indicating the dominance of quantum phenomena over mean-field behavior in this regime. Computational simulations are set up to validate our findings through numerical solution of the time-dependent variational principle equations, mimicking the characteristics of stationary states within the Jackiw-Kerman framework. The results of these simulations are in line with theoretical predictions, showcasing that variational approaches can efficiently model nonlinear dynamics by means of linearized problems in a quantum context. The effectiveness of this method in handling complex systems is illustrated through application to a mean-field H\'enon-Heiles model, where it is shown that it offers a more precise solution than other variational methods, closely approximating the existing solution, whereas for a true time-dependent solution, it displays a notable deviation, indicating that further improvements are necessary. The research concludes with an examination of whether the same variational approach can capture phenomena of quantum dissipation in interacting many-body systems. The possibility of employing variational principles in such complex scenarios is explored, along with the potential for incorporating damping terms into variational theories, thus providing a more comprehensive understanding of quantum dynamics in a broader context. The study suggests that variational approaches on a mean-field level can efficiently model nonlinear dynamics, and that further developments in this direction may pave the way for describing quantum dissipation in interacting many-body systems. The paper also highlights potential directions for research in this area, specifically mentioning the possibility of applying variational principles to study quantum dissipation in systems driven out of equilibrium, as well as the potential for exploring nonlinear effects in a broader range of phenomena, from quantum gravity to superfluidity and superconductivity. We've performed an in-depth analysis of three galaxy cores at $\rm z=2.91$ within a massive galaxy group, yielding high-resolution infrared and submillimeter data. This revealed that the galaxies exhibit extremely compact, actively star-forming cores at the centers of massive, irregularly shaped disk systems, both of which exhibit quiescent, lopsided characteristics. Consequently, these galaxies are witnessing `outside-in' quenching. We propose a theoretical framework suggesting that mass asymmetry, resulting from absorbed and irregular matter, is accountable for their diminished star-formation activity by channeling it towards their core. Furthermore, we observe that disk asymmetry is associated with gas streams that are feeding the galaxies and influencing their evolution. This is manifested by an aligned major-axis of galaxies in relation to nearby filaments, presenting observational evidence of accretion streams on galaxy evolution. This is demonstrated by bulge construction, combined with massive quiescent, lopsided galaxies in the current stage, until they collide with a major merger galaxy. Ultimately, this will result in a massive, elliptical galaxy. This process is comparable to a model featuring a massive, quiescent galaxy at $\rm z=3.48$, undergoing collisional quenching following a major merger. This occurred after a significant time lag following their assembly. This includes a massive, compact bulge constructed prior to quenching, combined with a massive, irregularly shaped disk system that became quiescent after it. Similarly, our near-infrared $K$-band morphological analysis, presented in a separate paper, has revealed that massive, quiescent galaxies in this galaxy group feature constructed or growing narrow, disk-like bulges in contrast to massive, quiescent galaxies at $\rm z=2.39$, where they are an elliptical, pseudo-bulge type. This provides significant insights into the processes of star formation and accretion in galaxy groups at $\rm z \sim 3$. This also offers a cosmological context to the various morphological transformations of galaxies in the COSMOS field. Moreover, it presents a local analog on the Earth to the galaxy construction that occurred during the cosmic dawn. This includes the construction of massive, compact quiescent galaxies at $\rm z \sim 7$, following a time lag of about 1.2 billion years, until they collided with each other. This led to the construction of massive, compact elliptical galaxies at $\rm z \sim 6$. This process is still ongoing

Recently discovered solar data from Bolivia (5250 m above sea level) and Mexico (4600 m above sea level) reveal significant neutron decay particle signals on November 7, 2004, correlating with a powerful X2.0 solar flare. Analysis of atmospheric data and satellite images suggests the particles caused a large, spreading cloud of condensation formed from neutrons decomposing in the atmosphere. Furthermore, evidence indicates this event may have resulted in the formation of a massive fireball in Kitkatla, Canada, which has been misclassified as a meteorite impact. The discovery of these particles, which have a short 687 second half-life, provides key insights into the conversion of solar energy into particles and offers a new means of detecting and monitoring solar neutrino activity. Additionally, it highlights the significance of maintaining historical data from ground-level particle detectors, which are essential for a comprehensive understanding of solar physics. The findings support the hypothesis that solar neutrinos can cause the decay of atmospheric neutrons into protons, electrons, and antineutrinos, and may help explain the exceptionally low observed neutron half-life in the 1980s. The event's significance also emphasizes the importance of collaborative scientific efforts and open data sharing and access. The accompanying database provides detailed data on the detected particles, related solar activity, atmospheric conditions, and geographical locations. It includes information on the discovered fireball in Kitkatla, as well as three previously reported similar events in 1872, 1937, and 1963. The data also reveal a notable 11-year cycle pattern in solar neutron decay particle activity, which anticipates an increased risk of such events during the upcoming solar maximum in 2025. The database is available at https://www.researchgate.org/publication/3597460-Solar-Neutron-Decay-Particles_observed_in_November_7_2004. The new 11-year cycle pattern of solar neutron decay particles identified in this study has important implications for emergency planning, particularly in high-altitude areas with limited access to infrastructure, and highlights the need for continued monitoring of these particles to ensure public safety. The discovery of the recent November 7, 2004 event and three earlier incidents in 1872, 1937, and 1963 in Bolivia and Mexico underscores the importance of maintaining historical data from ground-level particle detectors, which provide key insights into the conversion of solar energy into particles and the underlying physics governing solar neutrino activity. This study examines the linearized wave equations in relativistic hydrodynamics, specifically in both its first-order and second-order variants. For small excitations, these systems can be equivalently described using a set of semi-linear first-order equations. Both formulations are computationally expensive due to their extensive memory requirements. In contrast, a novel integrated continuation approach for boundary conditions is introduced, significantly simplifying the implementation while maintaining an accurate solution. This method enables a significant improvement in performance for both formulations, resulting in enhanced computational efficiency. In the case of the first-order theory, introducing an additional small parameter allows the development of a simplified, local boundary condition implementation, which is relevant for the majority of current applications. This enables a further improvement in performance, achieved through a direct numerical solution of the integrated equations at the boundary. In the high-resolution version of this scheme, an additional step is employed to eliminate the non-conservative term, leading to an expansion of the solution in the adjacent cell. This extension includes a modified Monent's method for the first-order theory and a new second-order variant. The former incorporates an additional term to account for the non-conservative nature of the equation, addressing the issue of divergence preservation. A corresponding modification for the second-order theory has been proposed, and both methods are shown to accurately preserve multiple conservation laws. The validity of these methods is verified through a systematic comparison with the full, nonlinear equations, using both an exact solution and a numerical approach. The implementation of the new methods is also shown to successfully reproduce the primary features observed in recent numerical simulations of relativistic heavy-ion collision experiments. Additionally, a new analysis is presented to investigate the onset of shock development in both theories. The results obtained with the new methods are compared to the full, nonlinear equations, and further include a numerical investigation of the effects of dissipation on both waves and shocks.
