Recently, end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition systems have achieved high accuracy, however, these systems demand considerable amounts of data and advanced computational power. Transfer learning has been proposed to overcome such challenges even across language boundaries, for example using a trained English model for German ASR. We explored this approach with much less related languages, specifically adapting an English model for Czech ASR, and discovered a simpler transfer method that significantly boosted the effectiveness. We used a modified alphabet without accents to make the transfer easier and observed this strategy to be extremely successful. Furthermore, our technique demonstrated potential when applied to Czech data as well. We employed a coarse-to-fine training technique to achieve this success, first training the model on a smaller set of phonetically diverse utterances and then on a full data set, and noticed this to be an ideal solution for low-resource ASR. We also examined other fine-tuning methods including pseudo-Self Supervised learning and a simpler alphabet without consideration of language boundaries, and our results indicated that our coarse-to-fine approach was the most successful even when compared to a model trained on substantially larger data set of 100,000 samples. We expect our technique to be highly useful for low-resource ASR and it has the added benefit of shortening the necessary computational time. We are also exploring other modifications to the neural network like additional hidden layers and also different decoding approaches like prefix matching and minimum average log likelihood. We expect such variations to result in even better outcomes even with smaller data sets. We are open to sharing our results and techniques with others in the ASR community and are eager to receive their feedback as well. We used PyTorch for our models and Kaldi for our data pre-processing. We used a single NVIDIA V100 16GB GPU for our training and testing. We utilized the Czech part of the Librispeech data set with 80 channel feeder network and 0.3 learning rate for our baseline model. We employed 10,000 samples for our coarse-to-fine fine-tuning and 20,000 samples for our cross-language transfer. We are willing to share our data set splitting approach with anyone interested. We hope that our approach will result in successful ASR solutions for other low-resource languages like Slovak, Polish and Sorbian languages. We are also exploring other approaches like multi-task learning and novel data set efficient neural network architectures like transformer and conv-tas network that could possibly achieve even better outcomes even with much smaller data sets. We are open to any feedback and suggestions from the ASR community

This framework suggests that primordial black holes make up the dark substance. Their mass should be no less than 9.3 x 10^12 GeV and follow a near-exponential distribution pattern. Given the vast number of black holes with original masses below the Earth's, it's clear that a significant fraction of the Universe's dark matter consists of these primordial black holes. Researchers investigated the crystal and magnetic characteristics of the single-crystal, hexagonal GdInO3 through an integrated approach that combined experimental and theoretical analysis. A centered honeycomb structure comprising triangular and honeycomb sublattices was formed by two inequivalent Gd3+ ions. The results from direct current susceptibility and specific heat measurements indicate two transitions into antiferromagnetic states at 2.3 K and 1.02 K. Additionally, the analysis of isothermal magnetization revealed a unique 1/3 magnetization plateau, corresponding to an 'up-up-down' arrangement of the Gd3+ ions. A notable increase in magnetic entropy was also observed in the GdInO3 system, originating from the inherent magnetic frustration within this compound. A model incorporating a classical spin Hamiltonian was employed to develop the theoretical phase diagram, showing a ground state dominated by weak easy-axis anisotropy and closely resembling that of an equilateral triangular-lattice system. This theoretical framework may be a valuable reference point for the interpretation of future experiments utilizing NMR, ESR, or muon-spin relaxation spectroscopy.

To improve dark matter detection, researchers are exploring "paleo-detectors," an innovative approach that involves reusing and re-purposing large volumes of ancient, high-sensitivity sodium iodide scintillation detectors from nuclear test detection sites. These detectors have already demonstrated exceptional sensitivity in detecting the rare events characteristic of dark matter interactions. Given their large size and ancient age, these detectors are less susceptible to artificial backgrounds and can potentially bypass the limitations of modern laboratory-based dark matter detection systems. As a result, paleo-detectors have the ability to tackle a more expansive range of dark matter mass parameters and have the capacity to directly detect the primary processes of dark matter interactions. For the most commonly hypothesized dark matter models, researchers forecast that the existing sodium iodide detectors have the capability to detect dark matter signals at an exceptionally low mass threshold of 100 kiloelectronvolts. Moreover, these detectors can significantly complement modern laboratory-based dark matter detection systems by directly detecting the primary processes of dark matter interactions, outperforming even the most sensitive modern laboratory-based detectors in certain scenarios. Group re-identification (GRI) is a sub-task of re-identifying individuals across a given dataset without any additional information. A key GRI challenge arises when the number of given images for each individual is limited, a problem that is further exacerbated by the large-scale datasets typically used. This limitation leads to a situation where the model is prone to categorizing individuals based on superficial physical characteristics rather than unique identifying features. To tackle this, we propose a novel large-scale unsupervised individual re-identification approach that leverages contrastive learning to encourage the discovery of distinct identifying characteristics for each individual. Our method employs a contrastive loss that combines an inter-personal and intra-personal contrastive loss to push similar images of the same individual closer together and separate dissimilar images from different individuals. To prevent the model from relying on surface-level characteristics, we introduce an entropy-based penalty term to promote diversity in the features extracted from each individual. Our proposed method is thoroughly evaluated on the FG-VUGA dataset and compared to multiple baseline models, revealing a significant improvement of over 20% in mean average precision (MAP) when the number of images per individual is increased to 150, and a remarkable 41.6% MAP improvement when the number of images per individual is increased to 300. Additionally, our approach is found to be highly efficient in terms of memory usage and number of parameters. To further illustrate the scalability of our approach, a further experiment is conducted on the MARS dataset comprising over 240,000 images from 12,000 individuals, resulting in a superior MAP score of 11.5%. Our approach offers a pioneering solution for large-scale unsupervised individual re-identification and provides valuable insights for researchers aiming to develop re-identification techniques that are both accurate and robust. These models have numerous practical applications including, but not limited to, long-term surveillance, activity monitoring, and large-scale database organization. Given the substantial advancements achieved, our approach serves as a ground-breaking framework that opens up avenues for exploring new methods to enhance the accuracy of individual re-identification on large-scale datasets. To facilitate further research, our approach is made publicly available on GitHub under the terms of the permissive MIT License. We also extend an invitation to researchers everywhere to collaborate with us and contribute to the advancement of individual re-identification. In line with this vision, we plan to regularly update the evaluation protocol and the code for further research into individual re-identification. This paper presents an original model that uses a unique threshold assessment framework to forecast Value-at-Risk (VaR) and Expected Shortfall (ES). The model's innovative component utilizes a Realized-GARCH model, integrating high-frequency data into a traditional GARCH framework. A specific parameter estimation method was developed for this model, involving a Zellner's Bayesian approach that utilizes a shock measurement model. A key feature of this model is the separation of its parameters into two distinct groups: one estimated directly and the other estimated conditionally. This framework's effectiveness was demonstrated through a series of forecasting tests, indicating that this model outperforms established GARCH and LEARCH models in predicting VaR and ES for equity indices and individual stocks. Furthermore, a case study was conducted to evaluate the model's performance during the 2007-2009 financial crisis, showing its ability to anticipate and adapt to changing market conditions and crisis periods. A step-by-step guide to this model's implementation is provided, including the selection of relevant data, parameter settings, and a diagnostic checklist to ensure accuracy and validity of results. External validation through a backtesting procedure complying with Basel II standards further confirms this model's reliability in predicting low-probability tail events. Overall, this model offers a groundbreaking approach for forecasting financial tail risks using a threshold assessment framework, leveraging the utility of high-frequency data and providing a clear pathway for implementation and validation. A primary application of this model involves use in portfolio risk management, for which a case study is presented. This model's innovative design, combining realized measures and a threshold framework, addresses existing limitations in GARCH models and extends the capabilities of LEARCH models to forecast extreme market outcomes. A key advantage of this model is its ability to handle long-memory effects, volatility clustering, and leverage effects, providing highly accurate predictions of VaR and ES through the integration of high-frequency data, a feature not available in traditional GARCH models. This model's effectiveness in predicting extreme market outcomes, especially during extreme market conditions, makes it a valuable tool for risk management. A further study is recommended to explore this model's performance in markets with multi-factor models. Recent discoveries of massive and ancient gravitational waves through the lens of pulsar timing arrays have significantly enhanced research in this field. However, recovering these signals is a complex task due to their faint nature and sensitivity to pulsar selection effects, timing array systematics, and internal parameters. Nonetheless, research has shown that wide-band pulsar timing array data can be effectively utilized to recover a signal's characteristics, including its amplitude and spectral shape, through a fully Bayesian approach that accounts for data losses and parameter ambiguities. This study investigates the feasibility of estimating timing array data's internal parameters, such as pulsar periods, spin downs, and Earth's gravitational wave parameters, in addition to a signal's characteristic parameters. Our research reveals that wide-band data and a robust pulsar model are crucial for accurate estimations, and we present a methodology for obtaining posterior distributions of all parameters of interest. This approach's performance was evaluated using simulated wide-band data for five different pulsar scenarios. Our results show that wide-band data enable the estimation of timing array parameters with a high level of accuracy, even in the presence of noise and model inaccuracies. Furthermore, we observed that wide-band data yield more precise estimates of pulsar periods and spin downs than their narrow-band counterparts. Our study also explored the effects of data sets, model inaccuracies, and pulsar selection on parameter estimation, and our findings have implications for future research, data set selection, and the development of wide-band algorithms. Overall, our study provides a methodological framework for the rigorous analysis of pulsar timing array data sets, encompassing both a signal's characteristic parameters and its internal parameters. This approach is currently being implemented for real data sets. That implementation will be the subject of a forthcoming study. Nonetheless, our study is a crucial step forward in the pursuit of discovering gravitational waves through pulsar timing arrays. That pursuit is likely to yield significant scientific breakthroughs in the future. Using lattice QCD, a method is presented to directly identify pairs of quark and anti-quark currents that contribute to the pion's correlation functions. This approach is utilized to isolate the impact of specific two-quark correlations on the pion's volume-dependent mass. Our findings demonstrate that the pion's volume-dependent mass can be expressed as the sum of the mass of a volume-scaled pion and a term representing the effect of two-quark correlations. This effect becomes apparent at smaller lattice spacings and is more pronounced at larger distances, where it significantly contributes to the pion's mass in the chiral limit. Our results also demonstrate how the two-quark correlations' influence varies with the inter-quark distance and include an explanation of the observed dependence in terms of the condensate density. Furthermore, we derive the quark mass's volume-dependent expression at the mass shell, which is in line with the observations made by the BESIII collaboration. This result implies that quarks' mass values, derived from the rho meson's mass, display a significant volume dependence that cannot be explained by the meson's volume-dependent mass alone. Our study provides a clear understanding of the origin of volume dependence in the light meson sector and highlights the importance of incorporating the effects of two-quark correlations when interpreting data from lattice simulations. This knowledge is particularly relevant in the context of current and future lattice simulations that employ smaller lattice spacings and larger volumes, which will yield more precise determinations of the strong coupling constant and quark masses. This, in turn, will lead to a more accurate calculation of physical observables in finite volumes, as required for the analysis of data from upcoming lattice QCD simulations that will utilize the BESIII collaboration's measurement of the weak vector form factor up to large values of momentum transfer. This new result, combined with the already available information, will allow for the determination of the light quark mass at zero temperature and in the massless limit. This, in turn, will enable the reliable evaluation of the impact of the light quark mass on the CKM matrix parameters, as is necessary in the context of the ongoing and future experiments that will precisely measure these quantities in two-body processes. This, in turn, is crucial in order to resolve the long-standing issue of the quark mass's influence on the CKM unitarity problem. It's essential to distinguish this notion from stochasticity within an individual's control. The opportunity for self-improvement exists unevenly across different socioeconomic spheres. This disparity affects individuals' ability to make informed decisions about risks, thereby influencing chance inequality. The interplay between chance inequality, risk tolerance, and income is complex and multi-dimensional, with implications for how income is redistributed. This thesis will explore the underlying factors of chance inequality through a probabilistic framework that considers an individual's willingness to take risks and their ability to make informed decisions about uncertainty. It will also examine the effect of income changes on chance inequality and identify the conditions under which increases in income could lead to decreases in chance inequality. This research has significant implications for how chance inequality should be measured and addressed in policy decisions affecting individuals' choices and opportunities. It suggests that simply providing more income without consideration for the underlying factors may not be sufficient to reduce chance inequality. This has important implications for the design of policy interventions aimed at mitigating the effects of uncertainty on individuals' well-being. Removing singularities from the space of Lagrangians in phase space gives us the space of bunched Lagrangians. This new space has a quantum K theory that can be used to study the bunched Lagrangians. In the case of the 6-dimensional phase space, the bunched Lagrangians form a variety known as a Grassmannian, and its quantum K theory can be connected to Schubert classes. By examining the process of removing singularities from the maxima in this variety, we can determine relationships between the Schubert classes. Our findings can be represented through an algebraic combinatorial formula, and this connection to quantum K theory arises from the relationship between the Hodge pole structure and the combinatorial structure of the Schubert classes. This relationship enables us to use the combinatorial formula to study the interactions between the Schubert classes. Specifically, we can use it to derive formulas for calculating the intersection numbers and the top Chern class of the hyperplane in this variety. This variety includes the Grothendieck's oneness test, as well as varieties related to Givental's quantum connection and Dubrovin's higher-spin gravity. Our findings also provide answers to questions related to the Witten's intersection point approach to quantum K theory and its extension to manifolds with singularities. Our methods involve using the Schur functor to translate the problem into a more manageable form, and exploiting the properties of the perverse sheaf to understand the relationship between the Hodge pole structure and the combinatorial structure of the Schubert classes. Our proof of the formula for the product of Schur functors, as well as our analysis of the combinatorial structure of the Schubert classes, can be of independent interest. This work extends and generalizes our previous findings in arXiv:2102.10202 and arXiv:2102.10203.

The Shapley value formula has been the basis for developing highly effective feature importance methods in machine learning, particularly for identifying the significance of data samples within a model. However, existing approaches have a major limitation - they are primarily confined to local model interpretation and do not account for the broader machine learning pipeline, which comprises multiple components that can greatly impact prediction outcomes. This study addresses this gap by introducing a novel framework that uses the Shapley value formula to debug machine learning pipelines by pinpointing problematic data samples and model sections. This framework is exemplified through the development of two specific protocols: 1) a data debug protocol that pinpoints samples with low Shapley value that differ from the predicted model outcomes, and 2) a model debug protocol that pinpoints model components with low Shapley value that produce unique predictions. To demonstrate the practical utility of this framework, two experiments were conducted - one on cancer prognosis and another on credit risk assessment. The results of these experiments validate the effectiveness of the proposed methods and highlight the significance of data in machine learning applications. The framework's versatility is further illustrated through a cancer treatment recommendation use case, and the study concludes with an discussion on potential future research directions. The code for this study has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/huang-acc/SMDebug. Additionally, a system demonstration video is available at https://www.ysdebug.com/. This study has been accepted for presentation at the 28th ACM Joint Meeting on European on Conference on All Things Distributed and on Data and Storage (ECOOP-PLDI-FASE), to be held in Madrid, Spain. The study has also received the Best in Track Award. We investigated the link between radio sources and the motion of stars in 27 globular clusters. To explore this connection, we drew from data sets including real-time observations from the MAVERIC collection, archival Parkes radio data, and catalogues of sources from the AT20G survey. By combining radio frequencies with kinematic and structural properties of the clusters, we identified patterns of radio source distribution within them. We discovered that radio sources generally emerged externally to the global gravitational influence of the clusters. Through statistical modelling, we found the distribution of radio sources to be evenly spaced around the clusters, suggesting they originated from sources that were externally positioned and moving in a curved path towards the clusters. This alignment supports a theory that extragalactic sources are causing the radio signals. The frequency of radio sources increased as the clusters moved through the Galactic plane, which could be the result of encountering a higher density of such sources in this area. The frequency of radio sources also varied based on the optical density of the clusters, with more optically dense clusters experiencing a higher frequency of radio sources, likely due to a higher density of such sources in areas with a greater density of stars. The frequency of radio sources also shifted based on the clusters' locations within the Milky Way, with clusters situated in the spiral arms experiencing a higher frequency of radio sources. The type of radio source most common in the clusters was a flat-spectrum one, indicating that the sources were likely powerful jets pointed towards the clusters. The fact that some sources showed evidence of movement greater than the motion caused by the clusters' gravitational pull implies that their own internal motion was greater than this. This led to some sources being bent into a curved path towards the clusters. The fact that sources with the greatest internal motion were more likely to be shaped in a curved path towards the clusters, and that such sources were more likely to be oriented in a way that their sides faced the clusters, with the former being 3.5 times more likely and the latter 2.5 times more likely. This implies that these sources were more likely to produce a radio source on the clusters' far side. The frequency of radio sources on the near side of the clusters was 2.5 times lower than on the far side, with this difference increasing as the clusters moved through the Galactic plane. This phenomenon is more pronounced in the southern sky. The frequency of radio sources also varied based on the clusters' structural properties, with radio sources more common in clusters that were optically faint and had a lower central density. We investigate a widespread issue in information integration that involves
reconstructing a hypergraph from a set of partially connected subgraphs. A
hypergraph is a complex structure that comprises multiple interconnected clusters
representing diverse relationships. To build this type of graph, we develop a
novel approach using a guided process that leverages both global and local properties
to optimize a non-Gaussian objective function. To achieve this, we draw on both
traditional optimization methods and cutting-edge GANs. Specifically, we employ
Bregman divergence to split the problem into multiple manageable sub-problems,
and then integrate these sub-solutions using a hypergraph extension of the
multinomial logistic loss function. We also introduce a hypergraph encoder-decoder
model that produces a probability distribution representing the connectivity of each
cluster. Our proposed method, in comparison to a non-optimized baseline, has
been shown to achieve better performance in both precision and recall on a diverse
set of hypergraph datasets. Our code is now publicly available online. To our
knowledge, this work represents the first explicit formulation and solution for the
hypergraph reconstruction problem, as well as the first application of Bregman
divergence in a real-world hypergraph learning context. Additionally, our study
provides the first comprehensive evaluation of a state-of-the-art algorithm on a
diverse range of cluster graphs. Furthermore, we introduce an innovative
distillation approach called guided hypergraph construction, which streamlines the
training process by prioritizing cluster connections over individual node
assignments. This strategy pays off during inference, resulting in a 5x performance
improvement in terms of computational efficiency. We expect this optimized approach
to become a standard method for enhancing the scalability of our model in the future.

The Bondi-Schay model, an early cosmological theory, proposes that the universe's matter density varies in response to changes in the universe's expansion rate. However, this model falls short due to its inability to account for the universe's current rapid expansion observed in the present day. A more plausible theoretical framework, the Hubble-Lema\^itre model, emerges as a variant of the Bondi-Schay model and is comparable to the Einstein-Lema\^itre solution. A study investigates the Hubble-Lema\^itre model's constraints by analyzing its predictions for the rate of mass density variation and cosmic expansion rates at different time periods. Based on the Hubble-Lema\^itre model's predictions for the present day's matter density variation rate and cosmic expansion rate, the study finds that: (1) the rate of variation in the universe's matter density at $10^9$ years ago is less than $3.5 \times 10^{-3}$ in units of $10^{10} M_\odot$ per liter; (2) the rate of variation in the universe's matter density at $10^{10}$ years ago is less than $6.2 \times 10^{-3}$ in units of $10^{10} M_\odot$ per liter; (3) the rate of variation in the universe's matter density at $10^{11}$ years ago is less than $13 \times 10^{-3}$ in units of $10^{10} M_\odot$ per liter; (4) the rate of variation in the universe's matter density at $10^{12}$ years ago is less than $26 \times 10^{-3}$ in units of $10^{10} M_\odot$ per liter; (5) the rate of variation in the universe's matter density at $10^{13}$ years ago is less than $52 \times 10^{-3}$ in units of $10^{10} M_\odot$ per liter; (6) the rate of variation in the universe's matter density at $10^{14}$ years ago is less than $104 \times 10^{-3}$ in units of $10^{10} M_\odot$ per liter; (7) the rate of variation in the universe's matter density at $10^{15}$ years ago is less than $208 \times 10^{-3}$ in units of $10^{10} M_\odot$ per liter.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual intelligence that is capable of navigating through complex texts. Current methods of evaluating text-based games are hindered by a critical limitation: existing simulation frameworks fail to maintain a high simulation rate, ultimately restricting them to only test simple tasks due to excessive computation time. This paper introduces TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of TextWorld that has achieved a remarkable simulation speed of one million actions per second on a single CPU core. This advanced framework builds upon the foundational optimizations of Fizzics and Montezuma, incorporating a ground-breaking action feeder module that significantly reduces system idle time and minimizes unnecessary computational expenses. TextWorldExpress has set a new benchmark for text-based game simulation, outperforming the existing Montezuma framework by a factor of nearly 25 while maintaining nearly identical performance metrics. This paper also presents a method for rating the difficulty level of text-based games based on the number of steps required to solve them at different simulation speeds, which serves as a foundation for future research in this domain. Ultimately, TextWorldExpress is poised to elevate the bar for text-based game challenges by incorporating a complex problem-solving component, thereby providing a more comprehensive evaluation framework for testing the all-around capabilities of virtual intelligence. This advanced framework is publicly accessible under an open-source license at https://github.com/cygnusdane/textworldexpress, and it has been incorporated into the TextWorld repository as a separate branch available at https://github.com/cygnusdane/textworldexpress-branch. This paper also presents a complex text-based game challenge at https://github.com/cygnusdane/super-adventure, which has been optimized for performance and serves as a benchmark for evaluating the capabilities of virtual intelligence. This game has been played through by multiple state-of-the-art agents, and their corresponding performance metrics have been graphically visualized through an interactive visualization tool called Bokeh, which has been embedded into the game repository at https://github.com/cygnusdane/super-adventure. This paper concludes with an analysis of the results obtained from testing TextWorldExpress with a cutting-edge language model, which has achieved a remarkable score of 247 on the difficulty metric for the Super Adventure game. This paper also explores alternative methods for enhancing the performance of text-based game simulations and examines the computational expenses associated with complex action feeders. Ultimately, this paper advances the development of highly optimized text-based game simulation frameworks that provide a rigorous platform for evaluating the all-around capabilities of virtual intelligence. Recent breakthroughs in NLP tasks were fueled by large-scale models and extensive datasets. However, certain NLP tasks are constrained by limited data, hindering the knowledge distillation process. To overcome this issue, data augmentation techniques can be an effective alternative to reach high accuracy in low-data settings. This research delves into the analysis of multiple data augmentation methods, including text inference, word substitution, and token removal, through the application of six widely-used models in NLP. The analysis included four tasks based on the GLUE benchmark and three tasks based on the SuperGLUE benchmark, using the AugMENT framework to evaluate the methods. The results revealed that word substitution and token removal outperformed text inference in all evaluation metrics, while the best method for each task depended on the task itself, with word substitution exceling in 9 out of 9 cases. Furthermore, the research uncovered insights into the relationships between model size, number of parameters, and performance, as well as the interconnection between data augmentation and neural network architecture. Finally, the findings suggest that word substitution is a versatile method capable of enhancing models of any size, whereas in contrast, token removal is more effective for smaller models. This research lays the groundwork for further investigation into data augmentation techniques in NLP under low-data settings. The code and models used in this study have been made publicly available on GitHub. Additionally, the team has released a high-level implementation of AugMENT, an open-source library called AugNLP, which is now accessible on GitHub as well. As the field of NLP continues to evolve, the need for empirical studies on data augmentation techniques will persist, given the growing prevalence of limited-data settings in natural language understanding tasks. As such, future research should continue to explore and evaluate various data augmentation methods in depth, with a focus on open-domain settings, with potential future studies aiming to examine other aspects of data augmentation such as ensemble methods and weighted sampling. This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a nonlinear term and an external potential in the exterior of a convex obstacle in all dimensions greater than two. We focus on solutions with initial conditions placed outside a critical radius and bounded by a linear function, and demonstrate that these solutions will spread at a maximum speed in the long-term. Our analysis holds for both dimensionally independent and dependent scenarios. In two-dimensional space, solutions with initial conditions located within a critical radius will also spread. In dimensions greater than two, solutions with initial conditions within the critical radius will instead converge to a stationary state. Our research also reveals a new, broader category of solutions that it terms 'explosive', where energy is released over time. We demonstrate that in dimensions greater than two, explosive solutions will spread at the same maximum speed as solutions with initial conditions placed outside the critical radius. In two-dimensional space, explosive solutions will instead converge to a stationary state. Our proof employs a variety of methods, including the Fourier-Bessel expansion, the variational approach, and the convex obstacle's geometric properties. Our results complement and extend previously known findings. We also provide an alternative, simpler proof for solutions with initial conditions placed outside a critical radius that they will spread at a maximum speed in the long-term. Our research provides a new framework for analyzing solutions to the Schrödinger equation in the exterior of a convex obstacle and may also be applicable to similar equations in the same environment. Altering the oxygen exposure leads to distinct changes in surface structure. At low oxygen exposure, the surface laminated structure is hidden due to bulk corrugation. However, at higher oxygen exposure, a clean surface structure emerges, associated with a more compacted bulk. This changes upon heating in vacuum. Our findings indicate that in vacuum, the surface structure returns to its initial state before heating, while the bulk structure reverts to its less compacted state, thus necessitating a larger energy barrier for this reversal. As a result, the modified surface layer becomes re-oxidized at lower temperatures than the bulk, triggering a metal-insulator transition at a lower temperature due to increased strain. Our study offers a deeper comprehension of the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ films and the intricate interplay between surface and bulk modifications. It also underscores the significance of surface structural changes in determining the electronic properties of transition metal oxide films. Furthermore, our study provides a previously unobserved phase diagram that governs the modification-induced metal-insulator transition, and may be a reference for researching this system. It is crucial that future research into metal-insulator transitions in V$_2$O$_3$ films considers the impact of surface modifications, especially given the relatively low energy required for such alterations, which may result in unexpected phase diagrams. Additionally, study of this system may offer valuable insights into controlling material properties by modifying surface layers in other transition metal oxide films. Finally, our study highlights the capabilities of low-energy electron diffraction combined with scanning tunneling microscopy as an incisive and non-invasive means of studying the effects of surface modifications on material transitions. To do this, we developed a temperature control system that uses a 780-nanometer laser and achieves a high degree of accuracy in temperature measurements.  By utilizing a diamond thermometry method, we validated our temperature control system and found that it accurately models temperature changes.  The temperature dependence of our diamond was calibrated by conducting a thermometry calibration protocol at various temperatures.  With this calibration in place, we were able to precisely control temperature conditions in our experiments.  We examined the optical properties of a high-quality diamond at different temperatures and discovered that it exhibits unique characteristics under certain conditions.  Specifically, we were able to observe odd-parity rotations of the diamond's spin resonance at certain temperatures, which may provide a basis for developing temperature-independent optical properties.  By controlling temperature conditions, a particular resonance can be transformed into a doublet, making it feasible for two-state quantum applications.  Our research also demonstrated the possibility of creating a quantum gate based on rotation in the plane of the diamond and demonstrated that this gate is highly resistant to temperature fluctuations.  Furthermore, we investigated the possibility of using a diamond's spin resonance to detect temperature conditions and found that this technique is quite accurate.  Additionally, we examined the possibility of using a diamond's optical properties to detect the presence of a paramagnetic ion, which could be an important sensing application.  Overall, our research demonstrates the high degree of control that can be achieved over a nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond, which makes it a versatile and reliable platform for the development of various quantum technologies.  This work could also provide a foundation for addressing some of the technical challenges associated with quantum computing, such as the creation of a large-scale quantum register, as well as overcoming some of the experimental difficulties in this field.  Furthermore, our research shows that optical detection of magnetic resonance can be more accurate than other methods, which could be an important consideration in the development of quantum technologies.  Finally, we would like to emphasize that while our research focused on a particular type of diamond, the principles and methods we described can be applied to other nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond or in other materials.  Therefore, we hope that our work could provide a useful contribution to the broader field of quantum research. Using a spin-restructuring term in a bilayer Heisenberg model, we transform the SU(3) magnetism on a triangular lattice into a system that can be easily analyzed using the sigma model. By integrating out the "chemical potential" parameter, we identify its range in which the SU(3) ground state is antiferromagnetically ordered. Additionally, we use bosonization to incorporate the Cheyney-Simons term into the model, and we find that it drives a transition from the antiferromagnetic phase to a more liquid-like phase. Notably, the CS term causes the triangular lattice to behave more like a regular lattice in terms of spin restructuring. A phase diagram resulting from our calculations indicates that the restructured phase has a more complex structure than a regular lattice would have. Mainly, the restructured phase includes two distinct antiferromagnetic phases and a more liquid-like phase, in contrast to the regular lattice which would only have one restructured antiferromagnetic phase and is not capable of supporting a liquid-like phase. Convolutional neural networks are integral to various safety-critical computer vision applications like human robot interaction and self-driving technology. Real-world deployments of these systems are hindered by the significant hardware variations that can occur due to electrical faults and the resulting inaccurate predictions. To facilitate seamless integration of CNNs into safety-critical environments, this research introduces a pioneering method to create a formal case for CNN hardware resilience. Initially, a theoretical framework is outlined to address unexpected electrical faults affecting CNN output via activation range supervision. Subsequently, a practical framework is developed to pinpoint and rectify precise ranges for specific CNN layers, demonstrating its utility with a renowned facial recognition network. Notably, this research is the first to tackle hardware faults in the context of CNNs through activation range supervision. The collision of two heavy ions at the LHC offers a unique chance to study real or virtual quark-gluon plasma in a limited time frame. Studying the collisions' production, particularly of particles like pions, kaons, (anti-)protons and $\phi$ mesons, can provide insight into the interplay of factors influencing their production. However, extracting precise information from experimental data is complicated due to the absence of distinct features in their spectra. Therefore, we use the JAM framework, which effectively models the collisions' production of various particles, and modify the parameters to fit data from the LHC's ALICE and CMS experiments. By comparing the results of these fits, we can draw conclusions about the collisions' production processes. Furthermore, we investigate the distribution of particles like pions, kaons, (anti-)protons and $\phi$ mesons across different variables such as rapidity, transverse momentum and multiplicity. Our analysis suggests that the collisions produce a significant amount of initial energy emitted sideways, supporting the halo picture of a heavy-ion collision. Additionally, we find that the production of particles like pions and kaons is influenced by the emission of gluons, while $\phi$ meson production is largely unaffected by initial and/or non-perturbative processes. A comparison of our results with the statistical model of Bose-Einstein correlations reveals that the volume of the interacting region is approximately $7800^3$ fm$^3$. Lastly, we observed that (anti-)proton production is overestimated when using the JAM framework, a discrepancy that may be attributed to an intrinsic failure of this model in capturing the properties of these particles or the necessity to readjust its parameters specifically for heavy-proton production. Moreover, it will be essential to integrate the statistics from the LHC's ATLAS and CMS experiments to draw more precise conclusions about the collisions' production processes. Mobile robots require a localisation system that can function independently and accurately, anywhere and at any time, by leveraging information from both visual and inertial sensors. Unlike traditional methods that rely on external information systems, we present a novel self-contained localization approach, using only the input from these sensors. This novel system uses an external memory attention mechanism to enhance context information utilisation and a vessel-oriented frame to streamline rotation prediction computations. Furthermore, we introduce an innovative boundary-integrity constraint for surface point reconstruction and a keypoint-matching score computation metric to assess and improve the system's performance. Our experimental evaluations, conducted in indoor and outdoor environments with varying lighting conditions, demonstrate the superiority of our system over state-of-the-art competitors and a basic self-localisation model. A particular highlight is the system's success in challenging environments with little initial data, achieving a mean localisation error of less than 10cm. All source codes and models are publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/kaist-vSLAM/EMA-VIO.

Throughout a solar-type star's lifetime, its rotation undergoes significant changes, following distinct phases. Upon reaching the zero-age main sequence, the star's differential rotation reverses in polarity. This inversion has been observed in young stars with slow rotations. However, the impact of this reversal on the star's dynamo process and magnetic activity cycles remains unclear due to the dipolar magnetic field's dominance. By combining extensive computational simulations and a simplified white-light flux model, we investigated the influence of this rotation pattern on the dynamo process and the star's magnetic activity. The results indicate that anti-solar differential rotation can impede the amplification of magnetic fields via the $\alpha$-quenching mechanism, suppressing magnetic energy accumulation and cyclic oscillations. Instead, the magnetic energy then follows a stable equilibrium with the kinetic energy. Additionally, this stable equilibrium is characterized by magnetostrophic balance. When comparing computational simulations with observational data, we found that stars with cyclic oscillations exhibit faster rotations. This study's findings are also consistent with the absence of magnetic cycles in the Sun's interior. Furthermore, we found that the Rossby number plays a crucial role in determining the star's dynamo process. All slowly rotating stars with a high Rossby number may undergo a similar differential rotation reversal, potentially inhibiting their magnetic activity cycles. This, in turn, may result in magnetic field evolution similar to that of the Sun. Nonetheless, these stars can still experience magnetic field bursts similar to the Sun's solar flares and coronal mass ejections. Consequently, this study's predictions may provide a scientific basis for anticipating the presence of magnetic cycles in such stars through their rotational periods and Rossby numbers. This, in turn, can further the understanding of their magnetic activity cycles and potential space weather. Additionally, this study highlights the importance of incorporating proper turbulence simulations in global simulations of solar-type dynamos and highlights the limitations of existing global simulations due to their computational constraints. We analyze the rank behavior of elliptic curves from the $S_4$ and $A_4$ quartic families over the rationals, focusing specifically on those with rational points of rank $\geq 4$. Leveraging computational results from the 24th Elmshorn Number Theory Conference, we reveal that for $S_4$ quartics, the rank of elliptic curves can rise by as much as $6$ units. Moreover, we establish that this rank increase can occur in $A_4$ quartic extensions as well. This achievement is made possible by our discovery and utilization of larger rank-4 subfamilies within the $A_4$ family, constructed through the application of Volker Zarkhi's rank-4 construction method. Notably, this successful extension of his approach allows us to find examples of rank-4 subfamilies in both $S_4$ and $A_4$ quartic families with the Mordell-Weil rank of associated elliptic curves being at least $4$. We also provide numerical data on the distribution of ranks for elliptic curves from these quartic families, including evidence suggesting that, as the quadratic field varies, the rank behavior of corresponding elliptic curves from $S_4$ and $A_4$ quartic families aligns with the predicted behavior of Gross's $GL_2$ main conjecture. Ultimately, our findings supplement and expand upon earlier research conducted by David Harvey and himself. Investigating the chemistry occurring on charged droplets offers valuable insights into enhancing two-dimensional reaction processes, a crucial aspect of many technologies. To date, research has primarily relied on analyzing the emitted light from these droplets, which provides limited information about the underlying chemistry. A novel method called reaction nanoscopy, built on our reaction microscopy technique, enables spatial resolution of ion emission within droplets. By utilizing this method, we studied the effects of temperature, size, and surface charge on droplets made of glycerol, mapping the areas within the droplets where ion emission is most active. Our findings show that increasing the temperature or the charge on a droplet leads to a larger emitting area, whereas changing the droplet's size has a minimal impact. Conversely, raising the temperature or increasing the charge on a droplet actually reduces the area where emission is most active, a counterintuitive result that could be influenced by the droplet's non-Newtonian properties. This research on reaction nanoscopy paves the way for a deeper exploration of the science behind two-dimensional reaction processes on charged droplets. The success of cancer diagnosis, treatment planning, and patient outcomes depends heavily on the properties and spatial organization of cells within tissues. Therefore, computer-assisted cancer care relies heavily on accurate representations of tissues that can capture key histological details. Building upon previous cell-level representations, recent approaches use hierarchical graphs to incorporate the spatial relationships between cells and their organizational structures. We review existing network-based representations of tissues, emphasizing the various types of graphs utilized, cell feature extraction methods, and spatial models that describe cell-to-cell interactions. Notably, we highlight the limited attention given to selecting optimal digital tissue segments, a crucial pre-processing step, and identify a shortage of methods addressing this issue. To address this gap, we propose a novel approach for choosing the best network representation of a tissue segment based on a quality assessment score that considers both local quality and global consistency. Our method, called BERT-QA, leverages a graph attention model to evaluate networks by combining self-awareness and inter-network comparisons. We validate BERT-QA through extensive experiments using 10 classes of digital tissue segments and demonstrate its superiority over alternative approaches. Moreover, we apply BERT-QA to improve the performance of a cell classification model by selecting the most accurate network representation for each superpixel, leading to a notable increase in classification accuracy. Our work lays the foundation for resolving challenges related to inconsistent cell definitions, ambiguous tissue regions, and difficult grading decisions, likely to arise when dealing with heterogeneous and disordered digital tissue segments. Additionally, we introduce an open-source repository that contains code accessible to the broader community and a comprehensive dataset consisting of over 20,000 digitally extracted colon tissue regions, along with their corresponding hierarchical representations, quality assessment scores, and classification annotations. This dataset, named DHSC (Hierarchically Structured Colon Tissues), fills a gap in current digital pathology datasets by incorporating tissue segments with globally coherent cell organization, obtaining which is a complex process due to the high degree of variability present in colon tissues. This dataset will serve as a valuable resource for further research aimed at enhancing cancer care. This framework was later expanded to incorporate a general theory of combinatorial differential forms. Our study builds upon their work, exploring the relationship between their combinatorial Pontrjagin classes and the classical definitions, especially in the context of smooth manifolds. We demonstrate that the two concepts coincide, which provides a foundation for further research in this area. Additionally, we investigate a more general aspect of this equivalence, discovering that it extends beyond smooth manifolds to a broader class of spaces known as PL manifolds. This understanding offers a combinatorial interpretation of the Pontrjagin classes in these spaces. We also identify a link between the combinatorial Pontrjagin classes and another geometric invariant called the signature, which originates from the work of Gillet and Soule. This connection enables us to provide a combinatorial definition for the Chern-Weil theory, a formalism that assigns invariants to vector bundles and maps based on their properties. Specifically, we show that when using the combinatorial Pontrjagin classes, this assignment becomes multiplicative. This approach also reveals relationships with other combinatorial invariants, such as the virtual rank of a vector bundle. We explore this interplay further, establishing an expression that relates the combinatorial Pontrjagin classes to the Euler class and the rank of a vector bundle. This expression serves as a combinatorial definition for the Euler class, which in turn enables us to provide a combinatorial definition for the Chern classes. This, in turn, allows us to establish an interplay between the combinatorial Pontrjagin classes, the Euler class, and the Chern classes, which originates from their relationship in the classical Chern-Weil theory. This study builds upon the work of several researchers, including those who have examined specific aspects of the combinatorial differential forms and the oriented simplicial sets. Our focus has been on the combinatorial Pontrjagin classes, but we anticipate that our findings will contribute to a broader understanding of the combinatorial differential forms. In this configuration, multiple LE units are combined to share a single image sensor. Each LE unit covers a separate area of the sky, with its reflective petal pointing in a different direction towards the sensor. This arrangement allows each LE unit to cast a non-overlapping shadow on the sensor, enabling the LE units to be time-divided and reduced in number. We present the results of a technical assessment, which showed that three to four times more LE units can be combined using this method without a significant decrease in their effective area. Furthermore, this configuration is highly compatible with the LE optics' typical manufacturing process, with minimal adjustments required. We outline an 1-100 keV wide-field X-ray monitor concept that incorporates this configuration and LE optics, which would feature a large area CMOS sensor, an 76 unit LE array, and an effective collection area of approximately 0.8 square meters. It would also incorporate a 1.5 degree field of view and provide a high count rate of 100,000 counts per second. This instrument would be suitable for observing a wide range of transient astronomical sources. We anticipate that this new monitor will be integrated into the Enhanced X-ray Timing and Spectroscopy mission (eXt-PCS) that is set to launch in 2029. We have developed a new numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, tailored for quasi-static simulations, bypasses the need for an operator splitting technique and explicitly solves the Einstein field equations via Roe's method in a conservative first-order conservative form. This approach is combined with a conservative second-order accurate finite difference scheme to model the star's interior, utilizing a linearised Einstein equations solver to provide boundary conditions at the surface. This implementation facilitates the evolution of stars in a manner consistent with their interior dynamics, recycling the information gained from outside the star to inform boundary conditions. Our code, dubbed GR1D-Roe, has been tested against several benchmarks, including the evolution of a rotating star in a binary merger scenario, where our findings align with existing research using operator splitting and the Lagrangian formulation. Due to its high resolution and conservation properties, our code offers enhanced accuracy and a more sustainable approach for developing future codes that will tackle even more complex astrophysical simulations. Furthermore, we have used our code to investigate the internal dynamics of rotating stars across various rotation rates, discovering evidence of nonlinear behavior in these simulations, a feature that is relevant to the analysis of gravitational waves emitted from binary neutron star mergers. The adverse effects of social determinants of health on the wellbeing of individuals are well documented, influencing up to 80% of their health outcomes. Accurate prediction of health status is possible when social determinants are factored in, as they provide insightful information on individuals' living circumstances. To build a comprehensive picture of community health, mapping SDOH across geographic areas is crucial. A common approach involves linking housing data with health data through unique identifiers such as addresses. However, this method is limited as it relies heavily on housing data and neglects other crucial aspects of SDOH. To tackle this limitation, our research introduces a novel framework for extracting social determinants of health at the neighborhood level solely from housing data, using a unique set of markers that can be easily identified within housing data. By incorporating this framework into a machine learning algorithm, we are able to predict housing characteristics across geographic areas with high accuracy. Our results show that, using a small sample of housing data with social determinants, we can achieve a 0.25 RMSE; and with no social determinants information, we can still accurately classify housing characteristics using a 0.25 threshold, resulting in an F1 score of 0.43. This framework integrates multiple features from housing documents, extracts relevant social determinants information, and embeds a dictionary-based approach that facilitates prediction in a neural network. This innovative solution paves the way for more effective mapping of social determinants of health across geographic areas. Our research has significant implications for non-profit organizations, community groups, and local governments seeking to promote healthy communities by identifying areas with limited access to healthy food, safe and affordable housing, and reliable transportation. These organizations can leverage this technology to prioritize resource allocation, launch targeted awareness campaigns, and advocate for policy changes in areas with the greatest need. Our research spans multiple domains, including computer science, public health, and environmental sciences, and we believe it has the potential to inspire a new generation of researchers to work at the intersection of these fields. This research was conducted at the University of Washington, part of the HubMap project led by Professor Diakov. This project brings together top researchers from some of the world's premier universities to advance state-of-the-art mapping technologies powered by artificial intelligence and machine learning. This work has far-reaching applications beyond mapping social determinants of health, as it demonstrates the ability to extract a wide range of community attributes using a marker-based approach. This approach can be adapted to detect various features in different areas, such as detecting deforestation in satellite images

We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen doped rutile TiO2 using accurate hybrid density functional theory.  The results show that N doped TiO2 maintains its ferromagnetic character with a magnetic moment of 3$\mu B$ at the N dopant site. In contrast, C doped TiO2 exhibits anti-ferromagnetic properties with a magnetic moment of 1$\mu B$ at the C site.  The optical studies indicate that N doped TiO2 has higher energy gaps (2.3eV) with intense absorption in the visible region (550-800nm), in contrast, C doped TiO2 has a lower energy gap of 1.5eV, with intense absorption in the near IR region (800-1500nm).  The atomic arrangement around the dopant has significant implications for the electronic and magnetic structures, with a key configuration being the Ti-N Ti bond, contributing to enhanced ferromagnetic stability, in contrast, the Ti-C Ti bond may favor antiferromagnetic ordering.  These findings have important technological implications for enhancing the ferromagnetic properties of TiO2 at room temperature, and for optical applications by controlling the dopant type.  Interestingly, C doped TiO2 may have potential biomedical applications due to its biocompatible nature, in contrast, N doped TiO2 may have potential use as a photocatalytic agent, due to its ability to absorb visible light.  Future research directions are also outlined, including the necessity of conducting experimental verification of these theoretical predictions, as well as the exploration of other materials with unique magnetic and electronic properties.  Additionally, the potential benefits of these materials could be further enhanced by suitably functionalizing the surface, a topic that also warrants further research. An infinite graph $G$ contains a $K_n$ factor $f$ if there exists a one-to-one mapping $f$ that associates each vertex in $G$ with a vertex in $K_n$. A set of Ramsey numbers can be defined based on this concept, where the objective is to determine the smallest number $r(n, K_k)$ such that any two nonidentical infinite graphs contain a $K_n$ factor. This paper focuses on the upper limit of this number for even $n \geq 4$ and provides a method to calculate it for certain $k$ values; otherwise, it provides an estimate. Notably, this study represents the first attempt to explicitly define the upper limit for infinite graphs containing a $K_n$ factor using a $K_k$ pattern in an infinite graph. The obtained results contribute to a broader category known as upper rich Ramsey theory. The paper also includes a section where various upper rich Ramsey-type problems are presented for both finite and infinite graph cases. These problems are related to upper rich Ramsey numbers with specific graph patterns and are available on the online database called the Ramsey Problem Archive. The upper limit for some of these problems within this database has not been previously reported. To demonstrate this, a $K_5$ factor containing a $C_{11}$ pattern in an infinite graph has not had an upper rich limit defined before now, where this study sets it at $r(\aleph_0, K_5, C_{11}) = 2^{5^7+7^2}$. The provided proof for this value relies on a more complex version of the tree embedding property. Additionally, this study defines a $K_6$ factor containing a $C_{13}$ pattern in an infinite graph with an upper rich limit at $r(\aleph_0, K_6, C_{13}) = 2^{6^7+7^2}$ and demonstrates that this value meets the requirements for a Ramsey number. Notably, both defined numbers fall within the same notations used for certain lower rich Ramsey numbers such as $g(\aleph_0, K_5, K_4) = 13$ and $g(\aleph_0, K_6, K_4) = 18$. The provided results for upper rich Ramsey numbers with a $K_k$ pattern in an infinite graph offer a starting point for potential further research and provide a foundation for more complex upper rich Ramsey-type problems dealing with multicolor cases

Long-lived magnetic structures maintained by ohmic dissipation in stars are dependent on a key stability criterion that involves the gravitational and magnetic forces. This criterion requires that the magnetic energy be sufficient to overcome gravitational forces in equal measure. While it is feasible for linear perturbations to temporarily satisfy this criterion, we have discovered that nonlinear developments ultimately violate the alignment of magnetic and gravitational potential fields, giving way to mode coupling and eventual loss of stability. This instability, which occurs when magnetic energy is marginally greater than necessary to counter gravitational forces, results in the oscillations evolving into a mixed $m=1$ non-axisymmetric mode that can lead to magnetic field decay through algebraic order and temporary internal heat release comparable to several days, potentially linking magnetic activity in stars with the oscillations themselves. This discovery is particularly relevant to the interior of long-period magnetic pulsars. LiDAR point clouds offer valuable measurements for complex environmental settings, allowing for updates to digital elevation models and applications such as glacial monitoring, detecting structural changes, forest assessment, tracking shoreline and beach alterations, landslide risk analysis, habitat mapping, and urban planning. One crucial step in these processes is the classification of 3D point clouds into basic categories. For example, the classification can distinguish between plant life, man-made features, and bodies of water. Our research aims to present an initial evaluation of a LiDAR-specific machine learning classifier that can effectively sort points into these categories. We utilized 25 LiDAR datasets from diverse settings, covering over 150 million data points, to train and test this model. Our results show that when using a conventional machine learning approach, the model achieved a 90% accuracy rate or higher in all settings, indicating that a single, universally applicable model can successfully classify LiDAR data with exceptional accuracy. Furthermore, we found that using a LiDAR-specific machine learning approach resulted in a 5-10% improvement in accuracy compared to conventional methods. This breakthrough has significant implications for the development of scalable, robust, and efficient classification systems that can handle complex real-world environments with ease. In addition to presenting our findings, we outline key considerations for designing a globally applicable classification system. We also explore the benefits of using a single, universally applicable model, as well as the potential of using latent features to enhance classification performance. We conclude by discussing potential research directions, such as incorporating color information, using auxiliary sensors, and integrating classification systems with feature extraction algorithms. These extensions could further improve classification results and enable the use of such systems in a wide range of applications. We hope that our work will serve as a starting point for the development of advanced machine learning algorithms that can accurately classify complex real-world environments from LiDAR data. We also anticipate that our findings will be valuable references for researchers working on similar problems, such as classifying multi-sensor data, constructing universal models for image classification, and developing robust methods for detecting and annotating natural language processing data. We are confident that our results will contribute meaningfully to the expansion of machine learning applications in various fields, including remote sensing, forestry, and urban planning. We are eager to share our work with the broader machine learning community and look forward to collaborating with other researchers on future projects. The source of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) has remained a major puzzle in high-energy astrophysics for many years. To shed light on this enigma, researchers are correlating UHECR arrival directions with high-energy neutrino sources. Here, we present findings from a comprehensive study of neutrino sources using 10 years of public data from IceCube Neutrino Telescope. The analysis examines neutrino flux and UHECR direction associations with six identified neutrino sources: TXS 0506+673, 3C 454, SSS 1101-333, SSS 1413+6259, 3C 760, and 4FGL J1407.3+5420. Statistical and systematic approaches were employed to investigate these connections, taking into account potential magnetic field deflections of UHECRs. Results show that two sources, TXS 0506+673 and SSS 1101-333, exhibit significant spatial associations with UHECR directions at 2.5σ and 3.3σ significance levels, respectively. No significant connections were found for the remaining neutrino sources. These results suggest that some active galactic nuclei (AGN) jets may accelerate UHECRs and produce high-energy neutrinos through hadronic interactions. Further analysis with expanded data sets and additional detection methods is needed to confirm these findings and gain a more in-depth understanding of UHECR and neutrino production mechanisms. Additionally, identifying specific targets for UHECR-Neutrino multi-messenger studies can be an effective approach in uncovering the sources and origins of UHECRs. Finally, we discuss the statistical methods and neutrino detection strategies employed in this study in the context of future large-scale neutrino detectors. These approaches can be used to investigate not just UHECR directions but also other high-energy phenomena, such as high-energy cosmic ray flux and energy measurements. In the event of a real-time detection of UHECR-Neutrino multi-messenger signals, these statistical methods can be used to quickly pinpoint potential sources and facilitate targeted observations in UHECR astronomy. In the process, we outline potential future research directions with large-scale neutrino detectors that can substantially improve accuracy and provide more comprehensive insights into the sources and origins of UHECRs. In the future, the PICO-based large-scale neutrino detector will significantly improve detection capabilities by enhancing the sensitivity to UHECR sources 5-6 times better than the current IceCube Ne detector

The flow of liquids is significantly influenced by surface characteristics, which can impede motion by various mechanisms such as adhesion, compression, or deflection of surface waves. This study focuses on friction within liquid foams when interacting with rough surfaces, whether they are solid or consist of additional layers of foam. Through a combination of theoretical and experimental approaches, we found that friction in these scenarios is mainly attributed to the obstruction caused by surface waves in the foam, rather than other factors. This insight led us to devise an applicable model that links surface roughness to the resistance encountered. This model demonstrates its relevance across diverse conditions by incorporating the influence of neighbor tube bundles and surface tensions. It also facilitates comparison with existing models related to fluid dynamics. This study is particularly relevant to the prevention of heat transfer in boiling fluids and the development of anti-ice and anti-frost technologies. Furthermore, it is anticipated that the model will be useful in the creation of novel surface patterns capable of controlling the flow of fluids through them. We utilized an innovative approach to overcome a significant challenge in measuring thermodynamic properties - the change in phase space volume. Instead of relying on macroscopic observations, we directly measured nonequilibrium thermodynamic properties by linking them to the thermodynamic rate of change in entropy, which is influenced by the system's anharmonic fluctuations. Our results, specifically free expansion data, corroborate our theoretical framework and demonstrate that the system's thermodynamic properties can be accurately determined using hamiltonian dynamics and without referencing its equilibrium state. Our study paves the way for investigating nonequilibrium thermodynamic processes and system fluctuations in various scenarios. We also outline an extension of this study to include thermodynamic transformations that are driven by external forces, which will enable us to thoroughly test our theoretical framework. Our research raises important implications for understanding nonequilibrium processes and fluctuations in microscopic systems and provides a new perspective on thermodynamics that is free from the limitations of the equipartition theorem. This advancement is particularly notable when considering the adiabatic expansion of a system that involves sound wave modes and results in thermodynamic instability. Our study is a significant step towards a comprehensive thermodynamic theory that can describe and predict nonequilibrium processes and fluctuations in macroscopic systems that are consistent with their microscopic dynamics. Our results also demonstrate the accuracy of our theoretical framework and support the proposal of microstate nonequilibrium thermodynamics as a unifying framework that integrates quantum mechanics, thermodynamics, and the principles of stationary action. This integrated framework provides a common ground for analyzing nonequilibrium processes and system fluctuations in macroscopic systems that are based on their microscopic dynamics. Our study is a critical test of this integrated framework, and the conclusions drawn from it have a profound impact on our understanding of thermodynamics and its relationship with quantum mechanics and the principles of stationary action. This, in turn, has a significant influence on our interpretation of the thermodynamic laws and their extension to microscopic systems. In neural machine translation, research focuses on enhancing output order issues.
A key constraint of sequence generation is that each element must be produced 
before the next, which can result in suboptimal outputs.
To address this, we propose a novel approach called look-ahead focus, 
which selects the most suitable part of the previous output to influence 
the next word selection.
Our method is an attention-based mechanism that identifies the optimal 
subsequence to produce the current word and includes a self-alignment 
component to capture local word relationships.
Experimentally, our look-ahead focus method demonstrated superior 
performance improvements, achieving +0.93 and +1.04 BLEU points relative 
to the baseline system on the WMT'14 and WMT'19 test sets respectively. 
Our in-depth analysis includes an investigation into why our proposed 
approach enhances neural machine translation and indicates that it can 
be applied across various model architectures. Notably, our method 
achieved better performance than a state-of-the-art system at the WMT 
2019 translation task while being computationally more efficient. 
This technique's effectiveness is attributed to its deep word 
representation properties, which enable better handling of noisy 
target sentences. Interestingly, our proposed method exhibits 
similar performance when compared to a robust baseline system in the 
presence of data noise. As a highly effective neural machine 
translation method, look-ahead focus has potential applications 
in other sequence-generation tasks such as summarization and 
chatbots. This method's simplicity and effectiveness make it an 
attractive solution for large-scale, real-world applications. 
Furthermore, our results suggest that target-language 
complexity plays a significant role in neural machine translation 
performance. To facilitate further research, we have made the 
source code and models publicly available online. In addition 
to this, we have conducted an in-depth analysis of neural 
machine translation loss functions, presenting our findings 
in a companion paper also presented at the ICLR 2022 workshop.

The significant disparity between technology researchers and practitioners led to a realization that a gap exists in bridging abstract concepts to actionable solutions. To address this, the Grid computing model was proposed as a fundamental framework. However, its high overhead and inflexibility made it challenging to apply in real-world projects. To overcome these limitations, a translation of the Grid model was necessary. By applying a transformational design method, our study shows that it is possible to successfully integrate the Grid concept into a practical computation framework. The resulting system, based on a layered architecture, provides a secure and reliable environment for complex applications and showcases a non-traditional approach to implementing the Grid model. A new unified model for dark energy and adiabatic matter has been developed, incorporating a non-de Sitter cosmological model that meets the requirements of the First Law of Thermodynamics. This model's validity is supported by both observational data and the absence of future singularities in the universe. Since the model's Hubble parameter equation does not have a fixed value, it may be applied to non-constant Hubble parameters, providing an expression for the deceleration parameter that is highly consistent with the values derived from supernova data. Ultimately, this model predicts a significant increase in the rate of cosmic expansion approaching the present day. Key parameters, including the equation of state for dark energy and adiabatic matter, are determined through a fit to supernova data, resulting in an average of -0.793 for dark energy and -0.217 for adiabatic matter. These values fit the expected minimum standards of -1/3 for dark energy and -2/3 for adiabatic matter. Additionally, a prediction for the model's reconstruction of the present day dark energy density density is made at a confidence level of 1 sigma. It should be noted that this model is an extension of a previous model introduced in 2007 and does not incorporate a big rip scenario or an antideSitter cosmological model that would violate the First Law of Thermodynamics. In educational settings, curiosity is a crucial skill that fosters creativity, a passion for learning, and a vital preparation for a future where lifelong learning and skill acquisition will be increasingly essential.  Unfortunately, many school systems are undermining curiosity by focusing solely on test-taking.  However, educators are seeking innovative ways to spark curiosity in their students, as they recognize the importance of lifelong learning in an ever-changing world.  One understudied aspect of curiosity is its link to peer interactions.  Our study introduces a pioneering theoretical framework that combines cognitive and social components of curiosity.  We developed an original scoring method for measuring curiosity in real-time through verbal and non-veronal expressions.  Our data analysis leveraged computational models to uncover the complex dynamics of curiosity in small groups, revealing how individual differences, task experiences, and social factors interact and shape curiosity over time.  Our results highlighted the pivotal role of personal interest, motivation, and anxiety in curiosity, while also showing how these elements respond to task challenges and peer influences.  Our work also demonstrated the intricate relationships between curiosity, learning outcomes, and anxiety, highlighting the critical importance of managing anxiety to achieve optimal curiosity and learning performance.  Ultimately, our study provides a foundation for developing computational models that capture the intricate dynamics of curiosity in social learning settings, a crucial step towards creating data-driven, curiosity-inducing educational technologies.  To facilitate replication and further research, our study also offers freely available, open-source implementations of all computational models and methods.  We believe that our work has far-reaching implications for the design of educational technologies that spark curiosity in real-time, as well as practical recommendations for educators on how to create supportive learning environments that foster curiosity through peer interactions.
