Gaussian processes have been widely used for tasks like regression and classification, and their combination with spline bases offers a comprehensive framework, covering traditional Gaussian processes and spline interpolation. This paper explores Gaussian processes integrated with Mat\'ern kernels on graph-structured data, providing a comprehensive framework that encompasses both Gaussian processes and isotropic Mat\'ern kernels. We provide a method for efficiently training these models through a combination of Gaussian process techniques and algebraic manipulations, and their predictive capabilities are shown to operate at a rate of O(n), in contrast to the typical O(n^3) complexity of matrix inverses. We demonstrate the efficacy of these models through synthetic and real-world data sets, showing them to be highly effective in comparing graph nodes and predicting global minimum cuts. Notably, we also apply these models to achieve state-of-the-art performance in the task of solving linear systems on specific data sets. We make available the source code for our models, along with the data sets and metrics used in our experiments, under the name GPonGraphs. This open-source package enables easy implementation of these models and can be accessed through https://github.com/StanfordVisualGeometrics/GPonGraphs. This work is a significant extension of our previous research presented at the 2020 IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR). It includes additional methodology for solving linear systems, a new approach for thresholding Mat\'ern parameters, a comprehensive study of these models in the field of Gaussian processes, as well as applications to the resolution of partial differential equations. These models have also been open-sourced under the name GPonGraphs at https://github.com/StanfordVisualGeometrics/GPonGraphs. This work has been supported in part by the Stanford Visual Geometrics Project, and it has been successfully applied to real-world cases such as the prediction of material properties and the reconstruction of electronic structures. It has also been recognized with an Outstanding Paper Award at the 2020 IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR). This paper provides a comprehensive review of state-of-the-art Gaussian process methods while also introducing novel applications to the solution of linear systems, matrix completion, and graph comparison. These models have achieved superior performance in various tasks such as the classification of remote sensing images, the detection of surgical tools, the segmentation of neurons, the reconstruction of electron structures, the prediction of material properties, the global minimum cut, and matrix completion, outperforming traditional methods by a significant margin. For optimal detection results, it is crucial to model the distribution of geospatial data effectively. A novel approach based on point process models has been previously introduced but can be computationally expensive due to maximum likelihood estimation. We instead propose a less expensive convex optimization method that achieves similar accuracy but significant reduces computational costs. Extensive evaluation of our approach under real-world data and conditions demonstrates its superiority in both precision and speed. Notably, we employed New York City taxi data from 2018, a large-scale dataset that surpasses previous study scales in terms of number of observations and time span. The optimal model we created can process over 260 million observations within 30 minutes. Compared to state-of-the-art methods, our approach yields nearly a 10-fold improvement in accuracy without sacrificing speed. Furthermore, we investigated how to model the spatial dependence of data using two popular methods and assessed the effects of parameter selection on results through a step-by-step analysis. The enhanced approach we introduced has the potential to be applied to other urban infrastructure detection tasks due to its flexible design that accommodates various feature types. For instance, we successfully adapted our method to use pedestrian traffic data for detecting road intersections, a task that previous studies have primarily focused on using ridesharing vehicle data. The implementation of our approach on significant-scale data also paves the way for real-time urban monitoring applications. In such settings, monitoring results will be obtained in near real-time, thus reducing delays caused by data aggregation. Additionally, our approach enables more precise estimation of the effectiveness of monitoring campaigns, enabling a deeper understanding of their impact. The significant reduction in computational costs achieved with our approach also creates opportunities for real-time visualizations that can provide an interactive overview of the monitored area along with detected infrastructure locations. This, in turn, facilitates faster exploration of data and improved interaction with stakeholders. Machine learning models, particularly those with neural networks, are prone to experiencing a significant adjustment in their accuracy when switching from a training dataset to a testing dataset. This instability is shown to originate from the models' reliance on optimization techniques that focus on minimizing loss over training datasets, without sufficient consideration for future data. Furthermore, we observe that even small changes in a dataset can result in substantially improved performance, as we illustrate through the example of adjusting the Sonar dataset's noise level. To address this issue, we propose the use of robust optimization methods that are less sensitive to specific data configurations. Additionally, we suggest incorporating diverse training datasets that cover a wide range of data conditions to enhance the models' ability to generalize. To achieve this, we explore the use of genetic algorithms for optimizing hyperparameters, and present an approach to create diverse datasets through clustering. We apply this to the Sonar problem, achieving notable improvements in model performance. We also explore the benefits of using a the K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) classifier as a diversity-preserving component in a machine learning pipeline. Finally, we introduce an open-source framework called UnstableModelDetector that flags potentially unstable models for further investigation. This framework is currently being expanded to handle classification problems as well. Through this work, we aim to bring attention to the significant issue of machine learning model instability and provide initial solutions that can be built upon by the research community. While deep learning-based image analysis has been gaining popularity for detecting and classifying biomedical objects, achieving high precision requires significant challenges due to the variability in object appearances, tissue background types, and image quality. This study presents a W-Net, a two-stage convolutional network that effectively identifies and extracts features from nuclei in histopathology images. This network is trained in two stages: first, a background subtraction stage that uses a background-based model to generate probable nucleus locations; second, a feature extraction stage that uses the initially identified regions to extract rich nucleus feature maps. This approach allows for efficient and direct use of prior knowledge about nucleus sizes and forms. This W-Net is evaluated using a large-scale dataset containing 54,000+ manually annotated examples, achieving impressive results of 0.813 AUC, 0.784 AUC, and 0.096 APE for single-image, multi-image, and whole-slice annotations respectively, outperforming existing state-of-the-art models. This work's key contributions include (1) introducing a dataset augmentation method called Random Background Selection, (2) proposing the use of background models for nucleus feature extraction, and (3) obtaining optimal parameter values using a novel approach called Random Search by Multiplying Grid Search. This research provides valuable insights for building high-precision deep learning-based medical image analysis models. Formulated in terms of ODEs, the model examines the dynamic biological processes that lead to pyroptosis and how they can be modified by anti-inflammatory interventions, providing valuable insight that can be obtained numerically through numerical solution methods. Given the model's novelty, there are no established analytical techniques available for solving it. However, we validate our model's effectiveness by simulating a typical time course of cytokine release in an infected cell. Furthermore, we investigate how different anti-inflammatory treatments affect the model's predictions, matching observed cellular behavior with calculated outcomes. Through numerical experimentation, we show that even though there is individual variation in how cells respond to infection, some treatments can consistently suppress the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation and subsequent cell death due to pyroptosis. Ultimately, our model offers a single-cell level understanding of pyroptosis in the context of COVID-19, providing a framework for assessing the effects of anti-inflammatory treatments on individual cells. This approach paves the way for further research into how infections impact cells at a single-cell level and the corresponding model-guided analysis of treatment outcomes. This knowledge can be employed to create more effective individualized treatment plans. In the case of COVID-19, cell death due to pyroptosis, fueled by a high cytokine storm, can be seen as a critical escalation that leads to severe complications including the deterioration of lung tissue and ultimately life. Therefore, it is essential to control pyroptotic cell death through anti-inflammatory treatments as part of the broader COVID-19 treatment agenda. A blockchain-based smart contract is an automated transaction program, utilized in various cryptocurrencies, that is gaining popularity. To guarantee the reliability of these contracts, a sophisticated validation tool is essential. This paper presents HELMHOLTZ, a sophisticated validator developed for Tezos smart contracts, that leverages refinement types to detect errors in contract code. By integrating a sophisticated type checker with a refinement type validator, HELMHOLTZ can accurately identify type-related mistakes in contract code. Additionally, HELMHOLTZ uses the PITA search engine to efficiently locate all occurrences of errors within large-scale contract codes. To facilitate seamless integration with the Tezos development ecosystem, HELMHOLTZ provides a refined type definition language that can be used to generate a contracts library. This paper provides an in-depth explanation of HELMHOLTZ's design, along with a practical application of the tool in validating a critical component of the Tezos blockchain protocol known as the baker protocol. Finally, the paper is concluded with an overview of potential future enhancements to HELMHOLTZ. We introduce a novel hierarchical approach, combining both goal-oriented and distance-oriented strategies, for solving chaser-evasion games in complex environments. Our method builds on the game's state space by creating a hierarchical structure of interconnected sub-spaces. Each of these sub-regions represents a target with its own obstacles and a focus on the pursuit's objective. A separate model tracks the relative distance between the chaser and evader within each sub-space. Ouroretical results demonstrate how this hierarchical structure can be utilized to devise efficient policies by selecting optimal outcomes and distance trajectories. We complement our findings with a practical example showcasing our approach's effectiveness. Notably, our method allows the inclusion of noisy sensor readings in the game's state estimation. We also observe that our method can handle a significant level of sensor noise. However, the amount of computation required increases exponentially with the number of sub-regions. To address this, we propose an optimization technique that can reduce the dimensionality of the game efficiently. However, this reduced version still demands a significant computational investment. To further speed up computation, we propose an asynchronous deep reinforcement learning algorithm that achieves a significant improvement but still lags behind human expertise. To overcome this, we incorporate human input into the learning process, leading to a further reduction in computation time. Overall, our results indicate that our method can tackle complex environments but may require a substantial amount of computation. Nonetheless, we believe that our approach has the potential to be applied to various pursuit games. To facilitate this, we plan to explore alternative efficient solutions in the future. Additionally, we will investigate other complex state space representations that can be decomposed into sub-regions. To get a better understanding, we will visually re-create the environments studied in this project using a 3D rendering tool called Blender. This will not only enhance visualization but also make it easier to modify and adjust the game's state space visually. We anticipate that this will also facilitate communication within the paper by making the game's dynamics more easily presentable. To this end, we will incorporate a more detailed description of the game's dynamics along with its underlying physics in the text. This, in turn, will make it simpler to suggest and analyze any modifications to the game dynamically. To achieve this, we will include a part of the game's dynamics in a separate file that can be executed in an environment called Pygame. This will make it possible to analyze the game's dynamics both visually and numerically. Nonetheless, this version may not demonstrate the level of complexity showcased in the later parts of the project

likelihood. Building upon work by Kadane and O'Hagan (2010), we demonstrate

mutually implicit components: a component representing a form of 'local expertise'
and another representing 'data-driven' influence. Consequently, our analysis
provides a more intricate understanding of nontransitive likelihoods by showing
that they are inherently connected to the concept of a cyclic likelihood and
thereby with the properties of a likelihood function. This, in turn, is a direct
consequence of the fact that a cyclic likelihood is itself a nontransitive relation.

Recently, deep learning techniques have gained popularity for enhancing low-dose CT images, particularly due to their impressive performance at a relatively low computational cost. A key method in this area, the unsupervised cycleGAN model, has demonstrated great promise in restoring regular-dose CT images from low-dose images without the need for paired training data. However, the use of two neural networks in the domain translation process can lead to a significant increase in model complexity, resulting in difficulties in real-world implementations. To address this issue, we present a new cycleGAN architecture based on a single neural network, which we call AdaIN-Switchable CycleGAN (ASC). In this architecture, we employ an adaptive instance normalization (AdaIN) layer to allow for the seamless switching of domain translation directions between the regular-dose and low-dose CT images. A proposed cycle consistency loss function, along with a domain-specific loss function, serves as the primary optimization target, effectively resolving the bidirectional translation issue through AdaIN. The ASC architecture achieves comparable restoration performance to state-of-the-art methods, while significantly reducing model complexity and reconstruction time. Notably, our results show that the ASC architecture yields comparable performance to current state-of-the-art methods, simultaneously cutting model complexity in half and shrinking the reconstruction time by a factor of five. This improved efficiency is expected to facilitate the widespread adoption of cycleGAN-based deep learning techniques in clinical practices. Moreover, the ASC architecture serves as a ground-breaking solution to the long-standing challenge of bidirectional translation in cycleGAN models. To validate the method's effectiveness, a comprehensive evaluation strategy that integrates numerical metrics with real doctor-patient pairs is employed. The evaluation indicates that the ASC architecture achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art methods, primarily due to its unique ability to efficiently tackle the bidirectional translation issue through the AdaIN layer. This is further highlighted by a numerical analysis demonstrating the significant space-time model complexity reduction achieved with the ASC architecture, obviating the need for two neural networks while maintaining comparable performance. This representation of the model's complexity is a key factor in facilitating model deployment across various computational platforms. Overall, the ASC architecture provides a high-performance, efficient, and scalable solution for low-dose CT denoising, accurately restoring detailed organs and enhancing overall image quality through a combined loss function. This is a key finding of this work, as the use of a single neural network has become a de facto industry standard for deep learning models. This strategy has significant implications for the further development of deep learning-based cycleGAN models in medical imaging

Recent successes in dialog understanding tasks can be attributed to pre-training methods with contrastive learning objectives, however current methods solely consider similar dialog samples as positive examples, forcing the model to distinguish between similar and dissimilar dialogs. To address this limitation, this study introduces SPACE-2, a tree-structured pre-trained model for conversations. It combines semi-supervised contrastive pre-training to learn dialog representations from labeled and unlabeled dialog datasets. To begin with, it proposes a general semantic tree structure (STS) that unifies diverse annotation formats, making use of all labeled data's rich structural information. Next, it suggests a novel multi-view score function to focus on similar dialogs while maintaining diversity. To extract unlabeled dialog's implicit semantics, the model incorporates structural consistency constraints. Experimental results show SPACE-2 achieves top-notch performance across seven datasets on four evaluation metrics for four dialog understanding tasks. Its code and model can be found at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/DAMO-ConvAI/tree/main/space-2 for reproducibility purposes. To show the effectiveness of SPACE-2's structure-aware dialog representations, it achieves state-of-the-art performance on three related classification tasks. Moreover, the model's expertise can be easily fine-tuned for few-shot learning on specific dialog understanding tasks. To verify the reasonableness of STS, the paper conducts thorough structural statistics and conducts AB/FB evaluation to validate the educational value of SPACE-2. Lastly, it observes SPACE-2's improvement over a strong baseline model diminishes with additional unlabeled data, suggesting there's scope for further research in utilizing unlabeled dialog datasets. To prevent the model from paying excessive attention to structural information rather than actual dialog content, future work could explore novel multi-view score functions. Additionally, investigating alternative methods to exploit unlabeled dialog datasets and incorporating external knowledge sources for dialog understanding tasks are also worthy research areas. Finally, the paper's key findings can be of interest to researchers working on related topics such as multi-task learning, cross-modal understanding, and graph pre-training. To study the rotational characteristics of unusual halo nuclei like $^{48}$Mg and $^{68}$Ni, we utilize a deformed oscillator potential modified for angular momentum projection. This approach allows for the formation of unusual halo structures and simulates rotational motion in nuclei. However, due to the presence of angular momentum, shape decoupling effects arise, leading to increased dimensional complexity. Consequently, multiple angular momenta contribute to the description of rotational motion in these exotic nuclei. Ultimately, we demonstrate that beyond the ground state, additional angular momentum components play a crucial role in describing rotational motion within these halo nuclei. Additionally, we observe that in cases where a high-lying state shares similar characteristics with the ground state, an intrinsic potential still fails to provide a complete understanding, necessitating the inclusion of angular momentum to capture its rotational properties. Moreover, we note that in $^{48}$Mg, both prolate and oblate deformed states arise from the contribution of angular momentum, offering a potential basis for deciding which shape dominates in this region. Furthermore, we suggest that in $^{68}$Ni, an oblate deformed state is likely present at an excitation energy of approximately 2.16 MeV. This study offers a comprehensive theoretical explanation for rotational motion in distorted halo nuclei and highlights the significance of shape decoupling effects that arise due to the involvement of multiple angular momenta. This insight holds vital implications for the interpretation of experimental data obtained through angular correlated spectroscopy. Ultimately, this study positions itself as a competitor to the conventional conventional collective model based on the invariant width approach, specifically the formula for moment of inertia within the deformed oscillator collective model. In our research, we upgrade BasicVSR by incorporating second-order information, utilizing a more advanced propagation method, and aligning features at both the feature and block levels. The improved model, named BasicVSR++, significantly outperforms the original by achieving a notable boost in PSNR metrics without employing external data, thereby demonstrating the effectiveness of our refined propagation and alignment techniques. Moreover, BasicVSR++ exhibits superior flexibility in accommodating various video scenarios, including single-frame and super-resolution tasks, with results surpassing those of the original BasicVSR and the renowned VSRNet. We also introduce a second-order version of the fast BasicVSR method, named fastVSR++, which offers a reasonable balance of performance and computational expense. The improved codes for BasicVSR++ and fastVSR++ have been made publicly available. Through extensive experiments and comparisons with the original BasicVSR and other top-performing VSR methods, our results convincingly illustrate the superior performance and versatility of BasicVSR++. With considerable enhancements in both intrinsic and extrinsic performance, BasicVSR++ is poised to become a leading framework in the video super-resolution community. Moreover, the faster fastVSR++ model it encompasses represents a promising future direction for accelerated video super-resolution. In addition to plain SR, the authors of this research also explore and present outstanding performance of BasicVSR++ on video denoise and deblurring tasks. With its cutting-edge performance and versatile applicability, BasicVSR++ is deemed a comprehensive solution that can tackle a wide range of image and video restoration problems. Specifically, for muon colliders, we show that using this approximation leads to significant improvements over the log approximation, particularly in high-energy environments. We examine how Godel, using his famous incompleteness theorem, proved the existence of an infinite number of undecidable statements within the system, and we explore how this achievement led several logicians to achieve the same result. Notably, we look at the contributions of Tarski, Carnap, and Rosser, highlighting their own groundbreaking findings and the subtle differences they made to Godel's original proof. Our analysis showcases the diverse methods these logicians employed to demonstrate the incompleteness of formal systems and the varying levels of undecidability they established. Furthermore, we discuss how their work laid the foundation for later developments in the field. Our study is particularly relevant to researchers in the history of logic and the development of Godel's incompleteness theorems. We introduce a novel task called direct image-based camera adjustment, where a single image is used to determine the optimal eye-in-hand camera position and orientation for a robot's grasping task. We develop a method to train a model to perform this task using only a large, general-purpose image dataset without relying on labeled data. This approach is tested on a real-world robot setup and demonstrated to improve its performance by integrating the model's predictions into an optimization algorithm. The results show our approach outperforms a alternative method and enhances the robot's ability to complete tasks in new environments. A key aspect of our method is a design to handle ambiguities in images, such as rotating objects that can be grasped from either side. This is achieved by evaluating a score that assesses a camera configuration's suitability for a specific object and task, without relying on precise positional information. The code and models have been made publicly available online. This research provides a method for the robot to refine its performance in new environments through efficient learning from a single image, paving the way for the development of more effective cross-domain training methods. These findings are illustrated with a video available on the project website. This work is a result of a research collaboration between a European university and a Japanese company. A well-known challenge in solving inverse problems arises from the existence of ill-posed operations, such as image reconstruction from limited data, where unique solutions may not be guaranteed. Researchers often employ regularization techniques to select a precise solution from possible ones. The goal of this study is to frame regularization in a different manner, as a conditional restriction on possible outcomes rather than a modification of the solution space. We introduce a novel framework based on regularized conditional GANs, which involves training a probability model to predict data based on given information and regulate the predicted outcomes with a conditional constraint. We derive a new algorithm from this framework that integrates an adversarial approach with a regularization method and demonstrate its effectiveness by applying it to image reconstruction and denoising problems. Compared to traditional methods, it achieves superior results in various scenarios. The advantages of this approach include avoiding additional parameter tuning and explicitly expressing the regularization term. We also provide theoretical justifications for our method and the unique properties of our results. We publicly release our code and experimentation settings at https://github.com/wherewong/RCGAN. The algorithm's performance is also compared to state-of-the-art models in the recent IEEE TIP paper "Image Reconstruction Using Implicit PDEs" https://doi.org/10.1109/42.3500613. New results are derived and the paper is revised based on the feedback from the reviewers. The revisions include the improvement of the energy function using a different time integration method, the validation of the algorithm's convergence, the enhancement of the discriminator using a different loss function, the empirical evaluation of the algorithm's robustness, the comparison with a non-deep learning algorithm, the identification of the over-smoothing issue and its solution, the image denoising experiment with the RAISE dataset, the source code cleanup and the documentation. The paper is further revised based on the additional feedback from the reviewers and the discussions at the IEEE TIP workshop. The revisions include the simplification of the energy function using a Euler method, the validation of the algorithm's performance on real-world datasets in image denoising, the comparison with state-of-the-art deep learning algorithms in image denoising, the identification of the over-smoothing issue and its solution, the demonstration of the algorithm's flexibility and the clarification of the terms. Additionally, we explore a new application of the algorithm to solve an optimal control problem and the associated inverse problem in fluid dynamics. This study examines the existence of invariant surfaces in a specific class of dynamical systems from the Caputo fractional order. We establish a condition for the absence of invariant surfaces by exploring the stability of the system's equilibrium point and applying a theorem from literature. Additionally, we provide a nonexistence proof for invariant surfaces in a particular dynamical system near its unstable equilibrium point. This proof relies on the Lie's method of finding first integrals. We conclude that the presence of a first integral in this specific dynamical system is impossible. Finally, we offer a technical appendix on the modified Bautin theorem. This research is an extension of an earlier study on invariant surfaces in conventional dynamical systems. That study's findings are shown to be a special case of our more general results here. We also highlight a notable difference between fractional and conventional dynamical systems concerning first integrals and invariant surfaces. This distinction arises due to the distinct characteristics of their respective equilibrium points. While the asymptotical stability of a fractional order equilibrium point can be unstable, it still serves as a necessary condition for the existence of a first integral. In contrast, the sole existence of an unstable asymptotical stable equilibrium point in a fractional order dynamical system is not sufficient to guarantee the presence of a first integral. This outcome demonstrates the complexity and variation introduced by fractional derivatives into the analysis of dynamical systems. This complexity stems from the nonlocal properties of fractional derivatives that make the system's behavior differ significantly from its local counterpart. Therefore, standard techniques employed for studying conventional dynamical systems are no longer applicable here, rendering the use of modern nonlinear analysis techniques necessary. In the case of a fractional order planar dynamical system, we leverage the Lie's method in combination with a theorem from literature to establish a condition for the absence of invariant surfaces. This condition is met when the specific determinant within Lie's method becomes nonzero. When this condition is satisfied, the system's behavior becomes similar to that of a conventional dynamical system. In the absence of a first integral, the unique features of fractional derivatives will not provide sufficient justification. In such cases, the nonexistence of an invariant surface can be attributed to either the system's hyperbolic equilibrium point or the specific determinant within Lie's method being nonzero. Next-generation wireless networks require exceptionally high data transfer rates that could be achieved by leveraging Terahertz frequency bands for communication. Traditionally, THz communication is confined to short-distance applications because THz signals face high absorption in the atmosphere. To overcome this limitation, researchers have explored the potential of multi-hop directional transmission techniques to extend communication range, albeit these schemes can experience high interference levels and complex channel estimation. To tackle this problem, this paper introduces a new approach that involves a cooperative multi-hop communication system with directional transmission using a simple and effective method for beam training. The objective of this approach is to maximize long-term spectral efficiency by dynamically determining the optimal number of training signals, transmission modes, and power distribution across each hop through a single robust training process. This strategy is further optimized using reinforcement learning, and a pioneering method is proposed that extracts a critical parameter expressing the level of training complexity and incorporates it into a multi-agent system, where each agent represents a separate transmission channel. The complexity parameter is derived from a rigorous analysis of the system's performance, and a pioneering multi-agent deep reinforcement learning algorithm is proposed to dynamically determine the optimal number of training signals and transmission modes by implicitly considering the optimal power distribution. The proposed deep reinforcement learning algorithm is an innovative multi-agent system that dynamically determines the optimal number of training signals and transmission modes by implicitly considering the optimal power distribution. The results of the proposed deep reinforcement learning algorithm show a significant improvement (up to 324%) in spectral efficiency over traditional methods and demonstrate the superiority of dynamic beam training over static approaches. The practical feasibility of this system is also addressed by applying a pioneering optimization method that reduces the complexity of real-world implementation. Finally, a demonstration of the proposed deep reinforcement learning algorithm in a real THz communication environment further validates the obtained theoretical results. The numerical and real-world test results demonstrate the effectiveness of dynamic beam training and reinforce the potential of applying deep reinforcement learning to solve complex optimization problems in real-world wireless communication systems. Additionally, a survey of recent research on the application of deep reinforcement learning in wireless communication networks is included, and an outlook on future research directions in this area is provided. Furthermore, a new research direction on the application of deep reinforcement learning in multi-hop THz communication networks is introduced, and several open research questions are posed. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent expanded convolution neural networks, while maintaining low computational costs. WN's success in the raw waveform generation task can be attributed to its flexible expanded convolution architecture, however its limited application to speech synthesis is hindered by a lack of pitch adaptation. Our proposed QPNet model overcomes these limitations by incorporating a pitch-dependent expanded convolution architecture in a WaveNet-like framework, achieving high-quality raw waveform generation and surpassing state-of-the-art TDF-WN in several speech synthesis metrics while maintaining a relatively low model size. Moreover, QPNet exhibits computational efficiency comparable to that of WaveNet. To facilitate general raw waveform generation, a stochastic pitch synthesis strategy is introduced and evaluated against a fixed pitch condition. Results indicate that both conditions yield comparable performance in objective speech quality evaluation, yet the stochastic approach outperforms the fixed pitch method in subjective listening tests. A publicly accessible code repository and model repository are provided for this paper. Experimental models are trained with the LJSpeech corpus and our proposed QPNet architecture is also applicable to other large-scale speech synthesis datasets. Additionally, a modified expansion factor for the first dilation in expanded convolutions is introduced, enabling the model to learn from longer input feature sequences. This revised architecture is found to enhance speech synthesis quality further. A detailed model complexity analysis, along with a parameter optimization strategy, is also provided, encompassing both convolutional and autoregressive components. A novel expanded convolution architecture called the Quasi-Periodic Expanded Convolution (QIEC) is introduced, featuring a pitch-dependent, stochastic pitch synthesis strategy that facilitates learning from longer input feature sequences. QIEC is found to outperform all previous WaveNet-style models in a range of speech synthesis objective quality evaluation metrics, while also exhibiting computational efficiency comparable to that of WaveNet. Notably, QIEC models with relatively low parameter counts match the quality of state-of-the-art transformation-based models, enabling a model architecture that is both highly efficient and versatile. As such, it is our intention to make this paper an open challenge for all machine learning researchers to participate in model improvements using the described architecture. Developing standardized annotations for Arabic texts and correcting their spellings presents significant challenges due to the language's complex characteristics, including a non-linear script and a high degree of variation in diacritical points and consonantal lengths. To address these issues, we present MADARi, a user-friendly web-based platform for collaborative annotation and correction of Arabic texts. The platform offers intuitive tools for marking morphological components such as roots, patterns, prefixes, suffixes, and lemmas, along with tools for correcting spellings and formatting. To facilitate collaboration, MADARi enables multiple users to work together on the same document, with features like real-time user tracking, assigned tasks, and an overview of the annotation process. Moreover, the platform allows for importing scanned or digital documents, along with tools for preprocessing texts and removing unnecessary pages. Additionally, MADARi provides tools for exporting annotations in various formats, including ANNOAR, ANNIS, TEI, PDF, and RTF. By providing a collaborative environment for Arabic annotation and correction, MADARi aims to accelerate the development of high-quality annotated corpora and dictionaries. The platform is an evolution of the MADAR platform, with enhanced features and a user-friendly interface, and is designed for use in various NLP tasks, such as machine learning, parsing, and semantic role labeling. Currently, MADARi is applied in the development of the State-of-the-Art Arabic Parse Treebank. The platform is available online at http://madari.seclab.nnu.edu and is an open-source project on GitHub. It supports multiple operating systems and can be accessed using popular web browsers. The instructions for installing the platform on a local server are provided on its homepage. The MADARi team welcomes feedback and suggestions for improving the platform. The contact information for the MADARi team is available on the platform's about page. The MADARi project is funded by the King Abdulaziz University Development Office's International University Grand Challenge and the National Science Foundation's Partnerships for Advanced Computing in Research and Education (PARE). By modeling various temperate exoplanets using this method, we've observed the presence of multiple gas species in their atmospheres and assessed the validity of their model parameters. This framework allows us to derive a novel equation that can be used to compute a node's representation by solving for its projection point onto the hyperplane. Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to personalize patient treatment and follow-up, ultimately reducing the risk of undetected invasive carcinomas. The process of polyp characterization involves assessing their appearance and pattern on histological images. Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved medical image analysis accuracy; however, training these models necessitates vast collections of annotated images. In this context, we've developed UniToPatho, an extensive dataset consisting of 9536 annotated H&E stained patches derived from 292 whole-slide images, designed for deep learning-based classification and grading of colorectal polyps and adenomas. This dataset serves as a resource for researchers tackling the challenging task of automating colorectal polyp characterization. To facilitate reproducibility, we've detailed the dataset creation process, extraction strategy, and annotation guidelines, including the implementation of a highly effective deep learning-based feature extractor. This feature extractor, integrated into a 2+1D Inception-like model, outperformed competing approaches in a 10-fold cross-validation study, achieving an adenoma grading mean average precision (MAP) of 0.34 and a polyp classification area under the curve (AUC) of 0.98. UniToPatho is a publicly accessible dataset that can be utilized for developing and evaluating deep learning-based colorectal polyp characterization approaches. Additionally, we've released an open-source code repository that provides implementation details and a user-friendly interface for exploring and downloading dataset components. This dataset is a significant contribution to the scientific community, providing a robust foundation for further research aimed at fully automating colorectal polyp characterization. This is especially relevant as the global healthcare community grapples with the rising incidence of colorectal cancer. A key aspect of combatting this disease is the characterization of colorectal polyps, a process that, when fully automated, has the potential to reduce diagnosis-related delays and improve treatment outcomes. This is, however, a complex task that requires significant specialized expertise and time to complete. As such, it is essential that researchers and practitioners in this field collaborate closely and share their knowledge and resources. This approach leverages a short-range asymptotic approximation, known as the geometric approximation, which serves as an explict relationship between the incident and scattered waves. A key aspect of this method is an adaptive technique for dividing the domain into finite elements, with the size of elements correlating to the local wavelength and geometric approximation's accuracy. This scheme focuses on resolving areas where the geometric approximation breaks down. Successful results have been obtained for various configurations, including smoothly varying material inhomogeneities and soft obstacles, using an element size which reflects the local wavelength and the accuracy of the geometric approximation. To further enhance performance, an iterative solver was employed, achieving significant reductions in memory requirements. Results demonstrate the method's capability with large grids, overcoming previous limitations of time-domain methods in terms of spatial resolution. For example, it has been possible to simulate wave interactions across 20 wavelengths in three dimensions. The paper also presents the results of a comparison with an alternative method, the boundary element method, for the case of a hard sphere. Specifically, we derive detailed proofs that the F-basis of the spin chain's eigenstates is closed under the action of twisted Yangian generators. This closure provides a explicit, recursive procedure for calculating form factors and scalar products. As an example, we compute a specific form factor involving N spin-1/2 operators. The analysis also reveals constraints on the excitations' rapidities, which arise from satisfying the quantum-group symmetry. These constraints can be used to simplify the computation of form factors and scalar products for spin-chain states built from higher-spin mesons. The twisted Yangian algebra's action may further be employed to extend our findings to spin-chain states constructed from higher-spin baryons. The algebraic Bethe-ansatz approach allows us to exactly determine the eigenvalues and corresponding central charges for higher-spin XXZ models, encompassing both compact and non-compact versions. The central charges' eigenvalue equation can be expressed as a symmetric function of the Bethe roots, annotated as Q. Currently, machine translation primarily focuses on written text, leaving room for expansion into spoken language. Our proposed task, zero-shot voice translation, aims to bridge this gap by combining voice-to-text and written translation. We introduce a new evaluation benchmark and methodology to assess this task's challenges. Our model, a state-of-the-art transformer-based approach with both parallel and series connection modules, achieves remarkable performance improvements over baseline models, exceeding 35% in BLEU score on the LSDEV dataset. This model also exhibits competitive performance on the NIST dataset, demonstrating that advances in one translation task can contribute to improvements in another. Our findings suggest that significant gains in written translation can result from applying techniques developed for voice-to-text translation. We facilitate open-source reproduction of our experiments and model repositories are available for the proposed zero-shot voice translation task. This work is a preliminary exploration into this new challenge and there are potential methodological improvements waiting to be explored. For example, incorporating both parallel and series connection models may not always yield the best performance in zero-shot voice translation. Additionally, our evaluation methodology solely relies on direct evaluation but there are arguments supporting the use of semi-supervised evaluation methods. We intend to delve deeper into these methodological aspects in future studies. We assess the applicability of three different methods for computing electromagnetic multipoles: Cartesian primitive multipoles, irreducible multipoles and spherical multipoles. Our findings suggest that the spherical multipoles provide the most accurate description of electromagnetic scattering behavior, as demonstrated with an example of an amorphous silicon sphere. These multipoles are utilized to model the optical force exerted on particles composed of semiconductors, dielectrics, and metals over a broad range of wavelengths spanning from the dipolar regime down to the Mie regime. Our approach enables a thorough examination of oscillator model approximations used to describe semiconductors and metals within the context of optical force computations. Notably, we observe that the oscillator model's limitations arise not merely from its inability to capture specific material properties but rather a fundamental constraint applicable to all materials which can be quantified. This constraint is identified as the intrinsic limit of oscillator models in excess of $10^5$ oscillations, which we mitigate by introducing a high-frequency cutoff in our calculations. This advancement allows us to expand the applicability of our method to compute optical force across an even broader wavelength range. Consequently, our approach becomes a powerful tool for accurately modeling the scattering and optical force of dielectric particles across all possible wavelength regimes. Additionally, we incorporate spherical multipoles to handle internal light intensity distributions within particles, thereby enhancing the model's comprehensiveness. This revised model is made accessible through a dedicated software library called MultipolarRts. Systematic validation is also performed across broad wavelength ranges and diverse material properties. This program is highly versatile and can be used for a wide range of applications including the computation of optical force and multipoles for arbitrary particle shapes and material properties. Furthermore, it provides an intuitive interface for users to easily set up and run multiple simulations in parallel, further accelerating its performance. This implementation is primarily designed to address the computational demands of high-fidelity modeling of dielectric microelectromechanical systems in optical environments requiring precise force and energy transfer calculations. This program is an essential tool for researchers and developers working with photonic and optomechanical systems, providing a robust solution for accurately modeling the interaction between light and material particles across all possible wavelength regimes. It is an open-source software developed using C++ and is compatible with most high-performance computing clusters and local high-performance computers. This program is an excellent example of how open collaboration can accelerate innovation in research and development. This software is available for download on the Argonne National Laboratory's GitHub page.

Given a particular setup in quantum geometry, we examine how these relationships change upon transforming to a related system through a process called birational transformation. Our analysis identifies the conditions under which the new relative phase angles align with the old ones, providing a basis for predicting phase shift when this condition is not met. Our findings suggest that such phase shifts could be utilized for controlling the evolution of quantum systems and their interaction with external environments. Furthermore, our framework facilitates the comparison of non-equilibrium states across different quantum systems. Additionally, we demonstrate that in certain situations, the phase shifts can be utilized for the development of a closed-loop feedback control system that adapts to the changing state of the system. Moreover, we show that in some cases, the phase shifts can be related to the changes in entropy, enabling the use of our framework for studying the interplay between quantum states and entropy in complex systems. ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization. It offers customized 2D visualizations of vectors in any number of dimensions, enabling users to define their own metrics for ordering data points. The tool is designed for linear and nonlinear dimensionality reduction techniques, including PCA, PCA with correlations, PCA with standardizations, UMPCA, Linear Discriminant Analysis, Multi-dimensional Scaling, and AutoPCA. ViDaExpert allows users to import data from Excel, CSV, and text files, and export results to R, MATLAB, Python NumPy, and CSV. It features an intuitive interface with interactive 3D visualizations using RGL and Trellis, as well as a function for embedding 3D visualizations in HTML web pages. ViDaExpert is available for download on Windows platforms. It comprises 12 R functions, which are also included in the package for users who prefer to install only the functionality. The application is suitable for a variety of data sets, including gene expression data, stock market data, and astronomical data. The software is open-source and free to use.
